A NEW YEAR OF ILPPINESS.

MHE Year Eighteen Hundred and Eighty-One has passed away unto the limbo of departed years, and one more is placed on the shelf—ticked off on the roll of Chronology, with its obstruction—Bradlaugh and bad trade, Parnell and Forster, Transvaal muddle and Mother Shipton's unfulfilled prediction. Eighteen Hundred and Eighty-Two opens with brighter hopes of returning commercial prosperity, peace abroad and remunerative employment for the people at home. The GRAND CLOTHING HALL CO3IPAINY enter on their fifth year of war against big profits; and they are pleased to recognize the substantial support they have received from the working classes—the class which bemfits most by the Grand Clothing Hall Com- pany's system of selling only their own Manufacture of Goods at a fair profit; and what they mean by a fair profit is not the 50 to 150 per cent. charged by Credit Tailors, but a mere fraction over the prime cost of production, to cover working expenses. A large turn over at a small profit is the aim of the Grand Clothing Hall Company; and they cannot, neither do they desire to, boast of the enormous profit they have made, bu-, that they have sold more Clothing, and given better value, and saved the pockets of the people more than was ever known in Warrington. This they will steadily and per- sistently pursue in the future, as in the past, to give the best value, to sell the largest amount of Clothing at the smallest working profit, and thus benefit the Working Man and add to the Happiness of the New Year.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

THE ELECTRIC LIGHT ON THE STAGE.—At the afternoon performance of " Patience" at the Savoy Theatre on Wed- , nesday, the Swan electric light was used for the first time on ' the stage. Between the acts Mr. D'Oyly Carte appeared be- fore the curtain, and after explaining the advantages of the Swan light in the event of a fire, proceeded to break alighted incandescent lamp enveloped in thin gauze. The result was the immediate extinction of the light without the gauze being at all burned. Several scientific gentlemen were pre- sent, and the lighting was pronounced to be an unqualified success. LIGHTING THE SUEZ CANAL BY ELECTRICITY.—The Borilvy Ga:ette says: —There is a fair prospect of the Snez Canal being lighted by electricity, so that ships may pass through it at night, instead of coming to an anchor as at present. Major Strutt, managing director of the Eastern Electric Light Company, is at present in Egypt arranging with M. Lemasson, engineer-in-chief of the Canal Company, for the lighting of parts of the canal, so that dredging ope- rations may be carried on at night instead of in the day- time. At present the traffic is very much impeded by the dredging ' operations. There is a fair prospect of a contract being entered into eventually between the Eastern Electric Light Company and the Suez Canal Company for the light- ing of the whole of the canal by the Brush system. There is a fair prospect also of the lighting of the Suez Dock by electricity for the Peninsular and Oriental Company. A TIME OF PEACE. Golden leaves and a golden day; (Lights are warm when the year is o 4:) Rushes whisper and branches sway, Gossamer shines and drifts away, And the empty fort is still and gray; (The river flows like a tide of gold.) long ago from that dim hill-crest (The year was young and lights were pale:) Brake the thunder that scared the rest Cast of the rich vale's languid breast, . Till day died faint in the clouded west; . (But only the river tells the tale.) Golden rays are about your face, (Mellow lights are the old year's crown:) Come to the old war-haunted place; Come with your spell of peace and grace To the heart where strife has scarr'd its trace; (The river sings as the sun goes down.) Golden ways are before our feet; (While the year wanes the rich light glows:) • Life is stored with the garnered wheat, All the bitter has turned to sweet, After the battle the rest is meet; (The song goes on as the river flows.) —Good Words. SARIS. DOUDNET.

As the salt does not evaporate (only the water) from the heat of the sun, there is no loss. This plan of salting stock is the least trouble and the most economical and the safest."— Farmer. "Two Cows ix °rim SKlN.—There is now manifested over the whole country a very lively interest in the im- provement of the milking capacity of dairy stock. There is a rage for importing the very best milking animals of Europe, with rapidly-increasing efforts to multiply and cul- tivate their superior qualities. These efforts are encourag- ing, and augur gocd results to our dairy interest in the near future. They foretell an enlargement of that interest with more certainty in its operations, and greater profits by way of cheapening the cost of producing milk. Larger yields per animal mean less cost in making them. If we can get 5001 b. of butter from one cow in a year, it will certainly cost less than it would to get that amount from two cows in the same time. The food from which the butter is directly derived may be the same in both cases, but while that food is being converted into butter, we have, in one instance, to support the body of only one cow, and in the other the bodies of two cows. Then there is the extra investment and the extra labour of milking and caring for two instead of one, all of which makes quite a difference in the cost of producing milk. There will be, according to the economy used in producing and using food, a difference of 20 dols. to 40 dols. (E 4 to £8) in the cost of the 5001 b. of butter, whether derived from one cow or two, in a year—equal to 4c. to Bc. (2d. to 4d.) on each pound of butter, enough to make all the difference between profit and loss, or profit and no profit. If one man can live by getting 2501 b. of butter per cow in a year, another can grow rich by getting 5001 b. But when we come to divide again and get but 1251 b. a year per cow, which is about the common average, the diffe- rence in cost will be three times as great—at the above rate, 60 dols. to 120 dols. (Cl 2 to £24) on 5001 b., or 12c. to 14c. (6d. to 7d.) on each pound. This makes dairying an up- hill business. It is the dairymen who keep these 1251 b. cows, who sell the calves of their best cows to the butcher, and raise what they cannot sell, who domplain of hard times and that dairying does not pay, and who get frightened at the introduction of oleo-margarine (you see they have their bugbears there as we have here), and, forgetful of the rights of consumers, petition the Legislature to pass laws for keeping the price of butter up, so that they can live.by dairying with such apologies for cows. But, thanks to the 1 enterprise of the times, their number is growing less.—New York Tribune.

BARROW-IN-FURNESS, MONDAY.—There is a steady re- quest for all classes of Bessemer and hematite pig iron, and the market is likely to be well supplied with orders for some time to come; but lately, makers of ordinary pig have sold next to nothing at all, nor is it likely that much will be done in selling till the season is further advanced. Ordinary qualities of iron are quoted at 625. 6d. for No. 3, with 645. as theAvalue of No. 1 Bessemer, ard 625. for manufactured parcels. Steelmakers, shipbuilders, and raisers of iron ore are fully employed, and there is a good inquiry in each department. Prospects are cheerful, and much activity is expected. LANCASIIIRE, Wednesday.—ln both the coal and iron trades of this district business during the past week has been considerably interfered with by the holidays. Both col. lieries and ironworks have been closed for several days, and at many of the pits operations have scarcely yet been fully resumed. But although the collieries generally Jaave not been working during the greater part of the week, the demand for all classes of fuel has been so dull that there has been comparatively little reduction of stocks. House fire coals still move off very slowly owing to the mildness of the weather, and with the stoppage of many of the works in the district for the holidays, requirements for manufacturing classes of fuel have been only limited. Although quoted rates are without change there is still a weakness in prices, sellers in many cases being open to offers at very low figures where buyers are in a position to take off anything like quantities promptly. The average prices quoted at the pit mouth remain about as under :—Best coals, 9s. 6d. to 10s. ; seconds, 7s. 6d. to Bs.; common house coals, 6s. 31. to 6s. 9d.; steam and forge coals, ss. 6d. to 63. ; burgy, 4s. 9d. to ss. 3d.; good slack, 3s. 9d. to 4s. 3d.; and common sorts, 3s. to 3s. 6d. per ton. In the shipping trade business con- tinues very quiet, both as regards the demand for steamers' use and for cargoes, either for export or coastwise, and at Liverpool and Garston coal is still being offered at very low prices. In the iron trade, although there has been only a limited business doing, there has been a very fair amount of activity for the time of the year, and both the closing market for last year and the opening market for the present, have, so far as prices are concerned, shown exceeding firmness. For forward delivery at present rates buyers have been offering freely, and makers both of pig and manufactured iron could have booked largely during the week had they been open to sell over the next six months on the basis of current rates. Makers, however, being mostly well sold for the present quarter, generally show a disposition to wait for better prices, which it is believed will be obtainable. Lanca- shire makes of pig iron are firm at 51s. per ton, less 21-, for both forge and foundry pig iron delivered equal to Manches- ter, and during the week they have had tolerably large offers at a premium upon this figure for deliveries up to the end of June; bat they still decline to go beyond the end of March. Outside brands of pig iron coming into this eistrict have also been firm at late rates, sellers as a rule showing no 'anxiety to secure further orders at present. In the finiehed-iron trade there is a strong upward tendency in prices, and some of the local makers, following the upward movements in other districts, have during the week with- drawn their quotations: Nominally, for bars deliyered into the Manchescer district, the price is £7 per ton, but, as a rule, further orders are now only being booked subject to the rates which may be fixed at the ensuing quarterly meet- ings, when it is expected an advance of 10s. per ton will be i put in force.

THE DIFFERENT DISPOSITIONS OF HINDOOS AND CHINESE. —Whilst the Hindoos possess a lively imagination, the Chinese exhibit in its stead a circumscribed but prac- tical worldliness. The former's conception of the world is po'etical and ecstatic; the latter's insipid and prosaic, with a puerile and pedantic trait running throughout. Whereas Chinese art is superficial, that of the Hindoo, on the con- trary, attempts to be profound, to fathom the connection be- tween mind and matter, uniting therewith a predilection for the transcendental; the fantastic, and the mysterious. Nothing can more forcibly demonstrate to us how intimately the growth of music is associated with the development of special characteristics and civilisation among nations, than the almost opposite method adopted by the Hindoos and Chinese, both in their treatment of musical theory, and in the manufacture of musical instruments.—The History of Music.

And, more than this, as compared with • other nations, men have three more years of life under the most favourable conditions for making provision for the future than other nations; for these latter require no less than three years of each citizen's life (say from eighteen to twenty-one) :to be devoted in compulsory military service, either to fight- ing or to getting readyto fight the enemies or the possible ene- mies of their country—a terrible burden, from which Eng- lishmen are happily exempt. And yet, in spite of all our immense advantages, the recorded deaths from sheer starva- tion are vastly higher in England than elsewhere. And be- sides this, we have continually before our eyes the fact that vast numbeis of persons, earning for the moment sums far greater than necessary to support existence, in practice totally neglect the duty of providence, even to the small extent of providing for a single month, or even a single week. I suppose there is not a town in England wherein the experience is not perfectly common, that a fall of snow which covers the ground to the depth of three or four inches will bring as claimants, either of suddenly collected charity or of aid from compulsory poor rates (which are no charity at all), not merely the actual agricultural labourers who for the nonce are really deprived of work, but, under the name of "frozen-out gardeners," a multitude ten times the num- ber of the actual gardeners in England, a large proportion of that beggarly multitude consisting of men for months in receipt of quite abundant wages, not one sovereign of which they have ever been willing to lay by. There are sufficient reasons to account fully for this dishonouring prominence of England amongst all other nations in the sin and shame of improvidence. For the present I am only concerned in drawing my feader's attention to the fact. —the Rev. W. L. Blackley, in the Leisure Hour.

PACKING ainTTER.—Mr. H. A. Willard, in the report of the Vermont Dairymen's Association, says, with regard to this subject, that butter, to keep well for any considerable time, must be excluded, as far as possible, from the air. The usual way of packing in tubs and casks will not do this in as perfect a manner as is required to insure nice, fresh flavour. A better way is to surround the butter with brine. in this plan the tub is made heavy, and heads are provided at both ends, so as to make A package that will not leak. In packing, the tub is turned on the small end, and a sack of cotton cloth is made to fit the tub, and into this the butter is packed until it reaches to within about an inch of the groove for holding the upper head. A cloth is now laid upon the top of the butter, and the edges of the sack brought over this and neatly pressed down; then the head is put in its place and the hoops driven home. The package is now turned upon the large end, and the sack of batter drops down, leaving a space on the sides and top. Strong brine is now poured through a hole in the small end until it will float the butter. The hole is tightly corked, and the butter is effectually excluded from the air. Bat- ter put up in this way will keep a year in sound condition. DISEASE AMONG VIOLETS.—In an article on greenhouses we recently referred to the diseases which are continually manifesting themselves in the vegetable world. An Ameri- can floriculturist in a large way of business is said to have been rained by a new and very unexpected outbreak of the kind. He had been remarkably successful as a grower of violets, of which he is reported to have had plantations of great extent. So extensive were his operations in this particular line that he was recognised as the "violet king," and appears to have enjoyed something very like a monopoly of the trade in this favourite flower. A single summer des- troyed the whole of his plants, and, of course, completely annihilated his trade. A change in the source of the water applied to the flowers was supposed at first to have occasioned the mischief. This, although a very remarkable result, would not have been unprecedented. Experiment, however, proved this hypothesis to be erroneous, and it became evident that this humble favourite of poets and moralists had fallen victim to a kind of plague of the most virulent kind. The petals of the flowers first become marked by a little circular blister, such as strong sunshine falling on flowers while globu- lar rain-drops are resting on them will sometimes produce, the heat of the sunshine being concentrated as by a burning- glass. The leaves next become limp and withered, and the whole plant in the course of a few hours is said to shrivel and die. The disease, whatever it may be, seems to be not only as contagious as the potato blight, the vine disease, and other vegetable maladies of the kind are found to be, but is even more virulent and rapid in its action. It will be inter- esting to learn whether this chief cultivator of the violet is the only one who has suffered in this way, or whether the blight is manifesting itself elsewhere as well.—Globe. THE AMERICAN CREAMERY.—The creamery takes away half the drudgery of the farmer's wife. But while it re- moves the drudgery it retains the income—the monthly in- come—not in store account, but creamery checks—good as gold. And the best part of it is that this income is derived from that part of the milk that the farmer can most readilly spare. It is a fact not generally known that for the forma- tion of the bone and muscle skim milk, buttermilk, and whole milk are practically equal. The fat removed by the cream can be replaced at a trifling cost in the form of oil meal or corn meal, and the farmer has the satisfaction of eating his cake and keeping the larger part of it too. This monthly income is therefore practically clear gain. Hav- ing thus received one profit from his cow—a profit fully covering the cost of her yearly keep and interest on the in- vestment—he has in the calf a cheap and available package in which to condense his grass and hay, straw and corn- stalks for shipment to the markets of the world. And this is the second great advantage of the creamery. When that calf is driven to market fully ripe, he carries in his hide acres of roughness and waggon-loads of corn, transformed into juicy, well-marbled beef, which draws gold from the pockets of Johnny Bull. But this is not all; the surplus milk, after the calf has been weaned, amends for the parsi- mony of nature, which seems to have strangely overlooked the marvellous appetite of a litter of thrifty pigs, and helps to prepare a number of smaller packages into which our farmer puts grass and artichokes—corn from the crib, slops from the kitchen, and oven worms from the field. But if the creamery blesses the farmer's wife in delivering her from the bondage of the churn, it confers an equal blessing on the farmer in prying him out of the ruts and compelling him to think. For he now must needs study how to get all the cream from the milk, how to feed his stock to the best advantage; and, rising higher, he is, before he is aware, balancing in his mind the merits of rival breeds and differ- ent systems of management—in a word, he begins to ac' quire an education which, though not recognised by the schools, will go further in fitting him for the business of life' than much that has favourable recognition, and all the* while is contributing his share to the producing of that grand cow of the future, which will combine great pail per; fortnance with greater beef qualities and become the desire of all people. All this requires, and .at the same time ren- ders possible, higher farming-80 bushels of corn per acre. instead of 40 bushels, and 25 bushels of winter wheat in: stead of 10 bushels in spring. Yet the cow must have pate:. ture of many kinds, of grass and meadow hay with sweetness unimpaired, and protection from the winter's cold; and summer's heats; she compels cleanliness and thrift and obedience to the law of kindness; she enriches the farni, covers it with a carpet of verdure; enriches the farmer antr lightens the labours of his wife; gives less work in Ott summer and provides more in the winter if she is kept ne* the creamery. The creamery is, therefore, the missing link in the farm system—not so much for any one great profit that it brings as for the number of smaller profits; not so I much for present advantages as for the future and incidental advantages that follow in its wake.—Henry Wallace, in Western Rural.

BREAD FROM A BARREL OF FLOITR.—The St. Louis Miller says that many assert that Minnesota flour will make from 270 to 280 pounds of bread to the barrel; while other wheats—Michigan, for instance—will not make over 240 pounds. Wheat consisting entirely, or almost entirely, of starch will not make so much bread as that containing a large proportion of gluten. It is a well recognised fact that Michigan wheat is almost entirely composed of starch, and that acounts for the small amount of bread to the barrel of flour. Fultz wheat has little or no gluten in it. It is largely grown in the Cumberland Valley, Pennsylvania, and has I been ruinous to the flour trade of the millers. Clawson wheat is very popular with farmers because of its large yield, but, like the Fultz, is nearly destitute of gluten. I The flour lacks strength, and will therefore make a stnall , yield of bread, and no miller making a high grade of flour can afford to buy it at any price, as it will ruin the miller. Sheep require great care at the present period of the year, especially in-lamb ewes. The differences in good and bad luck, as it is termed, in lambing are immense, and it almost entirely depends on the amount of care bestowed on the ewes before lambing whether a flockmaster will have one or the other. A case was reported some years since where three hundred ewes only yeaned one hundred live lambs, the Case being plainly referable to the sheep having been fed al,most entirely on turnips. How different was the state of things we chronicled last spring respecting the good fortune of Mr. Russell, of Horton Court Lodge, who had not a single death in his flock of 350 ewes from October to April, and who reared 412 lambs from 321 ewes. Mr. Russell is known as one of the most careful of flockmasters, always feeding his animals on suitable food, and never allowing a single head of live stock on his farm to go without either water or salt a single day in the year. SALT FOR CATTLE.—A northern farmer writes :--'s Our practice has been. for years to keep a tight box under the shed in the barn yard, in which there is a constant supply of salt. The cows help themselves to this, eating as much as they like, winter and summer. The salt being always accessible, the cattle are never salt-hungry, and consequently never eat too much, thereby causing unusual thirst, which is the case when they are fed on salt periodically. In winter this is injurious, hence we cannot recommend the practice of putting brine on straw to induce cattle to eat it in order to get the salt, because the effect is to create an unnatural thirst. When stock has free access to salt, they taste a little every day, which gives tone to the stomach and helps to make a steady atd healthful appetite. We use coarse salt, ipreferring it to the fine, as it does not dissolve so readily land does not absorb moisture so freely, which causes it to I waste. We have used rock salt, but gave it up on account of its high price. The coarse answers just as well, not costing half as much, and not dissolving much faster. Our salt box does not have to be filled more than once a month, which is quite a saving of time as compared with the sys- tem of salting occasionally ; besides, there is no forgetting. In summer time a tight box is placed in the field and salt put into it for the cattle to help themselves. Rain falling

div.p: AR .7. 1882. THE LAND QUESTION.

The previous articles have dealt chiefly with the privileged position of the Land Lord. We now come to the Church Lord; for our Land System and Church System are intimately connected, and the "Squire and Parson" are the great "I ams " in many a country parish. Referring to the subject of Tithe, Mr. Benett Stanford (formerly Conservative M.P. for Shaftes- bury), at a recent Farmers' dinner, said "Every sack of corn you and I grow, before we can get our livelihood, or interest for our money, labour, and risk, must first support a National Church and its 20,000 priests." Being taken to task for his remarks by a local clergyman, this exceptional Conservative wrdte in reply. "As we are on the sub- ject, I think the words National Church' do not express the meaning of the present state of the Church of England, because scarcely one-half of the population of England and Wales acknowledge its leadership. State Church more properly describes it." What is Tithe? Sir William Blackstone, in his celebrated "Commentaries on the Laws of England," describes "Tithe" as the tenth part of the increase yearly arising and renewing from the profits of lands, and stock upon lands, and of personal indus- try of the inhabitants; the first species being usually called Predial, as of corn, grass, hops, and wood; the second, Mixed, as of wool, milk, pigs, &c., consisting of natural products, but nurtured and preserved in part by the care of man; the third, Personal, as of manual occupations, trades, fisheries, and the like.

How did Tithe originate? It is generally claimed that it originated in the Mosaic Law, but there is this material difference between ancient and modern Tithes; among the Jews, nine-tenths of the Tithes were devoted to the support of the whole tribe of Levi who had no lands assigned to them, and only 9e-tenth of the Tithes—i.e., one-hundredth part of ;tile whole—was assigned to the clergy. As a recent ',triter has said, "Another and most important dif- ference is this—that Tithes in Israel were not en- forced by the power of the magistrate, by penal laws, by distraints, or by imprisonments." In this country, about the end of the 4th century—according to Stubbs' Constitutional History of England—the maintenance of the clergy was provided chiefly by the offerings of the people; for the obligation of Tithe in its modern sense was not yet recognised. It is true that the duty of bestowing on God's service a tenth part of the goods was a portion of the com- mon law of Christianity, and as such was impressed by the priest upon his parishioners; but it was not possible or desirable to enforce it by spiritual reme- dies, nor was the actual expenditure determined ex- cept by custom, or by the will of the bishop, who usually divided it between the church, the clergy, and the poor. It was thus precarious and uncertain, and the bestowal of a little estate on the church of the township was probably the most usual way of eking out what the voluntary-gifts supplied. To- wards the close of the Bth century the payment of Tithe was made compulsory, but the people had the liberty of paying it to the church, or religious house: or monastery, whichever they preferred. Mr. William Howitt says there was no general Act for their payment till the reign of John about 1,200, when the mode of appropriation was specifically defined in obedience to the Bull of Pope Innocent 111. The institution was perfectly Popish—ordered by the Pope himself, given by a Popish Monarch, and for Popish pretences. They were obtained in the first place by a species of holy swindling. They were granted, both by monarchs and private indi- viduals, not for the maintenance of the church and religion, but for a privatr and selfish object—for the expiation of enormous crimes, often crimes of blood, as in the case of AtheLstan, King of the West Saxons, to pacify the soul of his murdered brother Edwin, of which be was supposed to be guilty; and of Edgar, cruel to citizens, a seducer of women, and concerned in the murder of Ethelwold, that he might possess his wife, Elfrida ; of Caunte, guilty of the blood of Edward and Edmund, sons of Ironside. The clergy had persuaded these and other men that they could pray their souls out of Purgatory, and remit the punishment of such heinous offences—thereby creat- ing such sins against society; and to obtain these inestimable services, the powerful and the wealthy gave these pretended keepers of the keys of heaven and hell .the wages of tithes. They were therefore ' dyed in blood, both by the givers and the takers, who were the actual encouragers to bloodshed by holding out so easy a remission. But the gross delu- sion by which they were obtained was equally in- ' defensible. In this midnight of Popery, tithes were called the soul's ransom; and were so preached up by the covetous clergy that the credulous people gave them eagerly. Who, indeed, would deny the soul's ransom—endless life, if so to be purchased? By this fraud the church got into possession of the third part of the land; and but for the Statute of Mortmain, 1279 (which forbade lands and tenementsl to be made over to Ecclesiastical Corporations with- , out the King's permission), it is believed, would have ' swallowed up the whole. Such was the origin of tithes they were given, not with the pious view of affording an ecclesiastical maintenance, but in a pri- vate and selfish bargain for salvation, of which Mr. Howitt gives inStances from the reign of Henry 11. Many changes (of too technical a character for mention here) took place in course of time, but when the monasteries were dissolved by Henry VIII., the appropriations which belonged to them, amounting ' 1 to more than one-third of all the parishes in Eng- land, were given to the King, and many of the ap- propriations so vested in the Crown being afterwards granted out by the Crown to subjects—Court favou- rites, and those who had been the King's instruments in spoiling the Romish Church—are now in the hands of lay persons. Tithes are not now applied to their original uses. The Church, in its institution and officers, gobbles all all up; but formerly the officers of the Church used to regard tithes, not as their own, but as a property entrusted to them for distribution. As one writer has said, "At the first establishment of parochial clergy, the tithes of the parish were distributed a fourfold devision ; one for the use of the ' bishop, another for maintaining the fabric of the church, a third for the poor, and the fourth to provide for the incumbent. When the sees of the bishops became otherwise amply endowed, they were pro- hibited from demanding their usual share of these tithes, and the division was into three parts only." According to this, the incumbent was only entitled first, to a fourth part of the tithes, and subsequently to one-third of them, for they were as much intended for the poor as for the parson. Now, however, the poor must be provided for by a heavy rate, and a parishioner can scarcely attend a free and open perish church, however large an income the incumbent has from the parish, without having a collection bag put before him; while as for the clergy, some of them in receipt of large amount of tithe, employ underpaid Scripture readers, to save the expense of efficient curates, and do not scruple to make what revenue they can out of the church registers and the church fees. Sir William Blackstone also tells us that by the Act of Parliament 31 Henry VIII., C. 13, it was enacted that all persons who should come to the pos- session of the lands of any abbey then dissolved should hold them free and discharged of tithes, in as large and ample a manner as the abbeys themselves formerly held them, and this accounts for a consider- able extent of land in different parts of the country being now tithe free, having been exempted by such Act, and what Parliament has done once it must :d0 again when the Nation desires it. The collection of tithes under the old system led to much unpletisantness and litigation. The farmers very naturally disliked these so-called "successors of the Apostles" "gathering where they had not strewed," and gave them all the trouble and annoy- ance they possibly could in collecting their tenths of the crops and produce, and accordingly in 1830, what is known as the Tithe Co'mmutation Act was passed, which converted an uncertain and variable tax into a fixed payment, regulated by the price of corn; enabled the tax to be collected with more ease and less friction and irritation, diminished the num- ber of law suits, and removed some of the restrictions theretofore existing on the cultivation of land. To- day, over £5,000.000 is yearly exacted from the people, the greater portion of which (although it does not include all the revenues of the clergy) goes to the sup- port of the Established Church. Whether those who pay be Churchmen or Dissenters, whether they pay willingly or not, whether they regard the claim of tithes a just or an unjust one, they must, until the i law be repealed, continue to pay. Mr. William Watt, in one of the Prize Essays of the Mark-Lane Ex- press, shows that the tithe-owner has contributed _nothing to the agricultural value of the land on which he holds a preferential dividend claim. This prefer- ence dividend is very commonly equal to a fourth ,Or even a third of the landlord's rent. But there is a spacial kind of tithe known as "ex- traordinary tithe" (and a very suitable name, too), which is specially objectionable. Amongst their other duties, the Tithe Commissioners were to form the lands in any parish in which there were hop gardens, market gardens, or orchards, into a "die trict," within which the tithe rent charge was to be divided into two parts, ordinary and extraordinary. When fresh lands come to be cultivated for the first time as market or hop gardens, after the passing of
1 ,nol
is-

Act, they were to be rated wi• A 'harge, so as to bring up their , liability to the iiirunt of the extraordinary Dm charge per acre in district. Here was a new tax upon industry operatllg as a serious discouragement to the improved cultia.tion of the soil, and its evils were indefinitely exte4ed by an amending Act, passed 20 years ago, by which the Commissioners were empowered, upon th' application of interested parties, to declare the land' any parish of England and Wales a district, within Oich an extraordinary rent charge may be fixed by ti em if any portion of the parish has been cultivated RS hop gardens or market gardens since the passing. the Act of 1836. In its practical effect, the extraorkarY rent charge is virtually a tax on specific articlo.• Of the pro- ducts—hops, fruit, and vegetables—albject to this indirect tax, there are yearly importEti°ns to the value of five or six millions. To thatextent does the foreigner compete successfully in tt2 English markets with the overtaxed English rTioducers. The extraordinary rent charge acts as a bointY Thon importation and discourages improvement, farmer brings additional produce out of the land ~13e „Y cultivating and cropping it on market garden PIA": ciples, and no sooner does he begin eto reap his ward than the tithe owner, who has contribute nothing to the result, steps in to demand his share -Of the produce. There are some instances given at a .recent meeting of farmers in Maidstone. The extra- ordinary tithe upon hops amounts in some cases to 30$. an acre, on market gardens to 13s. 4c1., and on orchards and fruit land to 102. an acre. Last year there were 42,977 acres of hops in Kent; in Sussex, 9,409; Surrey, 2,328; Worcester, 2,760; Hereford, 5,934; Hampshire, 3,038; and some few acres in other counties, bringing up the total acreage in 1880 to 66,446. The annual value of the tithes with re- spect to hop land in 1880 was estimated to amount to £43,140, and the tithe upon orchard and market gardens amounted to as much as that on hops, so the aggregate amount paid in tithes might fairly be estimated at from £BO,OOO to £90,000 per annum. Within less than an hour's railway journey of London, there is much uncultivated land that will some day be turned to better account. It would probably be so at once but for the extraordinary tithe that weighs so heavily on the inferior soils to which it is applied. The metropolis and other great towns are but indifferently furnished with fresh fruit and vegetables, although the home supply is largely supplemented from France and Belgium. With a better supply the demand would increase, and there will be increasing scope for the development of this branch. Meanwhile the extraordinary tithe operates seriously to its prejudice. Alike in the in- terests of the producer and the consumer, it should be abolished. Ordinary tithe is bad enough, for it causes a farmer to suffer in bad years when he has quite enough to contend with without that extra ex- pense. Ordinary Tithe is distinctly a charge on the land, but Extraordinary Tithe is worse—it is n tax on production, and an impediment to the cultivation of the soil. Ordinary tithe should be changed into a fixed Moneyrent, subject to redemption, and payable directly to the landlord. Extraordinary tithe should be limited to its present area, and then redeemed where practicable, or allowed to die a natural death by the tenants gradually transferring special crops to other land where this tax could not follow them. Already a move has been made in the right direction by the farmers in the South, in the form of an agita- tion against these impositions and a newspaper started under the title of the "Anti-Tithe Journal," while a Bill on the subject has been prepared for in- troduction into Parliament.

When the Irish Church was set free, the Tithes be- came the property of the nation. Ought not this to be done with the English Church also? Make due provision for every clergyman of the Church of Eng- land, according to the work he does, and devote the rest as the tithes were formerly applied—towards the maintenance of the poor and the relief of the poor's rate, which would be a decided help to the handi- capped English farmer. If the Conservatives want to show themselves "the farmer's friends," let them take this up.
It is nof the most deserving clergy who get the biggest slices of the pudding; for, as George Combo says in Dr. Syntax of "the Rector"—

And while in wealth he cuts and carves, The worthy curate prays and starves. While Mr. Benett Stanford (the Conservative ex- M.P. before quoted from) wrote to his reverend cor- respondent: "What I maintain. is that any State Church should be supported by the State out of the general taxation, not out of the land alone—that is, the very food of the people should be as free as pos- sible of taxation. I will go further, and say the re- venues of any State Church ought to be paid into a common fund, as it was originally with our English Church, and the clergy should be paid in proportion to their work, and any balance should go to the relief of the poor. No one can convince me that it ivight that, standing on Shaftesbury Hill, one can count within a radius of five miles nve livings averaging £9OO a year, with five houses attached to them, and only populations amounting to about 300, while the unfortunate Rector of Shaftesbury, with its thou- /sands of inhabitants, has a bare £2OO a year. Here there is much room for reform." Really it is to be hoped that a few more Conservatives will utter the words of "truth and wisdom." In conclusion, it must be remembered— That our tithes are Popish in their origin, and were given for Popish purposes, very different to those to which they are now applied, and they are either national property, or should go back to the Romish Church.
That when the tithes were given by Parliament to the Protestant Church, that body included the whole nation, while now it is only one denomination among many.

Tliat the Established Church has a sufficient num- ber of wealthy members to be self-supporting, like the 'voluntary Churches. That if the Established Church were put on the voluntary principle, "the sale of livings" abolished, and the clergy reduced to "promotion by merit," it would terminate what Mr. Goschen recently referred to as "the despotic sway of the parish incumbent," which, he said, "was opposed to the spirit of the age and dangerous to the Church." And, finally, that the tithes are a tat on the farmer, who has quite sufficient to contend with in the shape of uncertain seasons, and certain foreign com- petition without this additional demand on his pocket, and, if the landlords or the public are to benefit from English agriculture, the farmer must be allowed more margin between his receipts and pay- ments.

Let Ireland tell how wit upheld her cause, Bee trade supported, and supplied her laws; And leave on Swift this grateful verse engray'ale "The rights a Court attack'd, a Poet saved. Behold the hand that wrought a Nation's cure. Streteh'd to relieve the Idiot and the Poor; Proud Vice to brand, or injur'd Worth adorn, tr. Au stretch the ray to ages yet unborn. —Popc. e have long felt an interest in Ireland and her people. h;ted amid the melancholy main, dishevelled and in tears, le* diadem dashed to the earth, her harp unstrung, way- alra•clid as a woman in the first consciousness of her beauty leer the Power it gives her among men, we envy not the th.legs cf the man who has no sympathy far this "gem of sea," which, instead of being a Paradise of bliss and ,12tY, seems rather a vessel of wrath, ' built in eclipse `l'igged with curses dark." We English people are too accustomed to speak in tones of supreme contempt of Irish people. " The mere Irish," -we say to ourselves, a are creatures of impulse, without a settled understanding, rereaeeeetlilig power, a moral sense, incapable of gratitude and ".PPreciating the beauties of kindness or the claims of "No Irish need apply"—an intimation which nPePwears occasionally in the advertising columns of our daily SPapers—aptly expresses this popular contempt. "Den- ":l3, boy:, said an English seheolmaster to his Hibernian " I fear I shall make nothing of you; you've no ppci,eatiort." " sure enough, sir," said the quick.witted '4a,e., '44% it myself that's always being told there's no th`,`,Bloll for it? Don't I see every day in the newspapers a 8; no for need apply at all, ell?' But such contempt is ea,slll,flal and a shame. The Irish undoubtedly have their oaults which are patent to• the most superficial d"'eemed erver of theirseciety4_ but these faults are somewhat re. uch th bY the splendour e`, their virtues. They have i at naive and noble, seniou • • enntnusias t'c and generoive, e Ist ..e_ and true in their consdtution. Their hospits I Y a . aces- its- .1° th ossendesive. Their orators, in thrilling, l_elinative, yet forceful eloquence, htave often saunded the d'ers have ejr_ltsBtirring tocsin of nationality. gheir,ze7nl I reeled Ven their bayonets through phalanxgc„:lo fell eiNn'erhowe n the shock of war before, and when e • • rs 4ell them they have never hesitate,' ariir r.ecipitate in great in t raceves tlPon the foe There must bed of Ir that .h Llamas Moore and h has given us songsterrthe rotators like Curran, Be„ Goldsmith. composers at s libhall great lawyers like I,';'_"el, Grattan Sheridan and 'unkett , • , er and Magee ; ouch art. such theologians tssaL"se'.nd Foley and Hogan; lets ri as stieh c.D ongall and , rrl by -• AT abr of Waterloo and of co elern ees as Lord Gough. l- a trivf Omnipotence, by whose t erajoaecie. The times haves tb,ere must be a relece these words were written, and yet ,i_hanged somewhat shome truth even now. Indeed,' eY are not without Serious to throw the veil of obli- eien'_.are many who are al cruelties and the lamentable Mb- over the wrongs, theint if this were done we should ils'o' , e,rrient of the past ; nt evils of Ireland to their four'. ne able trace the prese effectualremedies. bl t apply !it head, and therefore una e ° a' n that " it greatly concerned the was of the opinioobserve the prognosacs of StatePhe r ds of people to 'EI modern statesmen Who reprobate "II" But there ar,_ history of the past because it is a ' of referring to thltions which ought not to be re- of painful recollefever, to bury in oblivion the wrongs This desire, howthose benevolent recommendations i Ajured is one of .atended to cover a multitude of sins I Cheap charity is against justice, and the recommenda- himanity ancnore tender regard for the character of evinces a feeling of regret for the ills that have tha9a:;:r3dured. We shall display a higher wie- /Y _.gently studying the history of the past, for, we do not pretend that the questions which agitate . to-day can be settled by the events which happened ago' we cannot forget that the questions of to-day had an historical growth, and we shall understand better by seeing in what way they arose. Nor must believe that an act of cruelty can never be useful, of injustice never be necessary—we who bear in mind le remembrance of a single iniquitous condemnation, ales, " has traversed twenty centuries to sti,g- the judges and executioners "—be expected to ap- deeds done in Ireland, whose history has been mourn- epitomised thus the land, and all His works are coed; made the laws, and all they breathed was blood; Inlaid:owed annals of six hundred fears, • code-of blood—a history of tears. Swift, the first "Illustrious Irishman" we lee..g to introduce is not exactly so typical an Irishman as weehall endeavour to bring before otarreaders. "That war born at 7, Hoeys Court, Dublin, on the 30th of deer, 1667," says Thackeray, "is a •certain fact of noleedy will deny the Sister Island the honour and glory; but it seems to me he was no more an Irishman than a man born of English parents at Calcutta is a Hindoo. Goldsmith was an Irishman, and alwaye an Irishman. Steele was an Irishman, and always an Irishman. Swift's heart was"-.English and in England—his habits English—his logic eminently English." Still he accomplished a grand work for Ireland. It was he who first taught the Irish to rely upon themselves. It was he who led them to victory when robbed of all hope. It was he who gave a voice to their mute-sufferings, and traced the lines of their future progress. 11ence no one is more entitled to a loftier niche in Ireland?s Temple of Fame than Jonathan-Swift, Dean of St. Patrick'e. We shall,hetter estimate the work which the Dean accom- plished if wo notice briefly the condition of Ireland when he entered upon the duties of the Deanery. It is scarcely pos- sible for gsete conceive of a condition more deplorable than that inthich the Sister Isle had fallen. The Battle of-the &Yu° had ',been fought, Limerick had surrendered, and the Catholic population in consequence were completely pros- trated. Sarlefield and other brave fighters had joined the Irish Brigade, and were covering themselves with laurels while fighting under the French flag. But at home the Cattle- lies were sinking deeper awl deeper into despair, crushed by the most atrocious penal laws that ever disgraced the Legisla- ture of a country. The Irish Parliament was in-existenoc, but it was merely a Court in which bills were registered Which had -been approved and certified under the Great Seal of England. 'they had no power of rejecting a bill. They were compelled to accept it, however disagreeable it might be to them, and however inimical to the true interests of Ireland. ever en the offices of State and the Government situations might have been inscribed the words, "o Irish need apply:" " The only way to keep things quiet here," wrote Primate •Boulton," " is by filling the great places with the natives of England." "I must request your Grace," he wrote to the Duke of Newcastle. "that you use your in- fluence to have none but Englishmen put into the great Places here in future." The Viceroy dwelt in England the greater part of the year, and the rich landlords followed his example, spending in England the rents which had been wrung hem their Irish tenants. The resnit of this was a complete eabeenee of all public feeling and public spirit, while despair spread her raven wings over the land. The commercial aspect of • the country was no less de- plorable than the political. Until the reign of Charles 11. the Irish shared the commercial privileges of the English. Unhampered by Navigation Acts or disabilities, Irish com- merce began to thrive. A lively ceittle trade was established with Bristol. Salt -fish, salt butter, and salt meat were ex- ported to half the ports of Europe. Manufactures were Established and prospered. The population increased, and 'relabel at last appeared to be on the highroad to prosperity. But the English traders took alarm at this growing pros- perity, and regarding the " Emerald Isle" as a colony, to be administered, not for her own benefit, but for the conve- nience of the Mother -Country, the Government inaugurated a policy as suicidal to the interests cf England as it was to those oi Ireland. As the English landowners complained that .1-fish rivalry in the cattle markets was reducing the English rents, an Act of Parliament was passed in 1663, and made perpetual in 1666, by which the importation of cattle into England was forbidden. In the same year another bill was pamed by which Ireland was deprived of the whole Colonial trade. With the exception cf a few specified -articles, to European merchandise could be imported into the Britieh Colonies except directly from England, in ships built in England and manned chiefly by English sailors. No articles, with a few exceptions, could be brought from the Colon lee to Ireland without being first unladen in Eng- •P•nd. 1n,1C70 this exclusion of Ireland was confirmed, and in 1C96 it was rendered more stringent, for it was enacted that no goods of any sort could be imported directly from, the Colonies to Ireland. The Irish landlords then turned i their pasture land into sheep-walks, and encouraged a mann-I facture of cloths. Again did English jealousy interfere. They saw Irish manufactures competing with their own in the home market, in the Colonies, and on the Continent. Accordingly an export duty of four shillings in the pound was laid on all broadcloths carried out of Ireland, and half as much on kerseye, flannels, and friezes, amounting in it- self to a -complete prohibition; while to make assurance ra . re.sure, the English Parliament passed an Act prohibit- innglithee exPortation out of Ireland of either wool or woollen _8 ura.ctures to any country but England. The result of re.strictiou was to convert the Irish into a nation of srn,ugglera, and to make them, in the words of Swift, e n wers of Woodneighs„ and drawers of water to their vigorous Such was p the state of things when Jonathan Swift ape the Scene sc defende to be the undaunted and energetic r of the rights of templated the evil an oppressed people. As he con- -8 under which. Ireland was groaning, the fire burned Within • him* He beheld them with all the nata- ral ardour of a disposition which rose in opposition to it.paaup 6` Do not; said he to petany, "the corruptim

ast your and villanies of men eat into your flesh and exha, . ny, spirits ?" Delany replied in the negative. " W " an- swered the Dean In a fury, "how can You help it ,v, cause I am commanded to the contrary," repliedw his friend;? "Fret not thyself because of -evildoers." Braid the fire so ant speak, and burnedin 1720 whi et h n gaveth thhisa nhdei gcnoautli do n inotn, thr. short treatise, e ventD e a tno entitled," A. Proposal for the Universal Liege of Irish Mann. facture." In this pamphlet he urged the ;,(people to meet the restrictions which had been imposed or', , their trade by ab- staining from importation and using e xclusively Irish pro- ducts. "Fettered with restrictions, rgerbbed of her markets, blockaded round with prohibitions, hb, saw that if her people were worthy of her Ireland might e" till be sufficient for her-. self, and out of her own resources ,claight develop her indus- try. England might lay a veto g o on every healthy effort of Parliamentary legislation, but Tc.,England could not touch the self-made laws which the cons, =nee and spirit of the nation might impose upon themseljFves. By their own energy the Irish might still, if theyp chose' rise superior to their miseries, and by their suf. 2cess inflict the bitterest humilia- tion on their tyrants. England might close their ports, reject their tillage billrs, discourage the legislative efforts for the better maeageme- at of her lands, but she could not pre- vent them from plughing their own fields, wearing their own frieze jerkin rs, and buying and selling among them- selves." This v fas the drift of the whole treatise, urging the people to rise exclusively Irish products, and to burn everything tlfaat came from England "except their people and their cols." "I must confess," be added, "that as to the former -(the people) I should not be sorry if they would st,F iy at home; and for the latter (the coal') I hope •'in a little time we shall have no occa- sion f_in them." In a very ingenious passage he des- cribe( 1 the policy of England under the guise of a fable of " A-rchne and Pallas." "The goddess had heard." he said, one Arachne, a young virgin very famous for spinning rind weaving: they both met upon a trial of skill; and Pallas finding herself almost equalled in her own art, stung with rage and envy, knocked her rival down and turned her into a spider, enjoining her to spin and weave for ever out of her own bowels and in a very narrow compass. I confess that from a boy I always pitied poor Arachne, and could never heartily love the goddess on account of so cruel and unjust a sentence; which, however, is fully executed upon us by England with further additions of rigour and severity, for the greatest part of Our bowels and vitals is extracted without allowing us the liberty of spinning and weaving them." He concluded with an earnest appeal to the land lords to lighten the rent which was crushing so many of their tenants, declaring that " whoever.travels this country (Ireland), and observes the face of nature or the feces and habits and dwellings of the natives will hardly think him- self in a land where law, religion, or common humanity is professed." This treatise spread very fast, and was read with great, avidity. It shook the 'Council and the Castle Secretaries. The printer was seized for publishing such a "seditious, factious, and virulent pamphlet," and forced to give great bail. At the trial the jury brought him in not guilty. The Chief Justice sent them back nine times, and kept them 11 hours, until, being tired out, they were forced to leave the matter to the mercy of the judge. During the trial the Chief Justice, among other singularities, laid his hand on his breast and protested solemnly that the author's design was to bring in the Pretender. But the cause being so very odious and unpopular, the trial of the verdict was deferred from one term to another until, on the arrival of the Duke of Grafton, the printer was discharged, while a shower of lampoons assailed the judge. Had the politicians of that day known what belonged to their peace instead of .prose- cuting printers, they would have welcomed the development of Irish industry as a better guarantee against future troubles than a hundred Acts of Parliament. But they were purblind. They could not look beyond the next year's balance sheet. Hence they adopted the policy which Jonathan Swift assailed—a policy by which the English Government having sown to the wind has reaped the whirl- wind. North Shields.

The Chinese, Government has paid to Russia the first instalment of the compensation stipulated by the Kuldja Treaty. It is announced in a Constantinople telegramthatthe Porte is preparing a scheme for the unification of the monetary I system with a single standard. More,than.l.,ooo emigrants emigrants have already arrived in New York this month, from which it is inferred that the returns this season will show a large aggregate increase on those,of last winter. s The spanish Minister of Finance informed his colleagues in the Cabinet on Wednesday that the commercial treaty negotiations with the French Government were expected -shortly to lead to a satisfactory result. Telegrams from Vienna estimate that property worth ,a 'million of roubles, belonging to the Jews, was destroyed .or carried 61i:.during the riots in Warsaw last week, and that a thousand Jewish families are totally ruined. The negotiations for the conclusion of a Treatrof•Corn- ,merce between England and France were reoumed inTaris on Saturilay ; hut they led to no definitive result. It is stated that Mr. Crowe remains with Mr. Bateman, one of the secretaries, to examine the subject of the woollen duties in conference with M. Rouvier and the French'Commis- I-sicter.

Many v.i.l learn with regret that Guiteon't " reception," on Monday, was numerously attended by persons who were anxious to make the acquaintance of the assassin. The Court has now very properly ordered that ouch scandals shall cease, and has placed Guitcom on nrison,diet. It is said that the jurymen's faces "indicate that all have deter- mined' upon a verdict of guilty." Zlt is stated that the Guiteau trial is expected toqast two weeks longer, as the counsel for the defence intend-6U call as witnesses all the Washington physicians who have sent ;persons to acylums for the inssaie, and whese insanity de- veloped itself after Guiteau shot President Garfield. The .oumber confined in this category exceeds 40. The object of counsel is to show that their insanity is sithilar to that of .Guiteau. ,att Shaneville, near Cleveland, Ohio, a building.inArhich a." secret" - society styled the Knights of Pythias were ;celebrating a festival gave way. Two hundred persons were on the'lloor which gave way, and of these two were killed immediately,and three others met with a-more terrible fate in the ruins, which were set on fire lay the 'broken stove. Forty others were more or less severely injured. Before leaving the court on Saturday Guiteau, with un- surpassable effrontery, wished "a happy new year" to-every person present, and invited all and sundry to attend his "reception "in prison on Sunday. He protested on'Friday that the Amerizan people "didn't want to hong him any- how;" and read a telegram from "a ht.st of admirers" at Boston stating that in their Opinion he ought teloeTreSident. Something was said in the course of the -day as to the prisoner's demand for a consulship. He remarked that if such an offer hs.l been made before the Ist of June .it -would have-" settled the matter." The desolation in Warsaw is said to he almost 'beyond descrition. In :heir zeal against the Jews the rioters,de- molithed rows of houses and devastated whole streets. A telegram from Vienna to the Daily Xeres says that trade will suffer terribly from the riots. Many bankrupts have already been announced. The Czar has subscribed 100003 roubles for the distressed victims. The price of food is very high. The respectable inhabitants are deeply grieved at what has taken place. The priests and nuns immediately came to the assist&.ce of the distressed Zews. It isgenerally believed that the movement was prepared long beforehand, attacks upon Jewigh tradesmen having commenced simulta- neously in many parts of the city. A shrill whistle was heard, which was oberved during the encesses against the Jews in other cities. The riots have been far more serious than might at first have been supposed. Six thousand families arc said to have lost all they possessed.

At a meeting of the Ennis Town Commissioners, on Mon- day, the foliowing letter to Mr. Parsons, chairman of the Board, was ordered to be inserted on the minutes :—" Chief Secretary's olce, Dub 31st December, 16431.—Sir,—Inas- much as rny recent visit through Ireland was one of a purely private character and in nowise connected with the Irish Executive of Her Majesty's Government, I 'decided on not being interviewed in any form by public bodies or deputa- tions representing any pasticular opinions. For that reason declined receiving the eisputation of which you were the principal, and 1 now take this, the earliest opportunity to covey to you and those whom you represent that my refusal to receive your depaation was not actuated in the slightest degree 47 discourtesy on my part. lat glad I can reliably inform.you, from official information obtained since my return to Ireland, that crime is decreasing in the pro- claimed districts, and that the authorities look With a san- guine expectation to the time, not far distant, when the repressive measures now. in force can be abandoned.—' am, dear sir, yours faithtully, HERLITET GLADSTONE.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN: ri NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSION— - Mr. J. Fairelough, in the absence of the Chairman; pre- itided at the monthly meeting of this Board, held at the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Monday. There were ids° present :—Colonel McCorquodale, Messrs. Wood, Glover, Foster, Gillespie, Emmett, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and I Brierley (surveyor). HIGHWAYS, PU3LIC WORKS, AND SANITARY COMMITTEE, A meeting of the above Committee was held on the 19th December. Mr. Fairclough was elected chairman in the room of the late Mr. W. Pennington.—Dr. Watkins reperted , the spread of scarlet fever in Gas-street, and desired the Commissioners to impress upon the managers of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Schools, Crow-lane, the importance of at once closing the schools.—lt was ordered that Mr. Brierley write to the Rev. J. Lennon urging the importance of com- plying with the resolution of the school managers of the district, passed on the sth ult., viz., to close the schools for three weeks, from the 16th December. Seventy seven cases of scarlet fever and 10 cases of measles were reported at the meeting, and two deaths from fever during the month.—lt was ordered that Mr. Brierley be empowered to remove any fever patient to the hospital at Warrington, reported by the medical officer, on the certificate of a justice of the peace, where necessary. The condition of Park-road, south of the railway bridge, was again complained of, and Mr. Pardev promised to see to its repair.—The Committee recommended the Board to petition the Local Government Board in favour •of appointing inspectors under section 14 of the Alkali, tic., Works Regulation Act, 1881, to be resident in the neigh- bourhood of St. Helens and Widnes.—lt was ordered that in cases of emergency Mr. Brierley be empowered, with the concurrence of the chairman of the Committee, to instruct the Law Clerk to institute legal proceedings against offenders of the Commissioners' laws without the necessity of a special resolution of the Committee or Board.—lt was resolved that the tender of Mr. John Unsworth for the labour, drc" in paving, flagging, &c., of Stiez-street, Alma- street, and Grant-street, private improvements, be accepted. —The Surveyor having certified that the sum of £250 was' due to Mr. 5. Unsworth, on Crow-lane and High-street sewet contract, a cheque for that amount was passed.—A commung- cation was read from the Local Government Board requiring to know what loans, if any, the Committee were likely to require for the year commencing April Ist, 1881.—The com- mittee were of opinion that no loan need be applied for during that period.—lt was ordered that Mr. Brierley be in- structed to examine and make trial holes in the field known as " further six acres " on Newton Hall farm, and also pre- pare a preliminary plan with estimates of the cost of pre- paring a public burial ground for the district.—Plans of three cottages in Sefton-street, Crow-lane, for Mr. Robert Whitfield, were submitted and approved. The CHAIRMAN moved, and Colonel McConctronarx seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Mr. EMMETT asked what reply Mr. Brierley had received from Father Lennon with regard to closing the school. Mr. BRIERLEY said he wrote to the rev, gentleman on the following day, but he was sorry to say he had had no reply whatever.

Mr. WOOD asked whether there were many fever cases. Mr. BRIERLEY stated that the number of cases was de- creasing. Against 77 cases reported at the committee meet- ing there were now 44. Mr. GILLESPIE asked under what circumstances Mr. Brierbiy would be empowered to remove people to the lever hospital. Mr. BRIERLEY said it was in the event of a person not, having proper isolation and not receiving proper treat: ment. The minutes were conErmecl, and the Law Clerk was instructed to prepare a petition to the Local Government Board in favour of appointing inspectors under the Alkali, &c., Works Regulation Act.

The Earl of Derby was on Wednesday entertained at din ner by his feitow-members of the Liverpool Reform Club. The noble lord was elected a member of the club six months ago, his severence from the Conservative party dating some time earlier than that, but it was not until Wednesday night that he first spoke as a professed Liberal in an assembly of Liberals. Lord Sefton, the president of the club, occupied the chair, and among those who had assembled to do honou to the guest of tile evening were the Earl of Dalhousie, Mr. Rathbone, M.P., Mr. Cepfton, M.P., Mr. J. Roberts, M.P., Mr. S. Willinmson, M.P., Mr. Caine, M.P., and several other members of Parliament. Lord Derby, in regponding to the toast of his health, said that, though a change of political alliances must always imply some modification of political ideas, he had not much to unsay of what he had said in former years. He said : I have been a Conservative—a high Tory, or indeed a Tory at all, I never have been. High notions of prerogative and ecclesiastical privilege have found no defender in me, and still less have I ever sympa- thised with that curious development of modern sentiment whiclaas got the name of Jingoism, and of which I sup- pose the leading idea to be that no State can te in a healthy condition that is not occasionally pitching into its neigh- bour. (Cheers.) In one respect I have profited by expe- rience and observation. I have learned more and more the uselessness—to put it on no other ground—a attempting to resist the progress of popular ideas, and I have come to think more and more highly of the moderation, the fairness, and the general justice with which masses of men, includieg all conditions of life, are disposed to use their power. Con- sidering the great diversities of fortune in this country, I should have expected in 1867 a certain display of class feeling and of jealousy, not to say of bitterness against the rich, such as is visible in continental politics. I don't observe in England or Scotland a trace of any such feeling, and! believe that if the wealthy and educated classes will act with sense and prudence, if they will put themselves at the head of movements leading up to necessary reforms, they will not find their real interests exposed to much danger, and they may retain a large share of their former influence in the State. lam not going to waste your time by a con- troversial defence of the policy of the Cabinet. Criticism is the legitimate function of an Opposition, and it is a duty the performance of which they do not often neglect—(laughter): —but the duty of a majority, and a majority in possession of power, is not criticism, but action. It is not their busi- ness to dwell upon the past, but to provide for the future. (Hear, bear.) What was done in 1881 is now a matter of only historical interest: the question that concerns us is what is going to be done in 1882. I think there is a very general concurrence of opinion that the first work on hand is the improvement of the procedure of the House of Commons. There is another question con- nection with the constitution of the House of Commons which han already occupied more time and caused more bad feeling than its importance deserves—l mean the question of Parliamentary Oaths. For my :part, I utterly disbelieve in the value of political oaths. 1 .don't see that they ever caused any man in public life to do or to abstain from doing apything that he would have left undone, or that he would IPave done, if oaths had never existed. (Hear, hear.) But they are a custom all over the 'world, and they do no par- ticular harm. If we are to have any legislation on the sub- ject, the simplest plea would be to allow any body to substitute an affirmation for an oath, without assigning his reason. But it is not a very urgent question, and I shoulsl hope that, if Mr. Bradlaugh again offers to take the oath, as he did last year, there will 'be no fur- ther attempt to prevent him. (Hear, hear.) 4 There are, as we know, other matters to deal with, -such as Bank- ruptcy Laws, River conservancy, and that subject of licen- sing, which, as we have observed, excites many people to quite an extraordinary degree. It is certainly not the busi- ness of the Cabinet,laor of its supporters, to hasten to get rid of a House of 'Commons which is entirely in their interest, and which is full of reforming activity. (Hear, hear.) What cavnict wait is the work of restoring order and peace in Ireland. (Loud applause.) Those of you who know the opinions 'which I have expressed, know that don't take a very nheerful or sanguine view of the situation. I am afraid the discontent and the dislike of English rule, the vague but powerful sentiment of nationality, which we have so often witnessed abroad, have a deeper hold of the Irish mind than we on this side have been willing to admit. What is asked for under the name of Rome Rule is a sepa- rate Parliament; and I am afraid I must say I believe that is a very general wish among the 'lrish masses. (Hear, hear.) Well, what are we to do'? There is no escape from the dilemma. If we grant their wish we virtually break up the empire; for I suppose everybody can see that a Parliament, 'however limited at !first in powers, ence established in 'Dublin, would very -soon -shake off any dependence •on the Parliament sitting at Westminster. (Hear, hear.) If we resist and :personally I don't see that we have any choice—we must frankly accept the fact that we are overruling the will of a local majority, and for my part E-see nothing arbitrary or despotic in -so doing. The relations of England and Ireland concern not the Irish alone' but the "whole 35,000,000 'cC our population, :and I cannot doubt that of those 35,000,000 there is an overwhelming proportion 'in favour of maintaining the connection in its presect form. (Applause.) The will of the majority, it is argued, ought •to rule. Certaiely ; I accept thati'doctrine. Ido more ; I assert it. But, in a matter that concerns the entire community, it 'is the majority of the whole community,' and not any part of it, to which I defer. There is one thing that we have a eight•to ask, and that rise that in a time of distur- bance and difficulty the Government of the day shall have the supportcf all parties in the Stelte. (Cheers.) 'lt is not a time for calling names, for bitter and angry speeches about things which are done and which can't be undone. The latest charge aoainst the Government is that they:have been slack intheir efforts to preserve or to restore order.: I believe that a snore groundless accusation' never was brought against any set cf :men. (Applause.) Let us grant reforms by all means—decentralisation in any practicable shape--'hit let us hold out no false hopes of independence, or of a federal system which never can work 'between two countries so closely connected as England andilreland. (Cheers.) And, I on the other hand, let us have no more scolding. We are the stronger party and can afford to keep our,tempers. I have faith in time. When people see that seehat they wish foteis•fairly and finally out of reach, they cease first to try for it, and in the end to think about it at all. Let us hope it .may be so with Heme Mule. (Hear, bear.) In conclusion; his Lordship touched on the English land ques- tion. He said nearly everybody agreed that the present re- strictione on the transfer of !encl.-could not be maintained. He held the opinion that an increase in the number of land- owners woo desirable in the interest of the class itself. He was ready to support any fair plan of compensating a tenant for unevhausted improvemente,dant it would not ke wise to commit themselves to any scheme of allowing the tenant to sell what was called his interest, which really meant selling something that did belong to himeand a good deal that did not. But tke tenant was, in fact, inin better position to make his own terms than he had ever been in the memory of man; he was really master of the situation, for the excessive coin- petition for land which had always been put forward as the basis on wh:ch Irish land reforms were to rest did not exist in England.

A letter dated 7th December was read from the Clerk of the Peace's offices which stated that in reply to the Clerk's enquiry as to whether anything had been done >'with regard to the application of the Newton-in-Makerfield•lmprovement Commissioners to have certain roads in their districtdeclared to be main roads, under thencrovi9ions of section'ls of the Act, he begged to inform them that the County Highway Committee had classified all the applications sent in, and referred the same to the county surveyors for their reports, but owing to the difficulty of dealing with the ,question of main roads in so large a.county as Lancashire, the Highway Committee had not considered it expedient to recommend the Court of Annual Session to make any ordera for main roads at present. The LAW CLERK reported that he summoned Mr. Peter Mel:inley, of St. Helens, at the last Newton Petty-Sessions, for refusing to pay the tolls. At the sessions Mn McKinley acknowledged he was wrong, and he withdrew the summons on the payment of costs. A short conversation ensued, from which it appeared that Mr. McKinley was delivering goods in Newton with a van, bale refused to pay the toll when demanded, as he thought .he was not liable, the goecis having been purchased in St. Helens. Tha Ldw Clerk was directed to prosecute in future cases.

TRADE NOTES. A large meeting of South Males and Monmouthshire house coal colliers was held on Saturday at Llanvahon,at w:aich it was decided to continue the sliding scale apart from steam coal colliers ; and that, unleea certain improvements be made, notice to terminate the scala.be given to tie employer,c at the end ot,January. The,rollers' helpers employed at Messrs. Fox, Head, and Co'e. rolling mills, Middlesborough, struck on Moocaty for an increase of wages. The mills are consequently,stopped, but the puddling furnaces are -still in operation. A delegate meeting., representing 25,006 colliers of-Couth Wales ad Monmouthshire, was held at Aberdare, on Mon- day, when it was resolved that the mastero be requested to rectify the existing wages eliding scale, both as to basic and percentaa of scale advance.

THE ALLEGED EXTENSIVE DOCK FRAUD i• At the Everpool city pollee court on 30th salt., before:Mr. Raffles, stip =diary magistrate,Zohn Beckett, contractor; Run- corn, and coin Jones, machine weigher, in thc,employ of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, were charged on remar:d with having defrauded the Doak Trust of a .12s 6d. Mr. Carver (instructed by the solicitor to the Dock Board) ag- ed to protecute ; Dr. Commins, M.P. (instructed by Mr.

R. Bremnet)„.conducted Beckett'e defence; and Mr. Spence • (Messrs. Moore and Spence) appeared for Jonee.—Mr. Car- c-ver said that Eeckett for the past eci.-en years had been the , contractor for the supply of gravel to the Mercey,Docks and; Earbour Boardior their new works. The quantity of gravel' aanpplied to the Board of late had not been so great, but in, IEBO 100,000 tons were used, and.over 18,000 ,tons were, purchased during the first four months of the present year.; The price per ton paid to Beckett was 3s ,9d, and the, prizoner hired a vessel to convey the gravel from various: places to the Mersey, where it was unloaded at places to snit the convenience of the prosecutors, and the cargoes weighed by servaEts cf the Board. Soraetimes, however, the gravel was not weighed owing to pressure of buzinese, or to the absence of a weighing machine on the spot, and in such ease& the draft of the vessel was taken Sore and aft, ,with a record of the cargo, and these results were used for the 0ur.... poses of calculation on similar occasions. Beckett's custom was to bring the gravel from Barrow or the Isle of Man in a vessel called the Tarleton Lass, and on the sth inst a;cargo of gravel, which the prisoner had purchased at the rate of is per toa,arrived at Peel., The gravel went to the Alexandra Dock, and was there ,disokarged into tracks which were weighed ty the prisoner Jones about 100 yards away from the vessel. Jones sent in his returns, and, suspicions haying been entertained by the prosecutors, the stuff was re-weighed on the 20th alt, when it was discovered that the grams weight of the wagons was 194 tons and the amount of •the tare 53 tons JOcwt. The net weight, as made by Jones, was 149 tons 14,avrt, while the net, after re-weighing, was only 135 tons 8 ewt, thus leaving 14 tons 6 cwt. unaccounted for. The prosecutosa believed that the return made by Jones was a fraudulent one, that the sum of £2 12s 6d had thereby been paid in ez,cess by the Dock Board; and Beckett, it wauld be shown, knew of the improper rdturn.—Both Beckett and Jones were arrested by warrant on the 21st ult. ; Prior to that, however, they had been taken to the Detective Office in Dale-street for inquiry, and a piece of paper was then found upon Jones, containing the following words, "Be very careful about 'Vulcan weights; in fact, all vessels. Make this away after perusal.' Since his arrest Beckett bad written a statement, in which be stated that if the weighers bad properly done their duty all would have been right; that he was willing to do all in his power to assist the Dock Board; and that they could examine Itis papers at his office.—Evidence was called which bore out the above statement, after which Mr. RaGes said he believed there was a prinuz facie ease against the prisoners, but if on tinvesti- , gation other cases of a stronger character were found out against them, a further warrant had better be: applied ,for. The prisoners were th.en committe4 for trial to the se.ssiea,s, bail being allowed,
