div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

About 15,&poachers fishing in the Queenstown river;Mayo, on Tuesday night, were disturbethbv the bailiffs, one of the latter being severely beaten. Luke Armstrong, shopkeeper, Tubercurry, was on Wednes- day arrested under the Coercion V..,ct, and conveyed to Armagh gaol, charged with inciting to pay no rent. A large number of the Duke of Devonshire's tenants in the counties of Cork and Waterforc:, who a fortnight ago refused to pay their rent, have nos-,, paid it without any abatement.

The troopship Assistance left Eingztown on Wedneeclay with the let ffiattalion, Bedfordshire (late 16th Regiment), from Newry for Shorncliffe, and several detachments, num- bering 608 officers, non-conlmiseloned officers, and men. The house of a Scripture reader named Feeneo was Cred into on Tuesday night by a large party at Mygownagh, Mayo. Several bullets were foaled about the house. Five men were arrested on Wednesday morning on suspicion of being connected with the outrage. Mr. Herbert Qladstone, M.P., on Wednesday telegraphed to the chairman of the Ennis Town Commissioners, stating 'that the letter read the other day at the meeting of that .body, and purporting to bear his signature, was a forgery., A telegram was received on Tuesday from Major Bond, .who is at present in Dublin, stating that he had received an ,appointment as d 1 ice magistrate, at Balingarry, in Tipper- ary. The salary is £425 per annum, with a house and an , allowance of £lOO, for a horse. -

About 36 stands of arms have been captured out of a steamer and lodged in the police barrocks, Kilrush. The case was consigned to Mr. Glynn, justice of the peace, and an ex- tensive miller in the town. It is supposed that the address was intended to deceive the constabulary. A very large and influential meeting of landlords was held in Dublin on Tuesday for the purpose of pronouncing, in the name of the land proprietors of Ireland, on the administra- tion of the Land Act, and petitioning the Queen to take steps to relieve the landowners from the calamity with which they are menaced. About 3,000 landowners were present, and resolutions were passed in harmony with the objects of the meeting. The Dublin Corporation on Tuesday adopted a resolution, by 29 votes to 23, for conferring the freedom of the city on Mr. Farrell and Mr. Dillon. The Corporation of Cork, at a special meeting on Tuesday, conferred the freedom of the city on Dlr. Dillon, M.P. Out of 56 councillors 21 attended. It was agreed to send copies of the resolution to Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Forster, and all the Corporations in Ire- land. An atrocious murder was committed at Irishtown, near Mullingar, Westmeath, on Saturday morning. Entering a , house occupied by an old woman of 85 and her two daugh- ters, a stranger, described as "a tall, dark man," fired with a revolver at all of the inmates in succession. He missed thel mother, killed one of the girls, and dangerousiy wounded the other. The murderer bus not been arrested. His motive is unknown, but the crime is not believed to be of an agrarian character, The Irish Mayors were installed on Monday. The Dublin ceremony gave opportunity for a display of popular feeling in favour of Mr. Dawson, M.P., the new Lord Mayor; but he did not escape the attention of his opponents, for as he was passing Trinity College he—a baker by trade—was assailed with penny rolls and little bags of flour. At Lim- erick, which is always funny, there was a grotesque scene. The retiring Mayor, Dr, O'Sullivan, announced that he had

div.head: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.

These sessions were opened at Chester on Monday, Mr. Horatio Lloyd (deputy chairman) presiding. Mr. Lloyd, in addressing the grand jury, congratulated them on the light- nessof their duties, there being only 14 cases on the calendar, a number below the average, and the whole of them of an ordinary character.—The county treasurer's financial state- ment showed an estimated expenditure for the quarter com- mencing the 31st of March, 1882, as follows: Balance due to treasurer, £1400; county bridges, £835; main roads, £3000; prosecutions, £1200; repayment of loans, £1000; interest on loans, £1068; justices' clerks, £1100; coroners, £600; clerk of the peace, £400; lunatic asylums, £1200; reformatories, £150; purchase of land for asylum at Upton, £1800; cattle disease compensation, £200; and other items, making a total of £15,491. The estimated receipts were £l5OO from justices' clerks' fines and fees, £5OO from court fees, £5OOO from the River Weaver trustees, and £3OO from the Local Govern- ment Board towards maintenance of pauper lunatics. The balance to be raised was £Bl9l, and a county rate of id. in the pound was laid to produce this amount. A general police rate of fd. was laid, and local police rates in the various divisions, varying from fd. to lid. in the pound. The chief constable (Major leamersley) submitted his statement of the crime of the county for the quarter ended the 30th November last, which gave a bate' of 2534 apprehended and summoned, of whom 79 were committed for trial, 2094 sum- marily convicted, and 361 discharged. The Chief Constable said that since the adjourned sessions on the 22nd of Nov., four cows had been attacked with pluro-pnuemonia at:AshIOD, in the Eddisbury division, the first attacked having been an animal purchased at Chester fair from an Irish dealer. No cases of foot-and-mouth disease had been reported since the last sessions. Swine fever had appeared in two places, three animals having been attacked. Sheep scab existed on eleven farms, 67 animals remaining under treatment. The register of milksellers had been revised, and there were now on the register 2848 as compared with 3218 in 1880.—Colonel King reported that the sewage irrigation system of the asylum was in succesful operation, and that their crops of hay, potatoes, mangolds,,&c., were the envy of the neighbouring farmers. The Duke of Westminster brought before the magistrates the claims of the Discharged Prisoners' Aid Society. The annual report of the society, which acted for Denbighshire and Flintshire as well as for Cheshire, showed that the balance in hand at the end of the year was only £9 7s. 9d., and the subscriptions received during the year, amounted to £27 16s. Cd., a sum ludicrously inadequate to aid the dis- charged prisoners of three counties. The subvention given by the Government depended upon the subscriptions being at least equal to the Government grant.—The Hon. Wil- braham Egerton, M.P., brought forward a recommendation thatthe bye-laws relating to the passage of locomotive engines along the highway be altered. At present, agricultural locomotve engines were not allowed to pass aiong the high- ways after 5 p.m., but this was considered a great incon- venience to farmers, and by his casting tote the committee recommended that the prohibited hours be from eight p.m. to four a.m.—Mr. G. W. Latham seconded this, and urged that these were times when all possible aid should be given to agriculture.—Mr. Christopher Bushell and other members represented the dangers arising from the passage of traction engines along the road between five and six p.m., and the question was ultimately adjourned to the next sessions.

div.head: TRIALS 'OF PRISONERS.
div.p: TRIALS 'OF PRISONERS.
The Court then proceeded with criminal business, the Deputy Chairman presiding in the Crown Court, and Mr. U. Corlmt in the Nisi Prius Court.

THEFT OF LEAD AT FRODSULM.—Edward Antrobus, 23, farm labourer, Frodsham, pleaded guilty to stealing 88 pounds weight of lead, the property of Frederick William Dunsford, at Frodsharn, and was sentenced to sis months' hard labour.

STEALING A DECK NT FEEDSHAII.—SaMIIeI Twist, 17, labourer, Frodsham, pleaded guilty to stealing a duck, the property of Hannah Youd, atTrodsham. Lordship, and was sentenced to six months' hard labaur.

div.head: ABRAM COLLIERT EXPLOSION.
div.p: THE ABRAM COLLIERT EXPLOSION.

Another body was recovered on Sunday from the Arley pit of the Abram Coal Company, the scene of the disas- terous explosion on December 10th. The deceased had both legs cut off, but his body was not much disfigured, and he was easily identified as 'Peter Whaling, a detaller, of West Leigh, and leaving a widow and two children. He was found in the dibhole at the bottom of the upcast shaft. Johnson and Jackson, the two men whose recovery 13 hours after the explosion has already been recorded, stated that they spoke to Whailing immediately after the accident, and as they were then near the upcast shaft it was supposed that Whaling might have, in the darkness and confusion, rushed to the mouthing and fallen down the shaft, a distance of 130 yards. This surmise -has proved correct, but the work of recovering the body has been one of no small difficulty, owing to the great damage done to the upeact shaft by the explosion. The bricking in many places had been blown out, and about 15 tone of debris had to be wound out of the dibhole before the body was come across. It is reported that one person is still missing, John Shovelton, a collier, but no trace of his 'body has been found in the workings. Up to now 41 dead bodies have been brought out of the pit, and seven of those recovered alive after the explosion have since died from the-injuries received, making a total of 48 lives lost.

div.p: PRESCOT POLICE INTELLIGENCE. TrEmer.—Befcre Messrs. W( Pilkington and A. R. Gladstone.

A REFRACTORY PAPER.—Mary Riley was charged with being disorderly whilst an inmage of the Prescot Union Workhouse.—Mr. -S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, prosecuted, and in opening the case said the prisoner had been an inmate of the workhouse for more than three months. She had three children, and wac one of those women who had been deserted by their husbands. On Sun- day last it came to the knowledge of the porter that the prisoner had taken a piece of bread from the dining-room, contrary to the regulations. The porter searched the pri- soner and found a piece of bread in her possession, and reproved her for her conduct. Prisoner afterwards went to the day-room and attacked an inmate, dealing her a severe blow on the left eye with a piece of coal. She then bit the finger of another inmate, and tore the hair of a third, and threatened to kill her.—Prisoner was sent to prison for 14 days with hard labour. DISOBEYING THE ORDER OF THE COI:MT.—Wm. Thomas Cole was summoned for not paying the .noney he was ordered to pay by the court for the maintenance of his mother. The amount in arrear was £l2s. which, with £1 17s. 6d. costs, made a sum of £2 19s. 6d.—Defendant said he had had sickness in his family, and had been unable to pay.—Mr. Hartley, who appeared for the Guardians, read a statement of the defendants's wages.—Defendant said his average wage was 235. per week.—Defendant was ordered to pay 3s. per week until the arrears were paid off. DESERTING His WIFE LINTD FAMILY.—Jobn McDonald, for deserting his wife and three children in December, 1680, and never contributing anything towards their support, was committed to prison for three months. THEFT or A SHIRT AT HUTTON.—Thomas George Moore and Wm. M'Allister. two boys, were charged with stealing a flannel shirt, value 3s. 6d., the property of Charles Green, Blue Bell, Huyton.—Prisonera, who had previously been in a reformatory, on the afternoon of the 30th December • ook the shirt off a hedge in Mr. Green's garden, where it had been placed out to dry. Prisozers were met by P.S. Pin- cod', who searched them, and found the shirt in the posses- sion of Moore.—Prisoners were committed for trial at the Sessions.

div.head: pear,
div.p: pear,
TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [Sp s CIA L.] XXXII. BAALBEC.

The ruins of Baalbec, whether seen at a distance as you descend the slopes of the anti-Lebanon mountains, or as they tower in majesty above you on a nearer approach, can- not but excite wonder and admiration. The afternoon on which, after passing through the long vaulted passage, we emerged upon the spacious quadrangle around which the ruins are situated, and took our seats on the raised platform in the centre of the square, is one of the most vivid and cheris;led recollections of our journey. Our ponies had been led beck for stabling to the vaults within the passage; the Arabs, with the usual din and clatter, were driving the stakes and fixing our tents; while the noble ruins stood out against the sky or were scattered in broken fragments round. After a few minutes' rest we rambled over the wonderful ruins. We had not proceeded far with our researches before we discovered that we had the records of three distinct ages of the world spread out before us, patent to the most casual observer. The substructions which now form the platform of the great temple, are laid with stupendous bevelled stones dating back, probably, far beyond the Greco-Roman periods to which the temple itself belongs. These lelocks measure from 62 to 64 feet in length by 13 feet square, and are estimated to weigh about 1,500 tons each. How these were brought from the quarry and raised 19 feet high— their present elevation—it is difficult to imagine. It would be a rash thing to affirm, with results like these before us, that our own age is entitled to the credit of originating the hydraulic or any other lift. As we left Baalbec next morn- ing we saw, at half a mile distance, a block of stone 71 feet long and 13 by 14 square, lying just where it had been quarried perhaps 3,000 years ago, nicely squared and ready for removal to the temple, which had either been finished without it, or never finished at all. Such were the original foundations of the temple reared to the Sunegod in the Heliopolis of the Phcenician empire. In after ages, when Syria was overrun and colonised by the Greeks and Romans, and the worship of Baal bad been supplanted by that of Jupiter, arose this beautiful temple, executed in the most gorgeous style of Corinthian architecture, of which but six columns, with their noble entablature, remain. On so grand an elevation, the temple glittering with its smooth yellow stone in the golden sunlight, must have been very imposing for miles around. But ages rolled on, and Saracen hordes invaded and possessed the land: then arose upon the massive walls of the Acropolis and around the temple in a rude and barbarous admixture of stones of all sizes and shapes, the walls of a heavy fortress, behind which the Arab and the Turk sought protection from their enemies, while they must have spared no pains to desecrate and destroy the temples of the hated idolaters. Yet, strange to say, these Moslem invaders had no conscience in the matter of building their mosques out of the elegant fragments ttken from the demo- lished temples, or in fitting them together in the most rude and unartistic manner. It was in the village of Baalbec that we saw one of the most uncouth and unshapely of these structures. I have spoken of the majestic ruins of the great temple, but there is another, whose ruins far exceed it in interest and elaborate workmanship. It is called the Temple of the Sun. Its four walls, with much of the facade, are still standing, and display both without and with- in, an affluence of architectural skill, in the way of mas- sive ornamentation, far beyond anything I had ever seen. The coffered ceiling of the portico, in clearness and delicacy of workmanship, was more like carving in ivory than anythine. else. The portal of the temple is wonder- fully beautiful. It is about 20 feet in height; its doorposts are monoliths most lavishly carved with vines, garlands, and figures of various kinds. The architrave is in three pieces: the centre piece, fitted to the ethers like the key- stone of an arch, has sunk down, forcing the side pieces out of their place by its great weight and wedge-shape. This is now supported by rough brickwork, which one of our English consuls, after much negotiation with the Turkish authorities, got leave to run up within the doorway. The bricks and mortar in such a situation are a fearful eye-sole, but they certainly preserve in something of its original beauty one of the most exquisite specimens of architectural ornament ever wrought into a builaing. We crept through a hole left in the brickwork into the interior of the ruins where the massive fragments, some of them many tons in weight, which had formed the vaulted ceiling, were lying in confused heaps, while the half-columns, surmounted with noble projecting entablature, arose on all sides of the well- preserved walls. Outside, broken sections of smooth round columns, mingled with capitals in the finest relief, and beautifully carved heads from the ceiling of the portico were lying in splendid confusion. The columns had been had been in two pieces, bound together by heavy iron dowels, of which they had all been rifled, with one solitary exception, and that where the column had fallen inward against the wall, and was so firmly held together by the iron cramps that it was resting securely in its slanting position against the eetla, although several stones had been crushed and broken where the top of it was resting. The 'rain poured down in torrents through the night and during the forenoon of the next day, so we had to finish our explorations under dripping umbrellas; but our ardour was in no wise damped as we clambered about a scene which spoke to us se powerfully of the glory of departed empires —of the culture and refinement of. taste that ran parallel with gross idolatries and superstitions; empires which, in spite of a grandeur and elevation that seemed to reach the heavens, have been stricken down until the feeble flickering records connected with places like this, whose history is almost unknown, is all that is left to lift their memory out of utter extinction. Before starting, we gathered together in a group, and sangamid these relics of ancient heathendom "All hail the power of Jesu's name.", Then, at 11 o'clock a.m., we mounted, and after visiting the quarry in which the mammoth stone already mentioned lies, we struck for- ward across the mighty plain amid rain and hail and bitter cold. To us who had almost missed the winter, and been moving about, for the first time in our lives, under the scorching heat of February and March suns, the change was a little cruel. Before we reached the shelter of a shiek's house, two hours after we set out, we felt too much chilled to make it desirable to stand or sit in our wet garments, and most of the company rapidly promenaded the open archway of the house, and in so doing not only got up the circula- tion but prepared themselves for enjoying the good things provided by our dragoman in an adjoining apartment. After lunch the ladies were invited to visit the female part of the establishment. Then we had to wade through the slush and mire of the yard to find our ponies, and, being all refreshed and moderately comforted, we mounted, and again struck across the magnificent plains with the mountains of Lebanon clothed in mist before us, and the rugged Anti- Lebanon range in the rear. We encamped for the night at the village of Able, at the foot of the Lebanone, and experi- enced for the first time the exceeding discomfort of having to tent on grass dripping with wet, which not only saturated the carpets beneath our feet, but made our bedding and clothing and everything feel damp. After partially undres- sing, I think most of us wrapped our heavy coats around us, and, tucking the bed clothes well in, had a pretty comfort- able night. Although everything felt damp next morning, we all awoke refreshed, without having taken cold, and at eight o'clock started to ride along the fertile and undulating slopes at the foot of the Lebanon range. We were not long in passing through the important town of Zahleh, whose population, numbering about 15,000, is chiefly composed of Maronite or professedly Christian people. Its cleanliness and general appearance of domestic comfort contrasted very favourably with most of the towns and villages we had seen in the Holy Land. It has an English school and a telegraph office—both evidences of advanced civilisation. It stands at an elevation of 3,100 feet above the sea level, yet our way lay across the lofty peaks of Lebanon before we got a sight of the Mediterranean. Our, route to-day (Good Frilky), as yesterday, had been along the magnificent plain, 30 or 40 miles in length, that stretches between the Lebanon rend the anti-Lebanon mountains—the rugged beauty of the latter rising to the left, and the almost etherial stateliness of the former to the right, while before us, at the foot of the plain, stood Hermon, with his dark base shutting in the view, and his snow-white peak almost touching the clouds. A scene of greater beauty can scarcely be imagined. Soon after leaving Zahleb, we began to ascend the Lebanon range. Leaving Shtora on the left, in a few minutes we gained the fine carriage road which the French Carrying Company have made between Damascus and Beyrout. Following this, and before camping for the night, we bad reached an altitude a 5,000 feet above the sea level. As we looked from our tents that evening and saw the golden sun sink into the illumi- nated waters of the Mediterranean, a most glorious picture was presented to the eve. Twenty-five or thirty miles away, but apparently only five or six, the great sea lay with its broad expanse glowing in the rays of the setting sun—then as the burnished reflection in the line of vision faded away —there rested on the bosom of the sea, so much below us, the feathery clouds which, from a lower elevation, would have appeared above the horizon. Between us and the sea were spread out a succession of richly covered mountains, almost presenting the anpearance of an undulating plain. To our left the sombre hills of ancient Phcenicia reired their somewhat barren peaks, but on the right the northern Lebanon range arose with a majesty and beauty and variety of tint perfectly indescribable. The topmost peaks, covered white, and glistening with snow, deepened, as the mountains neared us, into silver grey, then into purple, then into deep olive, and ending, as they sunk into the last valley, into a sort of rich sable brown. Then in the Heavens there was as the poet describes it—
" That clerx obscure, So softly dark, so darkly pure, That follows the decline of day. As twilight sinks beneath the moon away."

- rhis was cur last night in the tents. In the clear bracity* air of the mountain tops, and in the joy of having finished our tent life, an unusual vivacity seemed to take possession of our party. Those who had health and stren.gth en their side spent the evening in all kinds of bodily feats and pedestrian exercises.' -It was enough to dissipate the rhzurn of a bilious sickness which had hung over me all day to • witness the hihrity and innocent recreations to which a few ' of the company yielded themselves, while some, the older ones, were nearly used up by the exhausting effect of two or three damp days in the Lebanon valley; the rest seemed invigorated by the cooler atmosphere, and thus enjoyed themselves. The night wits spent in tolerable comfort, although it felt somewhat breezy between the flapping of the tent corers and the almost incessant braying of the " donkey-asses," as thy were called in Cairo. Next morn- ing we bade farewell to our tent-life, which, with all its

freedom aad delightful novelty for the first few days, had. become very irksome before it came to a close ; what i- would have been if we had not been cared for with a foret sight aud readiness of resource wonderful to think of in their completenesb, I cannot imagine. When we came to compare notes afterwards with those who had travelled over the same ground in smaller parties, and who described the loneliness and monotony as almost unbearable, we must ever feel thank- ful that we seven, whe left England together, were not only a happy party in ourselves, but were associated with those who 112 the main contributed in a very high degree to the pleasure and profit of the journey. We had not proceeded far down the pleasant but circuitOus coach-road towards Reyrout before we got a sight of the beautiful city, sitting on the shore 20 miles away. The sands spread far and wide around it were red and glowing in the sunlight, while yott could almost trace the streets of the city itself as on a map before you. The road t2efore us was steep, and swept in anel out of the terraced hills, until reaching the plain, you saw it run in a straight line for five or six miles, bordered with mulberry trees, into the heart of the city. We arrived at the hotel by the sea shore in the after-noon considerably worn out, and wee thankful for the Sunday's rest that fol- lowed, and for Monday's rambles along the sea coast. On Tuesday the French stetmer anchored in the offing, and at six o'clock that evening we embarked. I must now draw my sketches of travel to a close. Had time and opportunity favoured, I should have liked to have occupied the columns of The Examiner fora few weeks longer in order to have given some account of our cruise along the coast of Asia Minor, and of our landing at Tripolo, Latakia, Alexandretta, Messina, ; our visit to Rhodes; our delight- ful sail through the Islands of the Grecian Archipelago to Smyrna; our visit to the ruins of Ephesus; thence to Syria, Athens, Constantinople; down the Bospherus, and across tke Black Sea to Varna; thence from Ruschuk to Vienna; five days sail on the Danube; and our rapid run home along the banks of the Rhine; but I feel that I have drawn upon the patience of the readers of The Examner long enough, while other duties make it desirable on my own account to suspend my labours in this direction. In conclusion, I may say that my recollection of Ephesus, and Athens, and Constantinople, and the Danube, are so dear to me as opening up stores of thought connected with past and present things, that I may find my way into print again before long in occasional papers descriptive of what we saw, that is if time be granted.

G. Y. T. STABBING A STEPFATHER AT ST. HELENS, On Tuesday, before Mr. T. Pilkington, John Gilooley, a middle-aged man, was brought up under remand charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm on Dennis Connor, hill stepfather, by stabbing him on the 24th ult. Prosecutor was called, and excitedly stepped into the box, and shouted to the bench, "Gentlemen, it was Christmas time, and I don't want to swear against him. I will not take the book in my hand."—Mr. Davidson (deputy magistrates' clerk): You will have to go to gaol yourself if you do not. Take the book in your right hand.—Prosecutor: No; it was Christmas time, and I don't want to swear.—With considerable reluctance he was at last persuaded to kiss the book. He then stated that he was a labourer, and lived at 17, Copperas- street, Eccleston. Prisoner had lived with him for about three weeks up to the 24th ult. Between eleven and twelve o'clock at night, Michael Gilooley, prisoner's nephew, got off the bed where he had been lying, and as he was crying, prisoner said to him, "I'll make you -that you won't be crying." Prosecutor said the prisoner should not touch the lad, aud went between them. He was then struck once on the shoulder and twice on the leg. Michael Gilooley then went into the street and shouted for prisoner to come out. The latter wanted to follow, but was prevented by a number of people. Prisoner, however, went upstairs (it being a low house), got through the window, and went towards Michael. Prosecutor told him to give over, and shouted "Police!" Prisoner then struck him on the thigh and in the abdomen, and he shouted out that he had been stabbed.— A niece of the prisoner said she saw the prisoner come out of a bedroom window in Cepperas-street. Her brothers— Michael and John—were in the street. Prissner went to them, and one of her brothers struck the prisoner, who re- taliated. The last witness, Dennis Connor, struck the prisoner with his hand about the head. The prisoner then gave a slight push below prosecutor's stomach, but she did not hear her grandfather say that he was stabbed. The prosecutor (her grandfather) then went home.—Mary Mere- dith, a widow, said she heard a disturbance in Copperas- street on the night in question, and heard Connor say "You've done it now, Jack; lam stabbed." She did not see the knife, or see the altercation. Prisoner, to whom the remark was addressed, went away, and prosecutor was taken away.—Dr. McNicoll, surgeon, said he saw Dennis Connor at his house in Copperas-street on the 25th of last month. He found a small wound about two incbes below the navel, and from the wound was protruding part of the omentum, which is part of the contents of the abdomen, and not part of the bowels. It was about the size of a walnut. He closed the wound at once, and it bad since done well. There was also a second wound in front of the left side. That wound had not injured any vessel, and had since done well. An iKstrument like the knife produced would inflict the wound.—P.C. Kendall apprehended the prisoner, who on the way to the station said " Before I'll be killed, I'll use fiats, feet, dagger, knife or pistol." He afterwards charged the prisoner with wounding Dennis Connor by strMng him with a knife. The prisoner replied, "I did not do it wilfully, the knife accidentally went into him when pushing him away from me." Witness, in answer to prisoner, said that prisoner told him that someone had been throwing bricks at him. Prisoner also said that if he had intended to inflict the wound the small blade would not be the one he would use, and be would not have been where he was when appre- hended.—Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the • sessions, bail being allowed.

div.head: NEW YEAR'S DAY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: NEW YEAR'S DAY AT ST. HELENS.

New Year's Day was ushered in with its usual accompani- ments, save the seasonable one of wintriness. This feature, as at Christmas, was conspicuous by its absence. The last few hours of the moribund year, and the first few of the one upon which we have now entered, were characterised by mildness of weather seldom known at this season of the year. The night was fine, and the light of the moon put to shame the lighted lamps of the street. According to custom, wor- shippers repaired to the sanctuary, where they spent the last moments of the old year in Christian devotion. Immediately after the advent of the new year, the musical bells Of St.; Thomas's set up a merry peal, and continued for some time) ringing out the old year and ringing in the new. The. ' solitary bell of the Parish Church also added its quota to the music of the night ; and the harmonious strains of a brass band in the street, discoursing music appropriate to the sacred character of the day, had a pleasing effect. The streets had quite an animated appearance as the people from the various places of worship weee wending their way homewards, wish- ing each other the oompliments of the season. Others took the new year ,n to their friends, and spent an hour in sociable enjorment. Blasts of dynamite were frequently heard after the clock struck twelve. People in general have more or less a passion for a loud report and a flash of fire, and these auxiliaries in the telebration of a new year's day, were not without their effect. New Year's Day being on Sun- day, there was perhaps less hilarity than usual, hut throughe out the day bands of children, intent upon keeping Chiist- mas up as long as possible, and extending it into the new year planted themselves at house-doors, and carolled their effusions until the appearance of the good woman of the house with the desired copper, or, as was pretty frequently the case, the appearance of the irate "head "or disgusted youth with the undesired consequences. In the churches and chapels appropriate pulpit references were made. At the Wesley Chapel, Corporation-street, a watch night service was held, at which there was a good company of people present The Rev. J. M. Walmsley conducted the service, which lasted from half-past ten on Saturday night to a few minutes after twelve. The Rev. Mr. Walmsley addressed some remarks based upon the 36th verse of the 13th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, "For David, after he had served his own generation by the v, ill of God, fell asleep, and wet laid unto his fathers, and saw cor- ruption." The preacher spoke of the character of David, whom he described as one who regarded himself as a servant, and not actuated with motives of selfishness. This trait was manifested in his writings. He then spoke of death, and the subsequent corruption of the body, and compared death to sleep. Death and corruption were simply the inermediate conditions between the life that now is and the life of im- mortality. Death was thus swallowed up in victory. After a few minutes of silent prayer and a hymn, the meeting broke up and the people dispersed. In the afternoon, an address was delivered to the young people. In the evening, at the Independent Chapel, the Rev. R. J. Ward preached from the text, "Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you."

div.head: AFRICAN HAIR RESTORER FOR RESTORING THE NATURAL COLOUR AND RENEWING SHE GROWTH OF THE HAIR.
div.p: THE AFRICAN HAIR RESTORER FOR RESTORING THE NATURAL COLOUR AND RENEWING SHE GROWTH OF THE HAIR.

Never known to fail in restoring the hair in eight or ten days. It promotes growth and prevents it falling off; eradi- cating dandruff, and imparting vitality to the roots of the hair. DEUI application of this preparation for a week or two will restore faded, grey, or white hair to its natural colour and richness. If properly applied it never fails; but it should be well shaken before using. It is not a dye, nor does it contain any colouring matter hence it does not soil the head, the scalp, or even white linen, but produces the colour within the substance of the hair.
When the original colour has returned, THE AFRICAN RESTORER should be applied•about once a week, which will be sufficient to sustain it.
N.B.—See that the words, "THE AFRICAN HAIR RE, STORER." are OR every bottle, as that is a " trade mark." PRICE ONE SHILLING PER BOTTLE.

div.head: EXAMINER
div.p: THE EXAMINER
SATURDAY, JANUARY 7, 1882:

Tam political campaign of 1882 has commenced with the speeches of two Cabinet Ministers, Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain, to their constituents at Birmingham, on Tuesday evening. No other oOn' stituency in the country possesses two representatives who can so ably define and defend Liberal, prinoiplea and methods of government, and Birmingham 11a8 good right to be proud of the influence it exercises, through its members, Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamber- lain, upon the councils of the Government, the action of Parliament, and the opinions of the British people. The present speeches of both right hon. gentleffell were well delivered, full of strong points arti good sense, and were received with the greatest approba- tion by all but a small section of a vast audience. Each dealt chiefly with the same overshadowing question, that of the state of Ireland and the best means for its pacification; and together Mr. Bright and his younger colleague placed the case as between the Government and the party of extreme men who set themselves to depose and supplant the Irish Executive Government, with singular clearness and fairness. Mr. Bright distinguished the three separate policies whieh are propounded for the government of Ireland. The first is that of a few English Demo- crats, which the Irish irreconcilables, for the sake of the personal immunity it would afford them, as a matter of course, heartily endorse. Mr. Bright has received some resolutions passed at a recent meeting of English Democrats, which indicate their view to be that under no circumstances ought a Government to resort to coercive measures in the shape of constramt upon the persons of agitators, however violent and dangerous their incitations to the populace may be. Ciovernments, the Democrats contend, have no right to interfere with the liberty of action and speech of the most reckless of demagogues, not even to prevent the country government from sinking into anarchy through their machinations. Rebels and revolu- tionists should be allowed the freest scope, and an unlimited length of .rope, by the very civil power they are plotting day and night to destroy. nu'B being the Democratic idea, Mr. Bright tells us he us no Democrat. Describing his position in a single phrase worthy to be recorded as an axiom for all advocates of constitutional liberty, Mr. Bright says: —" What I am in favour of is such freedom 58 Will

TIM peech delivered by Lord Derby at the Liver- Pool Reform Club will be read with more than usual interest, inasmuch as the occasion may be regarded RS that of his lordship's first public appearance as a Liberal. The outspoken manner in which he has • enunciated his views on the principal political ques- tions of the day will serve to dissipate any lingering doubt which may have existed as to whether Lord Derby would be found amongst the supporters of Mr- Gladstone's Government. He has plainly shown that his sympathies are with the present administra- tion, and we shall not therefore be surprised if dur- ing the next Session of Parliament he is found to be • one of its staunch defenders. Lord Derby, in coming over from the ranks of the Conservatives to those of the Liberals does not appear to have been obliged to make any very great change in his opinions. He says" I have been a Conservative; a high Tory, or indeed a Tory at all, I have never been. High notions of prerogative and ecclesiastical privilege have found no defender in me, and still less have I ever sympa- thised with that carious development of modern senti- ment which has got the name of Jingoism, and of ich I suppose the leading idea to be that no State can be in a healthy condition that is not occasionally Pitching into its neighbour." Referring to the changes made in 1867, he says that he found none of the "class-feeling and jealousy, not to say bitter- ness against the rich" which he expected, and he has learned by ex.perience and observation, like many other wise politicians, that it is useless "to resist the pro- gress of popular ideas." We are pleased to see that this hard-headed statesman has come to the conclu- sion that the present is an age of progress and reform, for this is a truth which all who desire to lead in public affairs must eventually learn, and the sooner thou do so the better. Lord Derby, however, is no half- hearted politician, for it is plain that he discusses many inevitable reforms with a heartiness which-'9s him infinite credit. He agrees with Mr. GlaL :Pea that a reform in the method of the transaction of pub- lic business in the House of Commons is urgently needed. He deals with the vexed oath question in a manner which shows that he is free from that intoler- ant bigotry which blinds too many of our politicians and causes them to act with a certain amount of tyranny, so that he is pre- pared to give justice to every constituency, and to view the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh into Parlia- ment with composure. Having dealt with the ques- tions of reform in county administration and the government a London, the noble earl went on to speak of the assimilation of the borough and county franchise, pointing out that as this appeared 4ievitable the redistribution of seats, when it took place, should be thoroughly done. His lordship also referred at considerable length to the Irish question, and warmly upheld the Government in its dealing with itreland, arguing that in a time of difficulty and disturbance the Government should have the support of all parties in the State. Dealing with the charge made against the Government that they had been slack in their efforts to preserve or to restore order, he says : " I believe that a more groundless acclimation never was brought against any set of men. :it is absurd, because the Ministry of the day, whoever they may be, hare more to lose by the continuance of disorder, and more to gain by putting an end to it, thanany other set of men can havo. They have, I believe, Acme what is plssible and necessary." Referring to dile Irish land- lords, Lord Derby says, "Leave the Irish people and

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

For some years Mr. Thomas Norman, of Runcorn, has led the van in the matter of improving the railway service to the town of which he is so useful a member, and we have to record another instance of his unwearied assiduity in this respect. For a considerable period the train accommodation provided by the London and North-Western from Runcorn to Manchester, has been of such a character as to call forth loud complaints from business men. The period which the journey was found to occupy, in these days of general expedition, called forth general astonishment. Mr. Norman, in answer to repeated requests, took the question up, and, with his usual good fortune, he has succeeded in bringing it to a successful issue. The company have consented to an arrangement, which will come:in force next week, by which a return ticket taken at Runcorn for Manchester will be avail- able for the passenger to return from that city via Edgehill, without any extra charge. Thus, instead of about two hours being occupied in the journey, as in the past has too often been the case, a passenger will be able to reach Runcorn in about an hour and ten minutes.

The performance of "The Messiah," which at this season of the year is brought prominently before the music-loving public, would suggest to a reflective mind the importance of music in civilised society. What in this vale of tears can so effectively touch the sympathies of man as some plaintive song, sung with genuine pathos? Who is not charmed by its power ? Managers of theatres found this out long ago, and so did political agents. Ought not its talismanic influence to commend itself to our churches? Some of them are already cognisant of it, and use it with effect. Perhaps it would not be well to turn places of worship into mere music places, but who wouldn't prefer good to bad singing? - -

As the paragraph about the dock at Widnes, which appeared under this column last week, has led to a slight misapprehension, it may be well to say that it related to West Bank dock, and the work will be carried out by the trustees of the estate of the late Mr. Hutchinson. It is said it will be proceeded with at an early date. Report has it that Mr. Pierpoint's coming concert in Run- corn will be one of the best that has ever been held in the town. The ratepayers of Runcorn may be congratulated on the fact that the Commissioners have succeeded in purchasing the books lately in the possession of the Literary and Mechanics' Institute at about one shilling per volume. As some of them are works of considerable value, the Board may be considered to have got a bargain. I understand that the block of property lately occupied by the Institute passed into the hands of one of the Commissioners a short time ago, and there has been a rumour that the Public Library would find a home in the building but from enquiries I have made, I believe there is not a shadow of 'foundation for the story. The Wesleyan Methodists of Widnes have realised the handsome sum of about £l3O by the sale of work which they held the other week, although they only required £6O. The manner in which the small bazaar was got up and conducted ,throughout is deserving of the highest praise. There is likely to be a rather lively discussion at the monthly meeting of the Widnes Local Board on Tuesday next, as one of the members has intimated his intention of "impeaching "the conduct of the Hospital Committee in the general management of that institution. On Monday, it is expected there will be quite a rush for seats at the Runcorn Police Court, as the case of Yarwool v. Code (or Codd) comes up for hearing. The matter at issue is certainly not of very great importance, but the " lively " proceedings of Mr. Code have caused a good deal of discussion both in Runcorn and Liverpool.

The Runcorn School Board do not appear to follow the plan adopted by most bodies of a similar character in the country, of doing their principal business in committee ; and the consequence is that now and then the representatives of the press, who have often several engagements in hand, have the pleasure of listening to lengthened discussions on sub- jects which are not of the slightest interest to the ratepayers, during which they are at liberty to bite their pencils, or adopt other methods of passing "the happy hours away." As an instance of this, I understand that at their monthly meeting on Wednesday the Board spent a couple of hours in debating on the respective merits of warming a small school- room. Stoves of high, and stoves of low degree, were brought on the carpet, and their respectiVif merits expatiated upon, from those whose price is about fifteen shillings to the more aristocratic ones at twelve guineas. The discussions at the Board are generally relieved by the witty observations and bonhomie of the Rev. Canon Barclay, but it would puzzle the author of "A Tramp Abroad" to be humorous on the prosaic subject of stoves. Matters were certainly rather dismal, but as they progressed the dreariness of the prospect was somewhat relieved by the sweet tones of a musical in- strament. At first the gentlemen of the fourth estate thought they must be under a delusion, having dropped off into the land of dreams, but the strains grew louder, and now they could distinctly hear the playing of several waltzes and gallops' mingled with occasional catches from popalar operas of the day. But the lines of the Vicar's face betrayed no cognisance of what was so plainly audible to every one in the room, and the discussion on stoves "dragged its slow length along." It appears that the building in which the members hold their meetings forms one of a block in which two rival teachers of music have lately locate themselves; and if the two happen to join their forces on a School Board day, the gatherings of this body are likely to become more entertaining than they have been in the past. FLACCUS.
We regret to state that Mr. William Harrison Ainsworth, the Lancashire novelist, died on Tuesday at his residence in. Surrey. He was born in 1803.

NEW YEAR'S EVE AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday night, the weather was'of a lovely description. The usual services to "welcome the coming guest" were held in the various places of worship, and were very well attended. Monday was observed as a general holiday by the tradesmen. WIDNES AND THE NEW YEAR.—On Saturday evening, the usual watch night services took place, and were very well attended. Several of the choirs belonging to the various churches and chapels paraded the streets, and sang at the houses of their friends. The Star of Temperance brass band also visited a number of places in the town ana played suitable airs. Monday was pretty generally observed as a generally holiday, only a few of the shopkeepers having their places of business open. There was a large traffic on the various lines of railway. CAUTION FOR NEW YEAR.—The recently published reports of medical officers of health show that the mild autumn weather and excessive rainfall have produced an unusual amount of scarlet and typhoid fevers throughout the United Kingdom. There is also in many districts ex- cessive mortality from measles and smallpox. Every cautious householder should use reliable preventive measures, and none are better than washing with Wright's Coal Tar Soap, recommended alike by the entire medical profession and the public. Let the soap be in every bed- room, bath-room, and nursery, and when you purchase, in- sist upon being supplied with Wright's. Refuse all imita- tions.—Advt.

WIDNES WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. The other evening a tea party was held in connection with this class, and the following ladies presided at the trays : Misses M. E. Smith, B. Jackson, A'. M. Brooks, M. A. N. Harper, E. Ankers, S. A. Bailey, J. Rogers, E. Whitby, C.. E. Youd, E. Hartland, S. A. Craft, B. Hartley, and S Goddard. Mr. B. Brown took the chair at the public meet- ing which afterwards took place. Mr. S. Jackson read the annual report, from which it appeared that the number of members was 45 and the average attendance 35, or 77 per cent. of the whole. Since last year there had been an increase in tae average attendance of 32. In connection with the class was a library possessing over 200 volumes and 60 subscri- bers. Appropriate addresses were delivered by the Chair. man. and the Revs. J. H. Cummings and J. Tessyman.

div.p: r 4 t fr it Till; EXAMINER SAT URDAY, JANUARY 7, 1882.

'f ST. Jomes PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN.— During the week, a series of special services, which have been well attended, have been held in this place of worship. WIDNES WEsLETAIT MISSION SERVICES.—A series of special mission services, in connection with'which the Rev. J. Wesley Evans has been the preacher, have been held in the Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel each evening during the week.

RUNCORN CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.— The members of this class had their annual tea, on Monday evening, in Camden school-room. Mr. H. Randle,:the presi- dent, afterwards took the chair, and gave a short address, in which he referred with pleasure to the work the society had been able to accomplish in the past, and spoke in encourag- ing terms of their future prospects. Mr. W. Dutton, the secretary, made a brief statement as to the labours of the class during the last twelvemonths. Mr. Randle was re- elected president, Mr. W. J. Shore vice-president, and Mr Thomas Page secretary for the ensuing year. • RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting took place on Wednesday morning. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present Messrs. Simpson, Prit- chard, Briscoe, Lea, and Rigby (clerk). Mr. Bowyer pre- sented his monthly return, which was as follows :—Certified Government accommodation, 2,289; number on the rolls, 2,781; average attendance, 1,9163; average attendance for December, 1880, 18024; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,252; accommodation in excess of average attendance, 3727; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 492. These figures show an increase in the average atten- dance, as compared with the corresponding period of last year, of 1139; and an increase, as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, of 664.3. The total number in attendance at private adventure schools under ninepence per week is 65. ENTERTAINMENT AT HUYTON.-011 Monday an en- tertainment in connection with the Huyton Quarry branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was given in the Huyton-and-Roby schools, by Professor Weber. There was a tolerably large audience. The entertainment opened with a marionette exhibition, the performances of the wax figures of which threw the juvenile portion of the audience into high glee, while the adult portion at frequent intervals testified in an unmistakable manner their apprecia- tion of the marvellous and dexterious feats of skill exhibited by Professor Weber at conjuring and legerdemain. A performance on the fairy bells was also given, and the entertainment concluded with a ventriloquial sketch by Pro- fessor Weber, introducing his automaton life-size figures (five in number). In the course of the evening the Rev. Canon Penrhyn stated that those who had not already joined the Scciety could do so at the close of the meeting. CHRISTMAS TREE AND PALE OF WORK AT WIDNES —On Thursday afternoon, a Christmas tree and sale of work was opened in the Parish Church day schools, Water- loo-road, for the purpose of raising a sum of money in con- nection with the class-room fund. The total cost of the alterations and additions, which have been previously des- cribed in our columns, is estimated at £4OO, including the cost of furnishing. Towards this about £133 has been raised. The Christmas tree was presented by Mr. Killcross, and it had been decorated by Messrs. J. B. Imison and Craw- ford, assisted by Masters John and Lewis Killcross. After a few opening remarks from the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, the vicar, the sale was commenced. Mesdames James White, Crawford, Mather, Lord, Treacey, Killcross, J. B. Imison, Jones, Shone, Parton, and the Misses Headley,lLea, and Kendrick, had charge of the stalls. Amongst those who presented fruit, smeetmeats, kc., were Mr. Clifton, Mr. Had- field, and Mr. F. Lawrinson. Mr. F. W. Wilkinson and Mrs. Crawford were amongst the donors of articles. The following ladies formed the sewing committee, under whose superintendence most of the articles on the stalls were collected :—Mesdames Imison, White, Jones, C. Jones, Balmer, Lord, Parnell, Thomas, Killcross, J. Wright. Williams, Miss Wrench, Mrs. Mather, Mrs. Crawford, Mrs. Barton, Mrs. Hunt, and Miss Boardman. The ariangement of the room was carried out by Mesdames Kilcross, 134 liner, Hagley, Thomas, Treacey, jun. THE VICAR OF WIDNES ON THE NEW YEAR.— Writing in the Liverpool Parish Messenger for this month, the Vicar of Widnes makes the following observations upon the new year :—" The days glide on so unceasingly and noiseless that it is somewhat hard to realise that we have passed into another year, and that hencefotward, with ratich painful endeavour, we must date our letters, accounts, and papers 1882. Perhaps, indeed, some among us write but few letters, or keep but few accounts, vet, even so, they cannot be oblivious to the change, as "A Aappy New Year to you" passes from mouth to mouth. Everywhere it is heard—in the street, behind the counter, among the furnace, and in the household,—Yes, the new year has come! Last year's al- manacks, diaries, and pocket books are now out of date, and the stationers' windows are filled with those for 1882. Those who keep such books make another start, the old ones are thrown to one side or carefully put away and forgotten, while the tidy housewife has already hung up the new pic- torial almanack. What solemn facts those forgotten old pocket books and almanacks are! Sometimes we hear of such old records furnishing, it may be in a court of justice, evidence alike damaging and unwelcome to the writer. Don't you think the years of our past life are something like these old pocket books? only we have written them day by day by our thoughts, words, and actions, and God has tliem in his possession—they are not forgotten—but will be pro- duced at the great Assize. In them we May say with all solemnity, "What we have written, we have written." And this must make us very thoughtful about the new year—the new volume of 365 pages now scarcely cut. What the leaves yet unopened may bear, what actions of ours, what deeds good and bad, what scalding tears whether of human sorrow or godly repentance, what leave-takings and farewells, may or must be there imprinted by oaggves before they at re- sealed, who but God can tell. And in this spirit we too may take up the general salutation, and wish to each other "A Happy New Year." But wishing without working is but a poor trade in arty line of life, and especially in the "happy new year" business. We must think out prayerfully, and work out carefully, as the first few pages pass under our hands. Note how our little people ear eager only to turn over rapidly, and haste to the end; middle life moves them slowly; old age, regretfully. May we, by God's help, serve Him this year more attentively than we have yet done. To do so, let us resolve—(l) Never to be absent from His House while He gives us health and strength. (2) To read a por- tiod of the Bible every day, be it ever so little. (3) To have prayer in the household; the Prayer Book collects are at our hand, that all may try. (4) To do something for God—in the parish, either in the church, school, or temperance society."

A NEW YEAR'S DRAMATIC BALL AT WIDNE & Considering the comparatively large population of the town of Widnes, the number of;devotees ti Terpsichore within its boundaries scarcely seems to be as numerous as in its rival, Runcorn, from which it is only separated by the river Mersey. Probably the inhabitants of Widnes are very few who can manage to become as enthusiastic as Sir John Suck- ling on this subject, who, writing in 1609 upon some splendid dancer at a wedding, says—

"Her feet beneath her pet icoat Like little mice stole in and out, As if they feared the light; But oh, she dances such away No sun upon an Easter day Is half so fine a sight." Perhaps the comparative scarcity of balls in Widnes, as compared with some towns of similar size, may be ac- counted for by the fact that Liverpool is within such a short distance, and those who are anxious to trip it upon "the light fantastic" can find their fascinating amusement in connection with all kinds of surroundings in that city, from the ball of the highest class to that at which the most in- discriminate company kick up their heels. On Monday evening the Volunteer Hall, which on ordinary occasions has very little interior beauty to recommend itself to anyone, was gay with bunting, scarlet cloth, and flags of all des- criptions, so that it had somewhat the appearance of one of those palaces of delight in which the fairies of the panto- mime choose to dwell. The cause of this pleasant metam- orphosis was the holding of a new year's dramatic ball. The services of Mr. W. S. Branson, who it will be remembered took the parts of Jacques and Shylock at the performance in aid of the Railway Benevolent Institution, had been secured by Mr. Sansom, the stationmaster to the London and North- Western, who had also promised his co-operation, and the Farnworth Glee Club were likewise present. About nine o'clock dancing commenced to the sweet strains of Mr. C. Powell's band—and "cheeks all pale blushed at the praise of their own loveliness." Amongst those present were Dr. O'Keeffe and party, Dr. Richardson and party, Dr. Brown and party, Mr. W. S. Branson, Mr. E. Sansom, Mr. Pierce Talon and party, Mr. and Mrs. Tebbut and party, Mr. and Mrs. Harrison and party, Mr. H. Cookson (Grimsby) and party, Mr. and Mrs. Catterall and party, Mr. Bennett (Run- corn) and party, Mr. E. M. Davies, Mr. McLeod (Birken- head), Mr. Poole:and party, Mr. H. Davies and party, Mr. E. Sankey and party, Mr. i3aialles (Ifiel Hill), Miss Reimer, Miss Tharme (Ditton), and Miss Fearney. Mr. W. J. R. Fowler, of the Central Hotel, had been entrusted with the work of providing refreshments, and these included so many of the choicest delicacies as to reflect the greatest credit upon the caterer. Shortly after eleven, a pause was made in the dancing, and the Farnworth Glee Club sang with much spirit "The forester's sound." Mr. Sansom then recited "The advice to tha players," from Hamlet, which he had himself evidently laid well to heart, for he was highly successful in its delivery, and won enthusiastic applause. Mr. Branson followed with the world-famous piece of. the poet laureate, "The charge of the Light Brigade" at Bala- clava, and threw into the delivery a fire and earnestness which electrified the listeners, and placed before them. as a graphic picture, the wondrous deed which will ever live in story. Next came the Glee Club again with "As the moments roll," and after that Mr. E. Sansom in " Hamlet's mad scene with Ophelia." Mr. Sansom rendered this with much taste. Mr. Branson then gave " Blackeyed Susan," infusing a life and character into the favourite old ballad which elicited well-merited applause from his audience. Dancing was now resumed and was kept up with great spirit to the small hours of the morning. Mr. S. R. Dexter acted as secretary to the Ball Committee. We may add that the total number of couples present was about 50, and many of toilettes were of the most charming description. Miss Tbarme, of Ditton, who wore a chaste-looking grey silk, wasgenerally 'considered to be the belle of the assembly.
/ RUNCORN VOLUNTEER BALL—This annual gathering, which had been but indifferently advertised was held on Tuesday evening in the Public Hall, and very poorly attended.
HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT

SOCIETY.—On Tuesday, a meeting was held in connection with the above society, when Mr. Miller gave a good essay entitled " Progress," the following members taking part in the discussion :—Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. R. Tandy, T Wright, and J. Hancock. OAKLAND-STREET WESLEYAN YOUNG MEN'S MUTUAL IM- PROTEMENT CLASS.—The weekly meeting of this class was held on Wednesday, when Mr. S. Jackson read a very inter- esting paper on "Self Education." Mr. Jackson sketched lmiefly the progress of education generally, and among the children of the working classes especially. He pointed out how inestimable were the benefits to be derived irons cul- ture, even for those engaged in manual labour. He urged upon the young men present the necessity of self-improve- ment. The paper was listened to with interest, and at its conclusion a short discttssion took place. HALTON PARISH CHURCH. A watch-night service was held in this church on New Year's Eve. After the usual evening prayers the Vicar delivered an address on the words, "The night is far spent, the day is at hand," to a congre- gation numbering nearly 200 persons, composed chiefly of young men. Private Prayer was engaged in for five minutes., At twelve o'clock the bell was tolled twelve times, indica- ting to the parishioners absent, as well as to those present, that the old year was passing away aud the new year enter- ing in. After a few words of congratulation, and the sintr- ing of a hymn, the Vicar gave the blessing, and afterwards shook hands with each person on leaving the church, wish- ing everyone a Happy New Year. HOPE OF APPLETON LODGE 1.0.G.T. WIDNES.—On Monday the anniversary tea party of this lodge was held at the house of Brother T. Reay. About 30 partook of an ex- cellent tea, after which threcinewmembers were initiated. Mr. Bradshaw gave a report as to the progress of the Temperance Mission, which it is proposed to hold. Two sisters were appointed to carry out the necessary arrangements in regard to the public tea. The following appointments had pre- viously been made, viz, chairman of committee, Bro. T. Harrison, Past Worthy Chief Templar; vice-chairman, Bro. Rescord ; secretary, Bro. W. Bradshaw, W.S. ; treasurer, Bro_ J. Fearley. THE PLEASURES OF RAILWAY TRAVELLING.—A "Con- stant Traveller" writes to a contemporary as follows : Whilst travelling by the 2.45 train from Liverpool to Hart- ford this afternoon, in company with four other gentlemen, we felt and heard a row going on in the next compartment (third-class). Five men were in it, one a smallish, active man, an Englishman, the other four sailors, drunk, and seeming to be Frenchmen. The Englishman tugged at the cord hard :no result. He was on the point of being stabbed when he got out of the window, and held on by our carriage, the train going down the incline to St. Helens, not stopping till Warrington. We let down the window and he got in— a sober, decent young fellow. I asked him if he thought he was in danger, and he replied that knives were drawn, kc. We also tugged at the cord, no whistle. However, by holding out a red handkerchief, and pointing at passing ‘St. Helens, we pulled up a little short of Earlestown Junction. lam astonished that a company like the London and North- Western, second to none, should not devise a better com- munication between guard and driver.
