HOLY TRINITY CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL-The scholars attending the above school had their annual tea party in the Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening. About 220 scholars sat down to tea, the tables being presided over by the female teachers. Afterwards a magic lantern, lent by Mr. F. Dalton, was exhibited by Mr. James Harding, and afforded much pleasure to the audience, the comic scenes creating great merriment. The remainder of the evening was spent in games.

PLEURO-PNEITMONIA.—It was reported to the clerk of the peace at Preston, on Wednesday, that this epidemic had broken out on the premises of Mr. John Hodgson, Old Swan, Liverpool, among 14 cattle; and also on tbe premises of Mr. John Hampson, Breightmet Hall Farm, near Bolton, among a herd of 17 cattle. One animal, valued at £2O, has been slaughtered at each place by order of the local authorities.

PERFORMANCE OF "THE MESSIAH AT ST. HELENS. —The choir of the Independent Chapel, Orrnskirk-street, gave their annual performance of a piece of high-class music on Friday night, in the Independent Chapel. It is a hope worth cherishing—and one which will no doubt be fulfilled if a good audience is a sustainer of such an institution that this custom will long be perpetuated. This year the work selected was Handel's "Messiah," which is famous as the masterpiece of the great composer, and which alone would have secured for his name an enviable immortality. At this season of the year this magnificent oratorio can be heard in many places, and it is now regarded as one of the indispensables which combine to make the season the hap- piest of the year. A musical performance has to be repeated again and again, Mr. Charles Hallo says, to be appreciated ; and this is pre-eminently true of the works of the great masters. Though selections from the great works are often given, want of time and the necessary weight of talent prevent their more frequent performance intact. Great praise is due to Mr. Elliott, the leader of the choir, for his indefatigable efforts in bringing the grand oratorios more prominently before the public. Tha body of the chapel was well filled, but we do not say that the performance was perfect. This was not expected, for the efforts made to render the piece were not of a very ambitious character. In the first place the situation of the performers was not one whereby the best effect could be produced, and the chorus was not strong enough for the occasion. The solos were all sung in a satisfactory manner. Mr. George Barton sang the tenor numbers with his usual ability. Miss Hewitt sang in a sweet manner "0 thou that tellest." Mr. H. Parr, though not pos9essed of a very powerful voice for the bass numbers, acquitted himself creditably; and the concluding air of the first part was feelingly sung by Miss Sharpies. Miss Smith, in the second part, sang the contralto air "He was despised " with pathoQ, and in a manner pleasing to the audience. Miss Ray, of Wigan, who is possessed of a fine soprano voice, sang remarkably well "1 know that my Redeemer." Mr. James Houghton sang "Behold I will tell you a mystery," but the voices that accompanied him were a little too quick. All the solos were sung with care and precision, and the choruses, especially "The Hallelujah " and "For unto us a child is born," were well executed. Mr. Hayes presided at the organ, and Miss Ada Sharpies at the pianoforte. The instrumentalists were Messrs. Gardner (3), and Mr. C. Hewitt. A collection was taken ea behalf of the choir funds.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held- on Tuesday morning, according to a special resolution. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Messrs. Norman, Williams, Dr. McDougall, Fsiher, Meadowcroft, Handley, Briscoe, Whit- taker, Linaker (clerk), Barker (surveyor,) and Brookes (secretary).

div.head: TILE NEW YEAR.
div.p: TILE NEW YEAR.
The CHAIRMAN said that as that was the first time they had met in the year 1882, he had pleasure in wishing them all a very happy and prosperous new year.
THE ADOPTION OF THE FREE LIBRARIES ACf. -

The CHAIRMAN reported that on the 19th December a meeting of ratepayers was held in accordance with a requisi- tion presented to him, when the Free Libraries Act was adopted by over IC3 against ten votes.
THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The MEDICAL OFFICER'S report stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 15. Six were due to pulmonary diseases; four to abdominal diseases; four to brain disease; and one to peritonitis, representing a death rate of 12 per 1,000 per annum. Nine deaths occurred amongst children of four years and under, and seven under one year. Two inquests were held, making the total number of deaths 17. During the past month, Dr. Mouritz reported that he had inspected, and condemned from 80 to 1001bs of left fore-quarter of beef, and eight pieces of beef weighing 43 lbs. ; also seven heads and plucks appertaining to sheep. All this was totally un- fit for human food, and subsequently ordered by a local magistrate to be destroyed.—ln reply to questions from various members, it was stated that the diseased meat, which had been seized, belonged to a butcher named Mcilvoy, of Church-street.

div.head: TILE BRIDGE SLOPE.
div.p: TILE BRIDGE SLOPE.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee showed that the Law Clerk had had an interview with Mr. Berry as to the slope to the railway foot-bridge. It was re- commended that Staffordshire paving bricks should be us!d in the footways in Portland and Cawdor-streecs.—Toe CLERK said that all he was waiting for now in connection with the proposed bridge slope, was a communication from the London and North Western Railway Co.—Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. Williams seconded a motion in favour of the minutes being adopted.—After a brief discussion. in which Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Fisher, Norman, Meadowcroft, and Handley joined, as to the desirability, or otherwise, of using bricks instead of flags, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: AMENDED CANAL BOATS' ACT.
div.p: THE AMENDED CANAL BOATS' ACT.

The minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee were passed, on the motion of Mr. HANDLE; seconded by Dr. MCDOUGALL.-A question was asked by Dr. McDouGILL as to what action the committee were taking in regard to the amended Canal Boats' Act. If the matter was sub judice, he would not press his question.—Mr. HANDLEy replied that the committee examined the various clauses of the measure before the close of last session, and made certain recom- mendations or amendments, and before the House met again these suggestions would be sent to the members taking charge of the Bill.—Dr. MCDOUGALL suggested that it would, perhaps, be well to form a strong deputation to wait upon the gentlemen in London. He believed that, with a few ex- ceptions, they had more boats registered in Runcorn than under any other registration authority in the kingdom. Steps ought to be taken for making a strong recommenda- tion on the subject of the Act to Mr. Dodson, president of the Local Government Board. He (the speaker) considered it a considerable hardship upon local authorities, who had no means at their disposal but the local rate, that they should be so severely censured by certain individuals for not carrying the Act into effect as they ought to do. The mea- sure was art imperial one, conferring national advantages, and the cost of the inspection ought to come out of the im- perial exchequer.—Mr. HANDLEY considered that until they knew whether the Government were willing to take under their wing the amended Act, it would not be wise to bring the matter so prominently before them. He was of opinion that it would be well if the boats could be assessed, in the same manner as dwellings, so that a fund might be provided out of which to pay for their inspection. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD ON THE COMMISSIONERS'

div.head: FINANCES.
div.p: FINANCES.

The Finance Committee's minutes, which were approved on the proposition of Mr. FISHER, seconded by Mr. BRISCOE, contained the following letter, which had been received from the Local Government Board:—" Local Government Board, Whitehall, 13th December, 1881.—Sir,—I am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to the loan ac- count in connection with the financial statement of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, for the year ended 25th March last, and to enquire whether the 'Board are correct in assuming that the loans included in that account have all been raised under the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852. If so, it would appear frem section 14 of that Act that one thirtieth part of each loan should have been annually set aside as a sinking fund for its repayment from the date of the original borrowing. If, however, the loans in the Loan Account represent the whole of the moneys borrowed by the commissioners under the Act, it is clear from the fact that none of such loans have been repaid, and that the total sum in the sinking fund is only £4l4—that Vie requirements of section 14 have not been complied with. In consequence of the precise date of the borrowing of the several loans not being given in the Loan Account, the Board are unable to satisfy themselves of the amounts which sheuld now be standing to the credit of the sinking fund in respect of each loan. They request, therefore, to be furnished with a statement showing all the sums which have been bor- rowed under the Act since the date of its passing; the date when each sum was borrowed, and the amount which should now be standing to the credit of a sinking fund in respect of it if the requirements of section 14 had been strictly complied with. At the same time lam directed to enquire why the amount in the sinking fund has not been inserted in Exchequer Bills, or other Government securities in ac- cordance with the requirements of section 84 of the Commis- sioners' Clauses' Act, 1847, which is incorporated by section one of the Local Act, and on what ground it is considered that the loan of £6,000 stated in the Loan Account to have been advanced in the year 1878, may be repaid by way of annuity, and not by means of a sinking fund, having regard to the provisions of the last quoted sections. I am, sir, your obedient servant (signed), J. F. ROTTEN, assistant secretary." THE PUBLIC Lil 3 RAM( COMMIT TEE AT WORK.

The temporary Public Library Inmittee re ported that the Library Institute Committee hail given the comm. s- sioners possssion of the Runcorn Public Library. The diii mittee also recommended that the baolis belonging to the institute, numbering upwards of 370 volumes, should be pur- chased for the sum of £IB 103. Dr. McDouGAIL moved that the minutes be approved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, which was passed. On the proposition of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. Briscoe, it was resolved that the following gentlemen should form a permanent Library Committee :—Dr. Steele, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Hazlehurst, Handley and Briscoe; with the following outsiders, the Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. John Simpson, George Rhodes, Daniel Worthington, and Thomas Riley.

THE GLYCERINE WORKS. The CLERK stated that the proprietors of these works had applied for permission t 3 carry on the manufacture within the limits of the Runcorn Improvement Act. The proprietor was willing that Mr. Abbott, of Messrs. Daglish's works, St. Helens, should examine the manufactory and prepare a report to the 130ard. Mr. HANDLEY said that some time since a slight nuisance was caused through the bursting of a man sewer in one of the principal streets of the town, but now the liquid which caused this state of matters would be used in the manufacture of glycerine. The new works would employ about 70 people, and this would probably mean that they would be the means of supporting about 300 of the towns- people. He proposed that permiision be given to the pro- prietor to carry on the manufacture, subject to the provisions of the Public Health Act. Dr. MCDOUGALL concurred with the observations of Mr. Handley. The motion was then car- ried, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.
RUNCORN BRANCH.

The annnal gathering of the friends Of this flourishing mission, which is under the management of Mr. Shaw, who has now become what our American cousins would describe as " an institution " in the town, was held on Mordav even- ing, in the Mission-room at the Bottom Locks. The building had been decorated with evergreens and mottoes, and from the ceiling hung a fine specimen of a Christmas tree. There was a good attendance at the tea, which commenced at about six o'clock, and the ladies who presided at the tables were Mesdames Preston, Meadowcroft, Whittaker, and Shaw; Misses Barclay, Mouritz, 'Williams, Norman, Garrett, Clarke, and Davies. At the meeting which subsequently took place' the chair was occupied by Captain John Pearson, and amongst those present were the Rev. A. A. Edmondson, assistant chaplain to the mission; Mr. Meadowcroft, agent to the Bridgewater Navigation Co. ; and Mr. Ravrlinson. During the course of the proceedings, the Rev. A. A. Edmondson delivered an address. The speaker, who was received with applause, first expressed the great pleasure it , always afforded him to visit his friends in Runcorn. He ' hoped they would all have a very prosperous new year. He felt regret that Mr. Patrick was not able to be present with them, but he had been called away by sickness. Though not there in the body, he was quite certain that gentleman was with them in spirit. He should have been better pleased if there had been a larger number of flatmen present, as he always felt at home in addressing them, having spent a considerable time at sea himself. He served his apprentice- ship in the training ship Conway. and he read the speech lately made by the First Lord of the Admiralty on that vessel, with the greatest interest, as he felt sure it would prove of the greatest value to their seafaring population. His Lordship, in the course of his observations, said that the safety of this glorious country of ours did not depend on our ships of war, but upon our merchant sailors—those to whom the mission desired to take the glad tidings of the gospel. If they would give him (the speaker) five merchant sailors upon a small craft, and put twelve men-o'-war's men on a vessel of a similar tonnage, he would undertake to "beat " down the English Channel many days quicker than his opponents. (Applause.) The superiority of the merchant sailors arose from the fact that the man-o'-war's man only knew his duty in relation to a particular part of the ship, but the former understood whatever was re- quired to be done on his vessel. Some of. those present might be inclined to the belief that their merchant princes were a greedy body of men, but, from his exper a very different ience of them, he was of

opinion. In support of this assertion he stated that, through the contributions of the merchants, the mission had been enabled to give a tea to over 900 men in the city of Liver- pool—(applause)—and he believed that if it had been required for 1800 those gentlemen would have gladly found the funds without any grumbling. Some of them might be of opinion that their sailors were "queer fishes," but he reminded them that they were merely the creatures of habit, like their friends upon shore. Mr. Edmondson then referred to the custom of taking intoxicants which was such a besetting sin in the case of sailors, and urged those present who were in favour of moderation to consider whether they would not be taking a wise step if they be- came total abstainers. The speaker concluded by referring to the fact that now a sailor who loved the scriptures could sit in the public room at the Sailors' Home, Liverpool, and read them without suffering the least persecution from his fellow-shipmates, whereas five years ago he would just as soon have thought of jumping from the royal masthead as have done such a thing. (Applause.) Mr. MEADowcnorr, who on rising was received with loud cheers, expressed the pleasure it afforded him to see a gentleman in the chair who was so clearly identified with the work of the men. He (the speaker) was somewhat sorry to observe so few sailors present with them that evening. Mr. Edmondson had spoken about the operations of the society in Liverpool, and the temptations by which sailors were beset in that city. He felt that what that gentleman had said was, to a great extent, borne out by their own experience in the particular locality in which those present lived. One reason why he should have been gratified to see a larger attendance of seamen was that the Mersey missions were fostered, to a great extent, by the parent society in Liverpool. In Runcorn the operations of the missions were even more particularly identified with the boat people. In that town there was a large field of work for Mr. Shaw, and it was only he, and such as he, who were so closely connected with the port and the navigation who could understand the evils and the temptations asso- ciated with the life of boat people and sailors. He felt sure that if the spirit which Mr. Shaw had manifested from the very beginning of his work there were continued, and his labours conducted in the same honourable and legitimate manner, success would inevitably attend them. If there was one thing more than another which reminded him of the happy period of the year in which they were living, it was the annual entertainment the missionary provided. They generally found that a tea party was prepared for the adults, and a Christmas tree handsomely decorated with presents for the boat- children who attended the school, suspended in the room. (Applause.) He felt sure they would all cordially support the resolution he had to propose, which was that tbey should , give theic best thanks to those who had contributed to their evening's entertainment by presiding at the tables, and to I those friends who had so beautifully decorated the room. (Applause.) Not only did Mr. Shwa', and his fellow worl;ers deserve their be,t commendation for the efforts they put forth throughout the year, but the various religious bodies of the town owed something • to their missionary, and the noble society with which he was associated, for their labours in attempting to reach the masses of the population. They were quite aware that the ministers in the town—whether they were Church or Nonconformist—did not reach the class of people which Mr. Shaw and the mission with which he was connected did. He could quite understand that their ministers would not care, day after day, to go down in the cabins of narrow boats and other fiats and vessels, as the friends of that mission expected Mr. Shaw to do. He (the missionary) had supplied the want which was felt in years past, by coming into daily intercourse with the boat-people who had not previously been reached by the ministers of the town. It was on this ground that he was glad to see Mr. Shaw was so well supported by the people of Runcorn. (Ap- plause.) Mr. RAWLINSON, in seconding the motion, said he felt personally thankful to those who worked through the year in connection with that mission. He had heard of much spiritual good having been done in that little room. The resolution was carried with acclamation.

During the evening Mr. Rhodes recited "The Spanish champion," rather cleverly; Miss Wright sang several songs, and was repeatedly encored; Mr. Pierpoint played several solos in a most charming manner; and ikliss Pier- pointalso contributed to the vocal entertainment. Several youths, including Masters Parsons, J. Howard, and Roger- son, sang songs or gave recitations. We must not forget to notice the capital execution of the band, under the leader- ship of Mr. Wm. Cooper. On Tuesday evening, a tea was given to about 240 chil- dren, after partaking of which they were arranged in full view of the Christmas tree. The proceedings were com- menced by the fife band playing a tune, after which Mr. Shaw said that some of the children who had gained prizes were away with their boats up the canal; he should therefore place their prizes in a large tin box where they would be locked up until the children returned. He then wished them all a happy new year, to which the children re- sponded. Mr. Shaw stated that the whole of the presents on the tree had been given by kind friends, and many of the useful articles were not only given but actually made by the donors. They had over 200 prizes before them, and he would call upon Miss Williams and Miss Garratt to dis- tribute them. The tree was very soon dismantled of its varied and valuable fruit. knong the things noticed were scarves, stockings, shirts, sweets, pinafores and petticoats, cuffs and caps, dolls and dresses, gloves and garters, neck- laces, and nice oranges, &c., &c. Mr. Shaw was assisted in his task by Misses Williams and G matt, Messrs. T. Hough- ton, G. Howard, C. Mort, and W. Lewis.

div.head: -WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: -WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.

I The annual congregational tea party of this church took place in the Public Hall, on Monday, when between 400 and 500 persons partook of an excellent tea. The hall had been elaborately decorated with flags and banners around the galleries and on front of the organ, whilst on the platform were a number of plants supplied by Mr. B. L. Pierpoint, so that the room presented a very gay and festive appearance. The following is a list of donors of trays :—Sir Gilbert Green- all, Bart. (2), Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P. (2), Rev. W. and Mrs. Quekett, the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Mr. Arting- stall, Mr. Peter Stubs, Mrs. Willcocks, Mrs. Jones (The Elms), Mrs, Nicholson, Mrs. R. Faircicugh, Mrs. Tauranac, Mr. Gill, Mts. Toft, Mrs. Porter, Mr. C. White (2), Mrs. Carleton, Mr. Genno, Rev. F. W. Cory, Mrs. Mackie, Miss White, De. Sherratt, Mrs. Robinson, Miss Brown, a Friend, Mrs. Carter, Messrs. firibson, Miss Hesketh, Mrs. Brundritt, Mr. Walton, Mrs. Brooks, MI. Wright, Mrs. Dooley, Mr. J. Tinsley, Mrs. Hunt, A Friend, Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, Mrs. Ilarrison, Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Ellison, Mrs. Coates, Mrs. .J. Chrimes, Mr. Gill, Mrs. Webster (Bridge-street), Mr. Samuel Davies, Mr. Joseph Davies, Mrs. Webster (Dalton Cottages), Mrs. Burgess, Mr. Spinks, Miss Woods, Mrs. Francomb, Mrs. J. Grice Craik, Mrs. Moores. Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. J. Marson, Mr. Deavhurst, Mrs. Jones (Bold- street), Mr. Speakman, Mr. J. Naylor, Mrs. Cawley, Mrs. Fraser, and Miss Atkinson. After tea the Rey. F. W. Cory presided (in the absence of the Rector, who is indisposed), and he was supported by the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, J. E. Vernon, W. H. Williams, and J. H. Davies, ctc. The CHAIM! tic expressed regret that the rector was unable to be present owing to indisposition, which he felt certain all would regret, but when they considered his ad- vanced age they could not be surprised that he did not feel able to be in their midst. He was very much pleased to see so many present. Their presence showed that they would come together to back up the old parish church. (Hear, hear). Some persons regarded tea parties as nuisanc?s, and said the sooner they were done away with the better. He could easily understand why some people objected to them. They were very troublesome affairs, and caused some anxiety, as they were a kind of speculation. But he thought them the best things out, and there were several advantages connected with them. That party had been organised for the purpose of making up the deficiency in the chureawardens' funds; and he hoped the resn't would be that they would have a considerable sum to hand over. (Hear, hear). Another advantage in connection with tea parties was, that they brought all together in a social and happy manner. There was, he was sorry to say, a good deal of stiffness amongst the members of the Church of England, and tea parties had a tendency to rub off that stiff- ness. (Hear, hear). They enabled them, too, to unite their forces. They knew that union was strength, and that the resources of the Church of England were immense. Gather- ings of that kind brought into the foreground the eminent qualities of the fairer sex. That tea party was due to the perseverance and energy of the ladies of the congregation, and he was sure they were much indebted to them. He could assure the ladies that that debt was not forgotten by the clergy and churchwardens of the Parish Church. (Hear, hear). He hoped the tea party connected with the Parish Church especially would ever flourish, and that they would meet upon many more happy occasions: (Applause). Mr. A. MACKIE made a few observations, in the course of which he spoke in eulogistic terms of the Rector, after which the CHAIRMAN read a telegram from the Mayor ex- pressing regret that he and the Mayoress would not be able to he present. He wished also to say that Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall were sorry that they were unable to be with them, and had sent a very handsome donation. (Applause.) " The Merry Peasants" (Schumann) having been fairly sung by the Parish Church choir, and "Twickenham Ferry." (Marzials) rendered by Miss Ethel Vaughan, The Rev. W. H. WILLIAMS, of Padgate, delivered a brief address, in which he referred to the fact that they all had a work to dp in the world, and he hoped they would all do it. The Rev. J. H. Davies sang a song which elicited a hearty,, encore, to which, however, the rev, gentleman did not respond. A flute solo, " Adeste Fideles " (by desire), was given by Mr. Peers Brimelow, and Mr. Richard Fairclough then rendered "Nazareth" (Gounod). The Rey. E. C. E. Cenr..EroN afterwards adaressed a few words to those present. It would be cruel, he observed, for him to take up their time, as he saw from the programme that they had a good deal to go through. He should like, however, to say how, in common with them all, he regretted the absence of the Rector. (Hear, hear.) The church choir sang "Holy Night," after which Messrs. Dell and Caufield rendered "Excelsior" admirably. A song, "At Last," having been sung by Ethel Vaughan, Mr. Lester Barratt sang "That is what we want just now," which created much merriment. Mr. Barratt then gave imitations of Mr. Frederick Mccabe, and impersonated the "Gossiping Domestic" in a manner which elicited hearty applause. The other items on the programme were:—" King Christ- mas," Mr. Price; "My Sweetheart when a Boy" (by desire), Mr. F. J. Dell; "The Miller and the Maid," the Rev. J. H. Davies; flute solo, Mr. Brimelow ; "The Roll Call," Mr.

Canfield: "Old and Grey," Miss Ethel Vaughan; and " The Burlesque Band," the choir boys. Mr. Barratt baying given "Christmas" (a pretty, witty ditty), and " Valking on de Promenade," another amusing character song, the CHAIR- MAN briefly thanked those present for their attendance, and the proceedings terminated.
LATEST NEWS.

--...-_,... A Cupar Fife telegram says the hurricane is working great distruction there. Houses and other property are greatly damaged. The Cemtral News states that summonses were issued yesterday for a Cabinet Council to be held at twelve o'clock this afternoon.

Yesterday, a large police and military force dispersed a Land League hunt at Foxbro', North Tipperary. Several illegal hunts took place in King's County, yesterday. All the members of the Cabinet, except Lord Hartington, who was unavoidably absent, attended the meeting yester- day. The Ministers sat from two o'clock until a quarter to six.

At a meeting of Conservatives at York yesterday, the Hon. Guy Cuthbert Dawney, of Baldersby Park, was selected the Conservative candidate for the North Riding of Yorkshire, for the vacancy caused by the death of Viscount Helmsley. The gale was experienced in full severity at Leith. At a brick works, the chimney stack was blown down, killing a man named Peter Smith, and injuring two others. Damage has been done to property in the town.

Judgment was given in Glasgow yesterday afternoon, in the Board of Trade enquiry into the loss of the Glasgow screw steamer, Craigrownie, on North Rock, County Down. The master's certificate was suspended for three months, and that of the mate fcr six months.

Thomas Cogar, ex-Mayor of St. Ives, appeared on remand before the Camborne magistrates, yesterday, charged with obtaining money from the St. Ives Town Council by false pretences. The Government auditor proved that the books had been tamperei with, and the prisoner was committed for trial, bail being taken.

The Hon. Mr. Bourke arrived in London from Constantinople, yesterday morning, and later in the day called on Mr. Hyde Clark at the office of the:council of bondholders. It is uncertain as yet when a meeting of the bondholders will be callid to ratify the en- gagements made with the Ottoman Government.

Four further arrests were made yesterday in connec- tion with the murder of Patrick Sullivan, near Skibbereen. Two of the men had been previously arrested and discharged. The prisoners were brought before the resident magistrate yesterday, and committed for trial. A respectable farmer, named Wiggins, living near Longford, was sitting in his parlour with some friends, when a shot was fired through the window, wounding Wiggins and another man, and a Miss Burns. Five men have been arrested.

A violent hurricane prevailed in Scotland, yesterday. At Glasgow a house and large chimney stack were blown down and other damage was done to property of every kind. Many vessels at Greenock were damaged by the storm. The tide rose to a great height, backing over our harbours, besides doing great damage on the northern shore of the Firth, where the full force of the gale is felt. Coasting steamers are unable to make their usual journeys. At Port Glasgow the low-lying streets are flooded and completely impassable. Tlie water has flooded the graving dock, and from the timber ponds and ship building yards large quan- tities of valuable material has gone adrift. An Ardrossan telegram says the tide has risen to a tremendous height and flooded workshops and houses. The Post Office intimate that telegraphic commusication with Scotland is greatly interrupted. .

The Central News says .—The intelligence that an at- tempt was contemplated to remove the bodies of the Em- peror Napoleon the 3rd and his unfortunate son, the Prince Imperial, from their resting places in St. Mary's Church, Chiselehurst, has produced the most intense excitement, I especially in the district. It appears that on Monday last Monsignor Goddard received a private telegram from .France ' warning him, and all in charge of the remains, that an at- tempt would shortly be made to move them, and bidding him to beware of body snatchers. The message was rather vaguely worded, and it might have been fairly inferred from its terms that a futile endeavour had already been made. There are, however, no outward indications so far i as at present ascertP:inrA thalti".! Ci...'flllt ;ere being in afly. way disturbed. Every care has all along been taken to guard again' the commission of any such outrage as that of wil'lZ‘n Dunecht has been the scene; but in view of all the circumstances it has been deemed advisable to provide far additional precautions, and the police have been in- formed of the matter. A constable has been set to watch the church, and ta-day Inspector Phillips, of the metropolitan police, and one of the local inspectors, visited the building in accordance with instructions from the authorities, the object being to ascertain what further steps might be necessary for the 1 protection of the Imperial remains. In addition to other precautions it is now contemplated to connect the coffins by i means of wires with an elect' fc alarum placal in the ad- joining clergy house, Sand it is hoped that the steps proposed to be taken together with the timely disclosure to Mon- signor Goddard, will effectly frustrate intents of the would be thieves. The body of the Emperor lies in the side chapel within a granite mausoleum. To remove the coffin it would be necessary to lift a heavy block of granite weigh- ing about three tons, and then to disengage a solid slab of slate, which is cemented and 'morticed into the stone work of the lower granite receptacles. In the case of the Prince's remains the task would be more easely accomplished. The corpse still lies in the coffin under the pall just as placed immediately after the funeral in the side entrance porch, which has been there converted into a temporary chapel. There is an iron rail doorway having the entranf e to the &lurch Whilst the doorway has been permanently blocked up, the rail door is also blocked, and the Imperial' seal placed over the lock. No communication has as yet been made to the Empress respecting the matter, but the chief members of her suite have been informed of the circumstances, and the tele- gram has been laid before the Scotland Yard authori“, under whose orders the police will act in the affair. _

div.head: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL COTTON.—Spot: A fair amount of business has been done without change in prices. Futures: The market is dull, and Thursday's circular quotations are barely maintained. LIVERPOOL CORR.—The market opens with a moderate de- mand for wheat at about previous rates. Indian corn slow, without material chano —Second report: The wheat trade was quiet, and only a mederate business was done; prices car.- not be quoted lower, but the tendency was rather in that direc ne w mixedDira ‘Mp e rixtranEAT. closing_ Bat Beef: s. : MANCHESTER tion. Mutton: Ist cla-ss, 9d; 2nd, 8d to ; 3rd, 61-d to 7id per lb. Veal: Ist, class, 84d; 2nd, 7}d to 81d; 3rd, 6d to 6t-ci per lb. Bacon pigs: Ist, ; 2nd, 50 to 6d ; 3rd, 5d to sid per lb. THE CASE OF STEALING FURNITURE AT RUNCORN.—At the Kuntsford Quarter Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. Horatio Lloyd, Margaret Cooke, who had been committed from Runcorn on a charge of stealing a dolly, two sauce- pans, two tables, and other articles, the property of Mary Ann Allaby, was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment.

TREATS TO TELE AGED POOR AT WAP.RINGTON.—As announced in our last issue, Mr. B. Sheridan, in accordance with his annual custom, invited the aged poor men and women to see the performance of the pantomime at his theatre. A large number availed themselves of the kind invitation, on Saturday afternoon last, and derived much pleasure in witnessing the admirable performance of "Jack and Jill." Mr. Harmston also generously invited the old folks, together with the inmates of the workhouse and schools, to witness the representation of " Cinderella " at the circus, on Monday afternoon. The circus was well filled, and the audience was much amused and gratified with the excellent performance. The old folks are greatly indebted to Mr. Sheridan and Mr. Harmsten, through whose thoughtfulness they have been enabled to spend together two most agree- able afternoons.

PRESENTATION AT WYCLIFFE CRITRCIL —During the past year the Rev. John Yonge has taught a Bible class, in Wycliffe Sunday school, composed of scholars who had attained the age of 15 during 1881 ; and on Sunday last, at the conclusion of the Church service, he presented each scholar with a splendidly bound reference Bible, containing 1 index,i o g inscription :_" and d re Presented na tpes. li presen- tation with a suitable address. Each Bible had the follow- ing accompanied the pastor of the panred the Church with the affectionate desire and hope that as she (or he) has now arrived at an age to understand the need and value of personal religion, she will henceforth endeavour to live as a true disciple of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour, making this book a • lamp unto her feet and a light unto her , path'." The number of scholars who received Bibles,was 16.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

-- The monthly meeting of the Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Alderman Holmes, in the absence of the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), presided, and there were present Aldermen Davies, Kean, Webster, Chandley, Burgess; Councillors Brown, Greening, Platt, Mackie, Pierpoint, Collin, W'allington, Francomb, Woolfall, Ashton, Monks, Dixon, Sutton, Barker, Broadbent, Jeans, Ridgway, Litton, Whittle; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Charles Chorley (treasurer), T. Longdin (surveyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager). WITCH COMUITTEE.-THE CHARGES AGAINST THE CHIEF CONSTABLE.

The minutes of the Watch Committee comprised the fol- lowing :—That this committee, after having carefully investigated certain charges made by the Relieving Officer against the Chief Constable and other officers of the force, of neglect in the execution of warrants issued at the in- stance of the Board of Guardians, are unanimously of opinion that there is no foundation for such charges; and further, that this committee find that the Chief Constable, and other officers acting under him, have performed these duties in a most satisfactory manner. Alderman KEAN moved, and
Alderman WEBSTER

seconded. the adoption of the minutes. The CHAIRMAN said he had a conversation the previous day with the Mayor, who seemed to think that the charges that were made against Mr. Hunt were entirely without foundation, and that Mr. Hunt had acted correctly in refer- ence to the proceedings referred to at the last meeting of the Board of Guardians. Alderman WEBSTER remarked that this subject was referred to the Watch Committee for their consideration by the Board of Guardians. The Chairman of the Board of Guardians was a member of the Watch Committee, and he brought this question forward. The relieving officers attended before the committee and made their statements, and the committee also heard what Mr. Hunt had to say. After consideration the matter was adjourned. In the meantime many members of the Watch Committee took the opportunity of going down to the police station to examine the plan adopted on receipt of warrants. The cornplaint was that warrants were wilfully kept from the eyes of the officers, and given to certain favourite constables for execution in preference to others and to the injury of the service. On enquiry it was found that it was altogether a mistake, as the warrants were not kept back, but were generally pl:ced in a rack; and that from some cause or other the relieving officers must have been in error as to the plan they supposed had been adopted. They also discovered that so far from there having been any neglect in the service of the warrants, tke police had served this year three or four times as many warrants as were served during the previous two or three years. When the committee met again the Mayor very properly said he thought there was no necessity for any further evidence, and the committee were unanimously of opinion that there had been no neglect whatever, but that Mr. Hunt had discharged the duties of his office in a manner in every way satisfactory to the committee, and they expressed their opinion to that effect to Mr. Hunt. Councillor MacatE asked as a favour from the Watch Committee that Mr. Hunt might attend a committee formed by the Guardians to enquire into this matter. He thought the Guardians, certainly himself and others, sympathised with the spirit of the resolution; but it only seemed fair and just to the servants of the Board of Guardians, and also for the elucidating of some collateral issue in connection with the matter, that more investigation should take place. It had been suggested that there would be some difficulty in Mr. Hunt giving evidence, as he was not the servant of the Guardians, unless he was empowered or r, quested to attend by the Watch Committee. He (Mr. Mackie) suggested that the Watch Committee at their next meeting authorize Mr. Runt , to attend and give any information in his power, and, if they did, he was sure that that which threatened to be a very unpleasant affair, and which had consumed a great deal of printer's ink at any rate, would he amicably settled. Alderman WEBSTER said Mr. Hunt full understood the duties of his office, and the Committee could not object to anything of that sort, but if the thine.' was to be gone into again before another tribunal, it could not be expected. The CHAIRMAN remarked that the right course to pursue would be for the Guardians to apply to the Watch Com- mittee, and they could determine as to Mn Hunt's attendance. No doubt the application would be courteously received. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE.
div.p: STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Committee contained a resolution that the following plans be approved :—Plan of two cottages in Guardian-street, for Mr. John Ellison; of ten houses in Wilderspool-road, and of 21 cottages in Scott-street, for Mr. J. E. 'Wright; of streets on land in Battersby-lane. for the Warrington Land and Property Investment Co.—lt was recommended that the report of the Lighting Sub-Commit- tee recommending that alterations be made, and new lamps fixed, be adopted. Councillor BROADBENT proposed, and Councillor PLATT seconded the confirmation of the minutes.

Councillor WALLINGTON thought it desirable that the Gas Committee should see that the lamps were fixed as soon t possible !he for weather wa....( prevailing. Several j -se'ia wia-1,0-: persons had got into the water through want of light, and a gentleman had told him that day that two of his tenants had given him notice in consequence of having no gas lamp in Hamilton-street. The CHAIRMAN said that, after the adoption of the minutes, Mr. Paterson would at once take action. It was to the interests of the town that the lamps:should be fixed in this dark dirty weather. Councillor BROADBENT remarked that there had been complaints that the lamps were in such a dirty state that they did not give that light they ought to do from the quantity of gas burnt. Alderman CHANDLEY thought the Council ought to have more specific complaints—the streets in which the lamps were dirty—before they proceeded to alter them. Alderman DAVIES admitted that the complaints were justifiable, and said their new lamps had not had a proper chance of showing what they could do, from the absence of cleanliness. The CHAIRMAN observed that he received notice from Councillor Dixon a for days ago, that he should ask a question at that meeting as to the dirtiness of the lamps; and he (the chairman) took the npportunity of seeing Mr. Paterson, who admitted their dirty ezte. In consequence there had been an extra staff of men put on for the express purpose of cleaning the lamps, and the?. had, he believed, commenced opereions that morning. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then carried. Wool) P.4.YEUENT TOR SANKEY-STREET.

'The Paving and Sewerage Committee'q minutes contained the following resolutions:—That the pip mover in Museum- street be continued to the west end of that street; that that portion of Sankey-street from the opening leading to the George Inn to Castle-street be paved with wood; that the 'dors be removed from the following streets, and a bur 1,, ation put in preparatory to paving the same with sets: —Queen-street, from Market-street to the intersection with Bewsey-street ; Mersey-street, from Church-street to Napier- street. Alderman KEAN moved the adoption of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and Councillor WooixeLL seconded.

Alderman WF,BSTEE remarked that he was glad to find that, at last, the committee were about to try wood pave- ment. Efe hoped that it would be successful, and that the streets in the centre of the town would be paved in the same noiseless way. The streets were now crowded with vehicles, and the noise they made was so deafenisg, that it was almost impossible to attend to business. Councillor MACKIE referred to the rejection of a similar proposal 20 years ago. The committee weredoing perfectly right in trying wooden pavement in this place, and he would suggest that the pavement should he extended to the Park gates. (Hear, hear.) If the members when going home that night would notice how many pools of water there were in tEe street, they would see how unpleasant it was for those who used the footpath, to have to step upon the road, which they were often compelled to do, the footpath was so narrow. Alderman KEAN observed that the committee were paving this portion of the street as an experiment. The cost would be 15s. 6d. per yard, while they could get setts for Ss. 64.; and until they saw how the pavement would wear, they were not justified in covering a larger portion. The minutes were confirmed. DANGEROUS FOOTPATHS. Councillor MONKS called attention to the dangerous con- dition of the footpath leading from Mr. Litton's mill to Atherton's Quay. It had already been the cause of one death, and he should like to know what the committee pro-

posed' to do. Councillor Wfurrna remarked that the footpath under the iron bridge in Arpley was in a most dangerous state. Alderman KEAN remarked that the London and North- Western Railway Company had acknowledged their liability to repair the footpath to Atherton's Quay, and they were preparinv, to build a wall. Councillor 3losits: They are not doing it. Alderman KF.AN said he was informed they were. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee, the Inspector reported that 47 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guar- dians, and school fees allowed for 88 children; that 41 cases had been taken before the magistrates, when fines were in- flicted in 33 cases, two adjourned, and one warrant ordered. The report of the committee for the year ended 31st October, 1881, which was ordered to be printed and submitted to the Council, appears in another column. Alderman WEBSTER, who moved the confirmation of the minutes, remarked that the report would be found a ' satisfactory one. Conmillor DIXON seconded, and the minutes were carried. MTISEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The minutes of the above committee recommended that Mr. Councillor Williams be appointed the secretary. The report of the Curator for November, was as follows: —Visitors to the Museum 2,097, an increase of 303, as com- pared with November, 1880; volumes issued to subscribers 2,657, an increase of 83, as compared with November, 1880; volumes issued to teaders 1,065, a decrease of 67, as com- pared with November, 1880. The following gifts were re- ported, for which the thanks of the committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—From Mr. Wheeler, a dipper; Mrs. Lawless, a hake and a haddock ; Mr. John Peers, a brass snuff-box, "The Pope's deadly wound, 1635," and a parcel of old newspapers, &c.; Mr. T. Mason (Glasgow), eight cop- per coins; Mrs. Dutton (Penketh), nine copper tokens; Mr. W. Fell, plaster casts, made and painted by himself, of hali- but and green wrasse ; The Liverpool Engineering Society, their "Transactions" Mr. J. P. Ryland', F.S.A., his paper

on "Armorial bearings at Prescot, &c."; Mr. T. Fletcher, "Proceedings of the Society of Chemical Industry "•' Vice- Admiral Sprott, C. 8., reports on the Mersey, 1879.80; Mr. Beamont, photograph of vase (The Log) found by Captain Warren at Jerusalem. It was resolved that the marble bust, executed by Mr. John Warrington Wood, of William Beamont, Esq., be accepted with thanks by this committee from the subscribers on behalf of the Corporation, and that the same be placed in the Art Gallery. Councillor GREENING moved the adoption of the minutes of the Museum and Library Committee. Alderman WEBSTER seconded the motion. Referring to the presentation to the institution of a marble bust of their esteemed friend Mr. Beamont, he said it was not yet in its place, but he hoped they should find a better place for it in the gallery than that occupied by his portrait in that room. He was sure that everyone must be gratified when he said it was the latest work of Mr. Wood—(hear, hear)—and that the portrait was an extremely accurate one—a speaking likeness he might almost say. It would add very much to the attraction of the gallery. There was also an additional attraction in a picture which had been lent for a short period by Mr. Wood, R.A. He hoped the gift of the bust would not be the only one they should have to chronicle in their gallery of art, for he observed that in other towns, every now and then, there were very valuable gifts to simi- lar galleries. Much benefit was•to be derived from a gallery of that nature, and he hoped it would be appreciated as it ought to be. Councillor MACKIE observed that Mr. Beamont, Mrs. Bea- mont, Alderman Webster, and other members of the com- mittee, had given a favourable opinion of the bust, and if other members of the Council would express their opinion, which could be forwarded to the far off city of Rome, where our young townsman was busily plodding his way, it would cheer him on in his path, and no doubt rouse the proper emulation of other young men who might at present be un- known in Warrington, but aiming to rise in that particular walk. We had connected with Warrington several men of considerable fame, and at least one lady; and he hoped the day was not far distant when they, by the combination of their funds, or by some marked manifestation on the part of some person of wealth, might be enabled to see their works in the Museum. The works, for instance, of such as Mr. and Mrs. Fildes, Mr. Woods, and Mr. Edward Brewtnall, junior. Councillor BROADBENT said he thought the presentation to the town of the bust of Mr. Beamont was an important occasion. (Hear, hear.) It was not saying too much to say that Mr. Beamont was the most distinguished man in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) His personal influence raised ' the whole social tone of the town. Everyone was exceed- ingly proud of him, and they all admired him. (Hear, hear.) The presentation of his bust to the town was, there- fore, a gratification to all of them; and it was made more in- teresting by the fact that it was sculptured by a young dis- tinguished Warrington man. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES remarked that what had been said was only the expressed feelings of everyone in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN : I have no doubt at all. The minutes were passed.

div.head: STALLHOLDERS' PRIZES.
div.p: THE STALLHOLDERS' PRIZES.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Markets Committee, Alderman CHANDLEY said it might be as well to explain to the Council that himself aud the vice-chair- man had been charged with partiality in the discharge of a little duty. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) In awarding the prizes to the stallholders, they were not led by pink piper and flimsy decoration, but by what they considered a mar- ket ought to be, that of having the best show of rare articles by which the public might benefit, such as apricots, melons,. &c.

Councillor WooLrA.m. asked whether the money given in prizes came out of the pockets of the chairman or vice-chair- man, or was authorised by the committee. (Laughter.) Alderman CHANDLEY : I am happy to say ;it came out of the pockets of the chairman and vice-chairman. (Laugh- ter.)

div.head: EXPENDITURE OF THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE EXPENDITURE OF THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.
Tha minutes of the Sanitary Committee comprised orders for the payment of accounts amounting to £839 17s. 9d.

Councillor Morms moved, and Councillor SUTTON seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor WALLINGTON called the attention of the Council to the expenditure of the Sanitary Committee. (Hear, hear.) At the last Council meeting the accounts brought before them as having been passed by the commit- tee amounted to £1.317 55., and he saw that the amount this month was £530 17s. 9d. He thought an explanation was due to the Council in reference to this expenditure, which was becoming enormous. Something should be done to prevent such an expenditure as this, which would be more than £lO,OOO a year at the present rate. The CHAIRMAN.: I expect that the accounts which are found here are all given in detail in the minutes of the Sanitary Committee, so that Councillor Wallington or any other gentleman can easily get at any one of them. Councillor DIXON said at the last meeting a sub-commit- tee was appointed for the Longford depot, and Councillor Monks promised they should have a report, but be had not seen it yet, and did not know when it would come. He thought they should have an account of what was going on. Some two months ago he wanted to go to Longford, but Councillor Milner said he should not go, and he wanted to know if the time had come when they could go there. lie I hoped sor4e means would be adopted whereby such a heavy I expenditure as the ',7esent TAW be put a stop to.

The CHAIRMAN :1 think the question Councillor Wal- lington has put is a very fair one. Councillor MoNxs, referring to the remarks of Councillor Wallington, thought if the Council watched the Sanitary Committee they would do no harm. It was a committee which had a large amount of money to spend, and must spend of necessity: and he thought no harm could come of a vigilant watch being kept over their expenditure. He was satisfied, if the members of the Council thought the expen- diture of the committee was excessive, it would not be cur- tailed except by their watchfulness. To a large extent the Council was responsible for it; the Sanitary Committee were simply the executive of the Council to carry out the various works whieh have beea entrusted to them. (Hear, hear.) As to Councillor Dixon's remarks, it was quite time he had asked for a report. But Councillor Dixon had a very happy knack of asking for reports at a very inconve- nient time, and he had no doubt he smelt a rat, and probably with some cause. He did not stand there to say that every action of the committee had been wise, or that they had never made a mistake. He thought they were just as likely to make a mistake as any other committee, and what he asked the Council to do was to give them a fair trial. There were members on that committee who were not dis- posed to rush into a reckless expenliture, but were disposed to advance cautiously. It was not cDnvenient at present to give the report asked for, but he was satisfied as soon as it was possible to give that report it would be given. The minutes were confirmed,

•ias COMMIrtEts 1 Tht proceedings of the Gas Commitfe comprised orders for payment of accounts amounting to £6,173 4s. lid.; and accounts on gas extension account amounting to £693 Os. 6. Minute' that the Borough Treasurer attended and submitted the following statement of the money re- quired for annuities, interest in bond debt and instalments for repayment of principal due 31st December, 1881:— Half-year's annuity on 1,510 shares, £1,510: half-year's annuity on 2.953 new shares, £1,033 us.; half-year's interest on £22,200 loans borrowed to redeem annuities, £444—£2987 us. Cr. by cheque, 27t1e Sept., 1871, £2500 £487 us. Second instalment for the redemption of annui- ties, £2,040; half-year's interest on £5,350 bond debt of as company, £lOB 155.; half-year's interest on £38,050 loans borrowed for extensions, £761; second instalment of debt contracted or to be contracted for gas works extensions, and on bond debt of the gas company, at the time of transfer to the Corporation, in all £45,350, £907—£4,304 6s. Amount paid for extensions to 9th December, £42,275 13s. 4d. Recommendation: that the tender of Messrs. Meadows & Sons, of Rainbill, for the purchase by them of all am- moniacal liquor manufactured at the gas works be accepted. Resolved that the General Purposes Committee be requested to furnish this Committee with a ccpy of a plan of the Borough which Mr. Longdin had been instructed to prepare. The average illuminating power of the gas for the fortnight ended 9th December, was equal to 181 candles, and for the fortnight ended 23rd December, 18.30 candles. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said Councillor Dixon had spoken to him in reference to the basement of the lamp column in Church-street. There had been some misunderstanding between Mr. Paterson and Mr. Longdin about it, but he believed the matter had been put right. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion. Councillor DIXON thought the committee were very sharp in pulling the old lamp down, but they had had to ask two or tinree times to have it put right. As an old resident in Church-street he did not thank the Gas Commit- tee for pulling the old lamp down, and he was quite certain if the Mayor and Corporation went to church,as they did in years gone by, the committee would never have put up such an insignificant lamp. (Laughter.) There had been some remarks about dirty lamps, but no one had spoken about the number of lamps which gave no light. Until the lamps were kept clean and well lighted they would not get the benefit from them they ought to do. He thought for the very large amount of money which the Gas Committee charged the Corporation they ought not only to have the lamps kept clean, but burners which would give more light put in. Alderman WEBSTER said it would be thought from Coun- cillor Dixon's observations that the top of Church-street was left in darkness when the old lamp was removed, but such was not the case. One of the best lamps the commit- tee had was put down in its place, and had been burning ever since. When the basement was fixed the light would be just the same, and it was as good a light as could be desired.

ICouncillor Platt drew attention to the deposits which gas consumers had to make before they were supplied with gas. The charge was 10s., and be could not help thinking the Gas Committee was standing in its own light in making such a charge. A great many persons were not in a posi- tion to pay 103. at once, and he thought if the committee could see their way to reduce the charge, they would have an equivalent, in the shape of a larger consumption of gas, for any small bad debts that might be made. The CHAIRMAN said he thought he gave a reason why the lamps were dirty, and that he als stated the committee had adopted measures by which the complaints would be obviated. As to the lamps going out he knew they fre- quently did so, but he was informed every lamp in the town was lighted each evening, and if they went out it could net be helped. In reference to Councillor I'latt's remarks, he could only say the matter should be considered by the com- wittee. The collection of accounts from cottagers was a

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 7,1
