If there was any likelihood of obtaining an increased consumption of gas the committee would be very glad, as it was to that object the gas works had been enlarged. The minutes were adopted. THE FLOODS PRETEIITION BILL.

The Rivers C-o-rm-niCt-e:'; minutes contained following report of the deputation appointed to have an interview with the Salford Corporation upon the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill. On December 2nd, a deputation consisting of Alderman Davies, the Town Clerk, and Borough Surveyor had an interview with the Rivers Committee of the Corporation of Salford. Mr. Alderman Davies intro- duced the question of the "Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill, 1880," particularly clause 37 of the Bill, which proposes to permit the Councils of the Municipal Cities and Boroughs, having a population of not less than 25,000 inhabitants, making application to the Local Govern- ment Board to be formed into a conservancy board corres- ponding with the area of their municipal jurisdiction. He argued that it would be a hardship upon many districts and watershed areas if such a clause was allowed to form part of any such Bill. He also brought forward the frequency of floods in the rivers Mersey and Irwell durin the past few years, ani considerei that Salford was as mach Interested as the town of Warrington in co-operating to use every effort to obtain the carrying of a Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill during the next session. After expressions of opinion from the various members of the Salford Committee, who endorsed the opinions of Alderman Davies, it was unani- mously agreed that Salford and Warrington should join in furthering the object sought; and it was arranged that the' Chairman of the Salford Committee and Alderman Davies ascertain, if possible, in what manner and by what means the joint Councils could influence the promotion of a Rivers Con- servancy and Floods Prevention Bill during the coming ses- sion. Minute—That Mr. Alderman Davies intimated that the Local Government Board would seriously consider the question involved in the 37th clause before introducing the Bill next session, and it was resolved to send a memorial to the Prime Minister as under :—" To the Right Honourable the First Lord of the Treasury,—The humble memorial of the mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of War- rington, in the counties of Lancaster and Chester, under their common seal, sheweth—That your memorialists regret that the pressure of business in the House of Commons last session necessitated the temporary abandonment of the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill. That this measure, if passed into law, would be of the greatest benefit, not only to this borough and locality, but also to the country at large. That the floods which have increasingly prevailed of late years throughout England and Wales have seriously injured valuable properties and manufactures, greatly hindered the production of food in this country, and caused great national loss. That it is impossible to remedy these evils until the before-mentioned Bill or some like measure is passed into law. Your memorialists therefore most respect- fully and earnestly pray that Her Majesty's Government will introduce this Bill at the earliest possible opportunity in the coming se.sion of Parliament with a view to its becom- ing the law of the land. And your memorialists will ever pray, &c.—Jon x RICIIA.RD PICKMERE, Mayor; Wm. Hy. BROOK, Town Clerk."

Alderman DAVIES moved the adoption of the minutes, and in doing so remarked that he had had an interview with the Local Government Board authorities, and he was happy to say the clause of which they complained would receive the serious consideration of Government. On the suggestion of various towns similarly situated to Warrington in respect to floods, they had sent a memorial to the First Lord of the Treasury, and he thought they should impress upon him the absolute necessity of the Bill being brought forward during the next session. Only that morning the Mayor had se- ceived a communication from the Mayor of Wisbeach asking that another powerful deputation from municipal bodies should wait upon the Government and press upon them the importance of this Bill. They believed by so doing it would be one of the Acts that would be carried through Parlia- ment during the coming session. Councillor SrrroN seconded. Councillor MacKIE asked whether the memorial had been already sent. Ihe CITAIRMAN: It has. Councillor INlAcum asked did it not seem in the face of it rather strange that a memorial of such importance should be passed merely by a committee and sent to the First Lord of the Treasury, stating that it was "the memorial of the mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warring- ton." It struck him there was something which required a little explanation; and his complaint of the whole move- ment, so far as it had taken place in Lancashire and Che- shire, was that it had been thoroughly at fault. Alderman Davies and other large landowners in the neighbourhood were no doubt willing to protect themselves against floods, which, according to the reading of the minutes, seemed to have come more than usual of late years. But he could tell them there was a very strong opposition to the movements and the chambers of agriculture sent a deputation to Mr. Dodson on the subject a few months ago. He strongly recommended the Council to be very wary in supporting the Bill as a whole, and suggested that it was not quite the thing to send a memorial to the First Lord of the Treasury in the name of the mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the town, when it only came from the committee. If it had been sent in the name of the committee, there could have been no objection whatever. He assured them this Rivers Conser- vancy and Floods Prevention Bill was going to be a huge tax upon the people—not onlv ordinary ratepayers, but those 'ffho happened to hold small properties contiguous to rivers.

Alderman WEBSTER hoped the committee would not 'lose sight of a still greater work, which he thought would be more effective in preventing floods than any bill before Parlia- ment, and that was the ship canal between Liverpool and Manchester. He hoped the committee, if they ever had the opportunity of giving their hearty support to that measure, would not fail to do so. It would be one of the grandest things that had ever happened to Warrington, and would in itself be the greatest engineering feat of the age. Alderman DAVIES, in reply, said the memorial they had sent was exactly on the same lines as one the Council adopted in July last. As to his being a large landowner, he supposed it was said in ridicule. He was not a large land- owner, and he did not know that he suffered more than his neighbours in Latchford and Howley. These were parts of the town that suffered very severely from floods, and were totally beyond the knowledge of persons who were at places of business in Sankey-street, (Laughter.) It was the bounden duty of the Council to afford those people who had property within the borough all the protection they could, and save their property from being destroyed by these floods. He granted there would have to be a tax, but they must bear in mind that instead of it being inflicted upon Warring- ton alone, it was proposed that the large areas which con- tributed to the floods should be compelled to contribute. (Hear, hear.) The bill, if passed, would bring relief to Warrinzton, and property would be increased in value. The minutes then passed. •GENIIIAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this committee was held on the sth Decem- ber, when the Mayor having received a letter from the secretary of the University College, Liverpool, stating that the Corporation had the right of nominating a Governor of that institution, it was resolved that W,.n. Beamont, Esq., be recommended to the Council as the Governor to repre- sent the Corporation of Warrington on the Board of Governors of the University College of Liverpool. The minutes also contained a resolution that the Borough Sur- veyor as soon as posible complete the map ordered on the 22nd November, 1880; and also provide 10 copies. z, The minutes were passed on the proposition of the CHAIR- MAN, seconded by Alderman WEBSTER.

discretion of the Committee it- meant it would be at the discretion of the Council. If gentlemen had considered only for a moment the result of the resolution, declaring the resolution free, they would have found that it was like tying their hands behind their backs. He supposed it pleased a good many persons to think that the hospital would be free, but gentlemen should have considered that the hospital had been built at a cost of £7,000 or £B,OOO to the ratepayers of the town. He thought with Councillor Wallington the Sanitary Committea were spending at a tremendous rate. The result was that the improvement rate had risen from 2s. 61.—which for many years was considered a high one--;- to 3s. 6d. in the L. Notwithstandinc, this they decided the hospital should be free, but he thought they ought to have considered the manufacturers and shopkeepers, who had to pay the rates, and indigent ratepayers who were groaning under the rate. He agreed that the Sanitary Authority who had to deal with infectious diseases could not be divided. They could not have two authorities responsible for the same thing, and the Sanitary Authority of Warrington was the Sanitary Committee, who were armed, as no one else was, with a special Act of Parlia- ment enabling them to do the work. They were told the Sanitary Committee had acted rather harshly in one or two cases, but the Act of Parliament did not allow the committee to do what they liked in the matter. It was left to the discretion of the magistrates as to whether the cases should or should not be removed to the hospital. It might be absolutely necessary in the interests of the borough that a pauper should be removed. He was happy to say the Guardians had now providedample hospital accommodation, and they should act in consort with them. If the Guar- dians bad a patient they wished to be removed, the Council could remove that patient with the conveyance they had, :4cad the Guardians were quite willing to pay the Cost. From what be had heard, the Board of Guardians would be satis- fied with the motion in every respect, and they would be quite prepared.to pay any reasonable charge the Corporation might choose to make. Councillor WALLINGTON seconded the motion which he I thought was one the committee could take no Objection to 4Whatever. By the motion the charges were left to the com- mittee, and he had confidence they would do justice to the ratepayers and those who had to send their friends or chil- dren to the Infectious Diseases Hospital. He reminded the Council that a great deal of these burdens fell upon the pro- perty owners, and while the rates increased property had a tendency to decrease in value. It had been urged that those who were well off should be charged, but they, he replied, had to pay the rates now towards the maintenance of the hospital, and if it were free to anyone it should be free to them. There wereothers, such as weekly tenants, for whom a small charge should be made. It was unfair to put the burden upon the owners of property, as rents could not be raised now.

Councillor PLArr said the motion really resolved itself into two distinct motions, and he thought it should be divided so that separate votes could be taken on them. As to the first part of the motion that the resolution passed in December, 1880, making the hospital free to the inhabitants of the borough who were compelled to go there, should be rescinded, he thought before a resolution of the Council was rescinded, and especially a resolution passed only 12 or 13 months with an overwhelming majority, very good cause ought to be shown why it should be rescinded. To his mind the resolution of December, 1880, had worked exceedingly well. Theyall knew the state of excitement the ratepayers were in before that time on account of the hospital, and he thought it was stated that a great deal of the objection to the hospital would be obviated if the charge then made for the maintenance of patients was abolished. He thought he might venture to say that had taken. place. The hospital was now doing its work quietly and well. The prejudice respecting the hospital had in a great measure passed away, and be thought it was now most inopportune to endeavour to revert to the old state of things. He thought they had better leave well alone. He admitted the cost of the hospital was a heavy one to the ratepayers, but they would not reduce the cost very materially if they again charged for the admission of patients. During the 12 months ending 25th March, 1880, the total amount of money collected from the persons who had been removed to the hospital was only a little over £32, and it was no relief to say they would reduce the cost by collecting that amount. He would like Alderman Davies to say what should be charged, and what amount they were likely to recover from those who went into the hospital. He thought so small an amount as he bad mentioned was scarcely worth collecting, nor was it worth while to re-open au old grievance and bring about the state of things that existed in 1880. The resolution would leave the charges to the discretion of the Sanitary Committee. In 1880 he was a member of the Sanitary Committee, and he knew when the poor people came up they had to lay bare the whole of their circumstances; and he was going to say thecommittee held a sort of inquisitioa,but it was as bad as appealing against the Income Tax. It was then found that in the majority of cases the people could not pay, and the Council must not overlook the fact that nine-tenths of the persons who were removed to the hospital were the poorest persons in the town. He did not think at the time a charge was made any account was unduly pressed for, but the very fact that these accounts were hanging over their hands, and that they were brought before the com- mittee time after time was a hardship. The people had really to apply for relief from these charges, and he main- tained it directly tended to encourage pauperism. They learued the. process by coming before the committee time after time. (Cries of Nonsense.") His opinion was that they did, and he had am good an opportunity as any other member of judging. It also encouraged imposition, and if the motion was carried they would want an enquiry officer to ascertain what the means of these persons were. He gathered from his remarks that Councillor Wallington was in favour of the adoption of a sliding scale, but that would in- crease the difficulties in reverting to the old state of things. He thought there was quite enough difficulty in working the hospital at present without increasing it. It was very difficult for the committee to get people into the hospital. It was a hardship to those whose children had to go into the 'hospital, and it was a hardship to the patients themselves. They were taken from home and kept at the hospital until they recovered entirely or died. It was a sArt of imprison- ment for the patients, and if the Cot:Licit made a charge they would be treating them worse than criminals. Councillor LirroN said prison was not a proper word to

div.head: COUNCIL AND THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE COUNCIL AND THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

Alderman DAVIES proposed the following motion :—"That the resolution passed by the Council on the 7th of December, 1880, which reads as flllows That in future no charge be made for the maintenance and treatment in the Infectious Diseases Hospital of patients removed thereto under the powers of the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879,' and the resolution passed by the Council on the 6th day of December, 1881, which reals as follows :—' That pauper patients be not admitted into the Hospital for Infectious Diseases, and that the Town Clerk require each of the authorities having the privilege of sending their patients to the Hospital to forward with each case sent a written undertaking that such patient is not a pauper,' be respectively rescinded; and that in future the amount of charges to be made for the removal, maintenance, and treatment of patients removed to Infectious Diseases Hospitals under the powers of the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1878, be left to the discre- tion of the Sanitary Committee." After asking the Council to bear with him if he. went beyond what appeared in the motion, he called attention to the Board of Guardians and referred to their able clerk, Mr. Sutton. He said Mr. Sutton, as they were all aware, when he laid his estimates for the gear before the Board of Guardians, very properly and very ably called their attention to the purposes for which the money that was to be raised by the overseers was required. He told them amongst other things very large calls were made upon the poors' rate by that Council, in fact all the borough rate was raised out of the poors' rate; and he showed that a large amount of the money went for the payment of municipal work. Mr. Sutton very well illustrated the very wide difference there was between money paid for poor rates and money for municipal rates. He simply named the matter with a view to showing that there was in the minds of the Guardians and ratepayers a wide difference between the corporate funds and the funds of the Guardians. As to the Guardians them- selves he thought the Warrington Board of Guardians would bear comparison with any other union as to the treatment of their paupers, and attention to their duties. Regarding the Sanitary Committee, be knew of no body of men who had stock to their work better than they had. It had been very disagreeable, and perhaps the most difficult work connected with the Council, and he asked them before using hard words about the Committee to consider the difficulties they had to contend with. It was some satisfaction to him to know that their work was spoken of far and wide. Speaking of Mr. Gornall, he said he did not think that gentleman was the best tempered man in the world—(hear, hear)—but he was the most conscientious public officer he had ever met. If Mr. Gornall erred at all, he erred in over doing his duty. (Hear, hear.) He went on to say that if they could help it they ought not to allow the Board of Guardians and the Council to come into collision, and with that feeling he had I drawn up the motion. He felt that, on the sth December, I 1880, the Council took a wrong step. He thought election cries, when they became law, in nine cases out of ten became bad law. The first wrong step was in charging too high for the admiSsion of patients into the hospital, but there was not a single case in which any one could say the money ' was unduly pressed for. If they charged anything in the future it should be left to the discretion of the Sanitary Committee, but they must bear in mind if they left it to the

Councillor PLATT said the patients were confined there, and it was necessarily a hardship. The CHAIRMAN said he thought Councillor Platt should confine his remarks to the resolution. Councillor PLATT said he was endeavouring to show there was great hardship and difficulty in the way without put- ting a charge on the patients. It was a mockery to do so after they had undergone all that trouble. [Councillor Monks: It is imaginary.] It was not by any means an imaginary evil. If the action was taken for the benefit of the patients alone, then there might be some ground for the change, but the action was taken for the protection of the public, and the public ought to pay for their protection. He was persuaded if the motion was carried there would be far more resistance as to removals to the hospital than there was at the present time. Councillor PIERPOINT said he had always been of opinion that the hospital should not be free, and he thought it would be much better if the charges were left in the hands of the Sanitary Committee or a sub-committee appointed to deal with the cases as they went before them. He, therefore, should vote for Alderman Davies's resolution, though it would be much better if it were divided. Councillor Platt had made use of some harsh expressions against the unfortunate people who were com- pelled to go into the hospital. To compare them to paupers, or the hospital to a prison, was a sad mistake. (Hear, hear.) A person was only taken to the hospital so that the disease might not spread to others; and, if he were left at home, would he not be kept as isolated as he possibly could be, and kept a prisoner in his cot? Councillor SUTTON annsunced his intention of supporting Alderman Davies's motion. There was no doubt, he said, that the making of the hospital free was a party cry at the list election, and used throughout the whole of the wards for the purpose of obtaining votes—(hear, hear)—and it met with the approval of the ratepayers generally. He supported the resolution on that occasion simply because he considered that the hospital was built expressly for the poor people in the town, and that the sum received from people attending the hospital was so small that it was not worth considering. With reference to the second part of Alder- man Davies's resolution, he objected to that when it was passed, for the hospital was intended for poor people and those pauper patients--(cries of "No, no ")—for people who were receiving a small amount of relief. (Hear, hear.) Although Alderman Davies spoke very favourably of Dr. Gor- nall as being conscientious in the discharge of his duties— and no doubt he did discharge his duties to the best of his ' ability—there was such a thing as over doing their duties. Dr. Gornall was disposed to do all he possibly could to pre- vent disease in the town, but his great mistake had been that he had not been content with having his own opinion, but he wished to prevent the Sanitary Committee and the Coun- cil from having an opinion on the same subject. The CHAIRMAN : I wish to remind you that Dr. Gornall is not before the Council. It is a financial question entirely, so you will be kind enough to remember that. Alderman BURGESS: Mr. Gornall has nothing whatever to do with the resolution before the Council. It doesn't ap- pertain to his duties in the slightest degree. This resolution arises from a different matter entirely. Councillor SUTTON said that since Alderman Davies had mentioned the matter, he wished to show that the Council did not oppose Dr. Gornall in carrying out his duty. Alderman BURGESS: That has nothing to do with it. Councillor SUTTON (continuing) said the pauper cases were those most likely to spread infection, and the resolution passed a month ago was inconsistent with the objects of the committee. Councillor MoNias remarked that the matter was a very simple one, and had nothing to do with Dr. Gornall or any one else. (Hear, hear.) He should support the resolution for the reason that the Corporation ought, in his opinion, to bear the expense of the hospital, but ought not to be called upon to pay for the food which the patients consumed (Hear. hear.) The food cost the Corporation ss. to ss. 6d. per head per week, which was not a large sum to ask a per- son to pay for the support of a child in the hospital. And when they talked about poor people they must bear in mind that the people who pleaded poverty,did not hesitate to spend ten times the money in indulgences which he should shrink from. It wal not true that the hospital was built for pauper patients, and he hoped it would not be used for that purpose. It was the duty of the Board of Guardians to at- tend to their patients whether in-paupers or out-door paupers; but the Sanitary Committee would provide them with accom- modation, provided they would pay a fair and reasonable charge. Councillor JEANS said twelve months ago a great outcry was made against tba hospital charges, and he voted for their

div.head: use.
div.p: use.

abolition, and it would be inconsistent for him now to for their reimposition. The second resolution which tht. were asked to rescind he looked upon as mere waste papei. It had no operation in law. Alderman DaytEs remarked that it was not intended to make a charge for admission into the hospital at present. They were in a difficulty with the Board of Guardians, and, if his motion were carried, this would be removed, and the Guardians would be prepared to pay for their pauper patients. Alderman WEBSTER said if the ratepayers desired an im- munity from contagion they must be prepared to pay for it. The Act of Parliament gave the Council power to compul- sorily remove persons to the hospital who were unable to procure the necessary means of isolation, which showed that the hospital was meant for that class of persons who were too poor to provide medical accommodation. He was sorry Alderman Davies had proposed his resolution in that form, as, if passed, the Council would have no power in the matter. He suggested that it should be altered to leave the matter to the Sanitary Committee, subject to the approval of the Council. The CHAIRMAN: That is the case in every committee. 41derman WEl:sir-ER said that, after proceedings had been taken by the Sanitary Committee, the Council would be unable to interfere, simply because its powers had been delegated to the committee. Alderman BURGESS: Nonsense. Alderman WEBSTER suggested that the discussion be adjourned, for the Sanitary Committee to further consider the matter.

Councillor BROADBENT complimented Alderman Davies for the manner in which he had introduced his motion, and said he gathered from the report of the last Council meeting that there was a difficulty with the Board of Guardians. He was glad to know there was no difficulty—(hear, hear) —and that the Guardians had plenty of accommodation. (Several voices, "No, no.") He gathered so from the remarks of Alderman Davies.
Alderman DAVIES: I appeal to some of the Guardians if it is not so.
Councillor JEANS: They have accommodation for house patients, but not for out-door patients. Alderman BURGESS: What accommodation? They have none.

I Alderman DAvrEs : They are quite prepared to pay for admitting patients to our own hospital. Councillor JEANS: I have no doubt that the Guardians would admit any charge of that kind, but the sole Alderman BURGESS: This is .not the meeting of the Board of Guardians. (Laughter.) Let us have one person speaking at once. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Broadbent is before the Council at this moment, if you please, gentlemen. Councillor BROADBENT (continuing) said it seemed to him that an amicable arrangement could be made by which the Sanitary Committee would use the power which they possessed, but which the Guardians did not, and remove pauper patients suffering from infectious disease to the hospital for a reasonable charge. With regard to again imposing the charges on persons entering the hospital, he considered the arguments advanced in favour of this aboli- tion, still held force. Some injustice had been done to Mr. Platt. It was said he had used undesirable expressions. The whole tenor of his remarks had been a plea for the poor—that they should be admitted free to the hospital. He had used the word " prison " in this sense—that when persons were placed in the hospital against their will they were not allowed to see their parents or relatives; and to that extmt it had the nature of a prison. (Cries of "No, no ;" and Councillor Platt: It is.) Although he (Mr. Broadbent) sympathised with nearly all Ald. Davies had said, he should vote against his motion, for the reason that it would not answer what they wanted. They wanted the Guardians to have a hospital of their own, to which the Council, with the powers they possessed,. would help them to remove their pauper patients in proper vans. - The Guar- dians were Willing to pay for thatassistance, and he thought Alderman Davies's intentions could be carried out without resci ading the resolutions. Councillor JEANS wished to make an explanation with regard to the Board of Guardians. (Cries of "No, no.") There was no difficulty with the Board of Guardians ; they had their duties to perform with regard to relief A MEMBER: We must not go into this. Alderman BURGESS (to the Chairman) : Will you let the Board of Guardians arrange their matters and the Council theirs, and not have it discussed in this.way ? Councillor JEANS: I don't want to take up the time of the Council, but -- Alderman BURGESS: It is too bad.

Councillor Jeans resumed his seat, and Councillor FRANCOMB said: I should like to ask Alderman Davies, if the resolutions are not rescinded, whether the Sanitary Committee have the power to charge the Guar- dians for any pauper patients that may go into the fever hospital. Alderman DAVIES : No. .n. ful

Several MEMBERS: We have, most decidedly.— Alderman DAVIES: On the contarary, if you will allow me The CHAIRMAN : I think you had better sit down. • Councillor FRANCO3IB: If the Sanitary Committee have power to charge at the present time, I think it is a pity to interfere with the resolutions, seeing that we only get £3O a year. On this ground I shall vote against the resolution. Councillor GREENING said Alderman Davies had stated that the Board of Guardians were willing to pay any expense incurred in removing patients to the Workhouse hospital. He, as a member of the Board of Guardians, was surprised that such an arrangement should be made with Alderman Davies unknown to the Board. Alderman 'Davies was in possession of information which a good many Guardians had not, and he should vote against the motion. The hospital was for the people, and they must bear the expense. ,Councillor DixoN announced his intention of voting against the motion, seeing that the Sanitary Committee had in the past done some acts whith had been scarcely approved. (" No, no," and hear, hear.)

Councillor LITToN remarked on the small amount of money collected and the great inconvenience to the Sanitary Committee, when charges were made for admission into the hospital, and said he could not support the resolution.

Alderman BURGESS said he expected anything, that might fall from him would have very little weight. Gentlemen who had had no experience of sanitary matters, and had never seen the inside of the hospital, knew a great deal more about it and how it should be managed than any member of the Sanitary Committee, and much more than the Chairman of the committee, who had spent the last ten years in trying to bring it into as good a shape as he could. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) But with reference to the proposal before the Council now, it was quite true that it was not quite in ac- cordance with the stability of things that a conclusion deliberately arrived at twelve months ago should be rescinded, and he did not think it was desirable they should adopt such a course. But when they remembered that, only a month ago they decided that pauper patients should not be admitted into the hospital, and the Council were now asked to rescind that resolution, it appeared to him there was a weakness somewhere. Twelve months ago he was one of those who ventured to oppose the resolution declaring the hospital free. (Heir, hear.) He held the same opinion still, that it was not within the province of the members of that Corporation to do such a thing. It was an illegal act. (Cries of "No, no.") That was his opinion, although he knew the Town Clerk allowed the resolution to be passed, and to be enforced. He had a high opinion of the Town Clerk's legal knowledge and ability, and bowed submissively to what he allowed; but at the same time he had not been able to discover by what authority the Council took upon themselves to tax the people. (Hear, hear.) That was a thing that in his judgment they had no power to do. it had been said if they compelled people to go into the hospital to prevent the spread of the disease they were hound to pay the cost. That was. all very well to look at, but he maintained that the public of Warrington had done their share when they erected that hespital and paid for its main- tenance. It was not for them to take money out of the pockets of every ratepayer in the borough to keep a sick person in the hospital. (Hear, hear.) They spent money year by year on the institution irrespective of the cost of maintenance, and he contended they were not justified in charging the ratepayers with the maintenance of those per- sons using the hospital any more than they wonld be justified in asking for contributions to keep them in their own homes. For that reason, and for many others, he had no difficulty whatever, however unsuitable it might seem, in voting for the motion. Councillor Monks had referred to the charge of 16s. per week for maintenance, but they had ascertained that the cost was not nearly so much as that. But it was quite clear if the Council reduced their charges the Lymm Local Board and the Newton Commissioners would at once ask for their charges to be reduced, as they expected the Corpora- tion to maintain their patients at the exact cost. The charge of 163. was an all-round charge; and if a reduction was made they would have to reduce all the charges. The committee have acquired greater. knowledge since they last discussed the question, but infectious diseases hospitals were new, and very few people had had any experience of them. The Council would have to be patient. The persons to whom they committed the management of the hospital were expected to find out many things, but there was one thing he had to impress upon the young members, and it was that they did not know everything. (Laughter.) He should vote for the motion, although he was a member of the Sanitary Committee. He asked. the members of the Council to read over the second res9lution with very great care, so I that they might properly grasp its true meaning. They I would find .that it referred to patients besides those who I lived in Warrington alone. It was very much more exten- sive. So far as pauper patients and the Sanitary Commit- tee wefe concerned he had nothing to retract. He had never I had the slightat difficulty regarding the question, but he had always been ready to take into the hospital all patients I suffering from infectious diseases residing within the limits of the borough of Warrington. To show them that this was not a recently-formed opinion, he quoted from the minutes of the Sanitary Committee of September Ist, 1880, the following minute, "A deputation from the Board of Guardians attended the Committee to inquire whether the Corporation are willing to receive pauper patients into the Infectious Diseases Hospital, and if:so,upon what terms. After conferring, the consideration of the subject was deferred." On the 28th September, 1880, there was passed this resolu- tion :—" Referring to the inquiry of the Board of Guardians, made by the deputation which waited on the Board on the Ist September last, as to the terms upon which the com- mittee would receive pauper patients into the Infection Diseases Hospital, the committee, having well considered the question, determined that it is not expedient to enter- tain their proposal." He (Alderman Burgess) drew up that resolution with the object that, should the condition of things change,. they might, at some future time, receive patients of all kinds into the hospital on proper and equit- able terms, and tie believed that if the Bea:d of Guardians

the Board of Guardians they were—(loud laughter)—and not have pushed themselves into this matter, the difficulty would not have arisen. As a member of the Council, he should vote for the reception of people of all conditions who were suffering from infectious disease into tL "le hospital upon fixed and equitable terms. (Hear, hear.) might be asked why he, as a member of the Sanitary ' amittee, consented to this resolution which denied the Con • ssion of pauper patients. a4"1" ncillor JEANS: Well, it is certainly a most extraordin- Cou. lotion. ary reso ,an BURGESS: We are not now at a meeting of the Alderm.uardians. The sioners had entered with 'tie right in the interests of the Committee did not think If Alderman Davies would let ratepayers of Warrington. e, he thought the Board of the matter rest a little whi, nlanation, and possibly a way Guardians wouid give some ext. l could be satisfac- might be found by which the wh. o e thingHe should vote with Mr. torily arranged. (Hear, hear.) • not allow the coffers of Davies if only to show that he wont,. Warrington Corporation to be plut idered by Warrington Board of Gnardians. Onion of the Council Alderman DAVIES said if it was the opi s quite prepared that the question should stand over, he wa to consent, but, having heard what he bad to say, if the matter they majority of the Council considered it was a allowed to could decide at once, he hoped it would not be I: members hang over. After remarking that be thought deciding should wait until the end of a discussion before •emarks how they would vote, he proceeded to reply to the take to of the various speakers. He thought it was a great mis If describe the hospital as a place not desirable to go int ,olar he were stricken down by disease he would, give partic riot instructions for his removal to the hospital, as he did look upon that institution with that horror which had bee expressed. It was said that there was a great cry math against the hospital on accoult of the charges which were made for admission. That was a great mistake. On the contrary, the members of the Council knew that the great cry against people being forced at.° the hospital toJk place after the institution was made a free one. (Cries of "No, no.") He maintained that it did.

Councillor SUTTON: To a large extent it did. Alderman DAVIES : As to its being made a party cry, we all know that on the walls there were placards to this effect, "Vote for so-and-so and a free hospital." Councillor SurroN : On both sides. Councillor PIERPOINT : I spoke against it. Alderman BURGESS: It was " Vote fer Pierpoint, a free hospital, and no School Board." (Loud laughter.) Alderman DA.VIES: I think I must remind Alderman Burgess that this is not a Board of Guardians' meeting. (Laughter.) Councillor Platt had made some reference to the receipt of i'32 a year paid for admission to the hospital. It was not a question of £32; it might be a question of hundreds of pounds. As long as they had a resolution on the books forbidding them to charge anything, they could not charge the Board of Guardians who were prepared to pay. Councillor PLATT asked the Town Clerk if there was any- thing in the resolution of the 7th December, 1880, which would interfere with their making an arrangement with the Guardians to take their patients at any charge the Council thought proper to make ? Was there anything in the reso- lution to prevent them making an arrangement with the Guardians, without rescinding anything? The TOWN CLERK: Not as to the paupers outside the borough, but there is as to those in the borough. Alderm al DAVIES said the Council could net charge, then, for those persons who ought to be taken care of, and paid for, by the Guardians; and what they had been doing that night was with the view of avoiding a collision between two valuable bodies in the town acting in the interests of the ratepayers. So long as there was a free hospital the Guardians would be justified in refusing to pay for the admission of outdoor paupers. Sup- posing there were some outdoor paupers on Town Hill, and an epidemic broke out there, would they refuse to remove those people? If they did a Government enquiry would be keld quickly and the. Corporation, as the responsible authority, charged with neglecting their duty. If they did as he wished they wonld have power to charge the Guardians a reasonable sum for the maintenance in the hospital of either indoor or outdoor paupers. Alderman WEBSTER wished to adjourn the debate, but the Chairman ruled that that course con d not be taken. Alder- man Davies having repleed,

The motion was then put to a division when there vote 4 for it Aldermen Burgess, Davies, Chandley, Kean, Holmes; Councillors Monks, Brown, Wallington, Pierpoint, Sutton, Woolfall, and Collin against Alderman Webster, Councillors Greening, Dixon, Ashton. Francomb, Jeans, and Platt. The motion was therefore declared carried by a majority of five.

div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The following report for the year ended October 31st, 1881, was presented to the Town Council on Tuesday : "The committee are glad to be able to report that the average attendance of children of the several elementary schools in the borough is steadily on the increase, as will ba shown on examination of the accompanying return of attendances at the various schools. It may be pointed out that the average attendance for 1880, was 4,785, this year it is 5,422, an increase of 637. The average attendance at the end of 1877 (the year in which your committee was appointed) was 4,180, thus giving the very satisfactory increase in four years of 1,242. The average attendance just quoted, is confined to public elementary schools exclu- sively; but there are in addition 886 children attending private uncertified or non-government schools (including the Grammar School, the Blue Coat, and the Workhouse Schools) which will increase the attendance for the year, at both public and private schools to 6,308. Your committee have also much pleasure in submitting for the information of the Council the accompanying tabulated return of the number of children preented for examination in the several ; standards at the elementary schools. In 1880, the number presented was 4,738, this year the number is 5,207, being an increase of 469 children, for whom a Government grant is allowed ranging from 17s. to 21s. per head. The committee have held 21 meetings during the year, and have given case land attention tu the routine duties devolving upon them. 409 parents, representing over 600 hildren who have been labsent from school or irregular in their attendance, have been summoned before the committee, and due considera- tion given to the reasons and excuses submitted for such labsence or irregularity, and with the exception of 19 cases, in which the excuse was satisfactory, orders as to atten- dance at schools were made. 305 cases have been taken before the magistrates for adjudication, and in most of them fines were inflicted, amounting in the aggregate to £62.2a., in sums varying from 2s. 6d. to ss. in each case. Last year the number summoned was 180. The committee, whilst regretting the heavy increase in the number of prosecutions, feel that every endeavour was used before having recourse to this extreme measure, and that they were cases in which no other course would avail. Twenty-one incorrigible children (boys) have been committed to industrial schools during the year, of these 'l9 are now under detention (two having evaded apprehension), for which the Council contributes a sum not exceeding in each case 2s. 6d. per week. The Board of Guardians have allowed school fees during the year for about 500 children, amounting to £215 3s. 11d.; the amount allowed last year was £245 12s. The entire cost of the working of the department of your committee, taken from the Borough Treasurer's accounts for the year ended 25th March, 1881, was £162 14s. 7d., but from this sum there should be deducted the amount received for fines, £62 25., which gives £lOO 12s. 7d. as the total cost of the year; or including the school fees paid by the Guardians, £315 15s. 6d., which upon the present rateable value of £128,033 is considerably under a penny in the pound. The Council will remember that an application was made to the Education Department in June last for their sanction to a proposed reduction from the 3rd to the 2nd standard for par- tial exemption. The application was made to enable chil- dren over ten years of age to be employed as half-timers on passing the 2nd standard, and it was believed that that standard would fully meet the requirements of the district, and would not in any way interfere with the ultimate amount of education which should be acquired by the chil- dren. An opinion was also expressed that the relaxation would conduce to a better attendance at school up to the age of partial exemption. The Department, howevei, declined to sanction tha alteration. At that time there were about 420 half-timers employed in the borough, and there was a continuous demand for them but latterly this demand has decreased, and the number of 1:alf-timers is considerably reduced, the number at present in actual employment being under 200. Your committee cannot but feel that the results of their year's work are exceedingly gratifying, the more especially because they have been obtained in the face of many difficulties with which your committee have had to contend. The town has scarcely been free during the year from sickness and disease amongst children—skin disease, sore heads, measles, and scarlet fever having been very pre- valent. As many as from 70 to 80 children have been in- mates of the fever hospital at one time, and in families in which fever has occurred the rest of the children have been kept away from school upon the advice of the medical attendant until the sick members have recovered. In addi- tion to this the school attendance officers have had to use great pressure with careless and indifferent parents to com- pel them to send their children to school. In conclusion, the committee would draw the attention of the Council to the fact that the estimated number of children of school age in the borough is 6,900, and that there is school accommoda- tion for 8,314, or for 2,892 more than are now attending school. It may be further remarked that two .new elemen- tary schools will be•opened early in January next, which will afford further accommodation for 300 children, or a total of B,6l4.—Signed on behalf of the committee. S. M. WEBSTER, chairman.

This may be seemed at a cost of one halfpenny for a large breskfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated and starchy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest packet making fourteen breakfast cups of strong Cocoa.—Advt.

40, MARRIED TOO EARLY.—An awkward domestic difficultolf has arisen in Long Island, New York, and has aroused inuchh sympathy owing to the peculiar circumstances under whiclt it has occurred. It sees that a married woman, who f° 1 that her end was approaching, and who was unduly sol: one as to the fate of her six children, implored her hushanecdt yto marry her younger sister, she being the only-person fitt d in her eyes to take charge of her family. Her bus au promised to act in accordance with her wishes immediatelY after the funeral, and the sister also gave the sameProraise• The sick woman, however was not satisfied. She feared theY would not be as good as their word, and entreated them to_ give her the consolation of knowing that her children would. certainly be cherished after her departure. Worn out with her importunity, they finally consented to be married at once. Notwithstanding the boisterous state of the 11?eall„8/4a1 stiarge numbers of people turned out of doors on isat''"er,n night, and there were abundant signs of merriment kt h,tircigny houses in the town. The advent of the New Year is' N.". ..minently the season of rejoicing in Prescot, far more so lila at Christmas, for while on the latter occasion the re- ngs are attended with much solemnity, at New Year all il ` alloyed joy. In accordance with an old-established et, om the business in connection with the staple trade of tC own—watch movement making—has been suspended for hole of this week, and as there has been a considerable ict rovement in many of the branches during the past year, ill oubt the holiday has been thoroughly enjoyed. From early hour on Saturday evening bands of music paraded e streets, and companies of carollers assembled at the doors their friends to cheer and rouse them to a consciousness that a new year was at hand, and that prudence and fore- thought recommended oblivion of some scenes of the past, and hope and exertion in the future. While some spent the time in feasting and merriment, a portion of the towns- people spent the dying moments of the old year, and the beginning of the new, in devotion, there being special ser- vices at midnight at several places of worship in the town. Altogether the little town was, just as lively as it usually is on such occasions.

LITERATURE. \NAL, SPENT LIVES (London: Kegan, Paul, French, and Co.).—Under this title we have a brief series of modern biographies by Herbert Edmunds. The author says that the principle by which he was guided has been a desire to map out the different provinces in which the human mind has exerted itself in recent years to take from each an illustrious example of patient and successful toil, and in doing this he has produced an interesting and profitable work which is Well worthy of being placed in the hands of our young people. The biographies are well written, and being inter- spersed with pleasing and characteristic anecdotes form very attractive and serviceable reading for young men. The author has introduced the religious element in a very happy way with much good taste, so that it is entirely free from that peculiar style which renders the many written lives of good men tiresome reading. The examples of the modern Poet, general, philosopher, admiral, statesman, physician, schoolmaster, explorer, geologist, surgeon, lawyer, and the . man of business, have been admirably selected, and we hear that the work which has already passed through one edition Will be extensively read. It is well printed on good paper and bound in an attractive cover, forming an appropriate reward book or present. . HANDBOOK FOR WRITERS AND READERS (London: Whittaker and Co;)—This is a very useful triplicate little volume by Mr. L. C. Gent, who has evidently bestowed a very large amount of labour upon the work he undertook. The first part is a dictionary of daily blunders, containing a collection of mistakes often made in speaking and writing, corrected from the best authorities and conveniently arranged in alphabetical order. The second part consists of a handy book of common English synonyms, comprising about 33,000 ordinary words in general use; whilst the third portion is a handy classical dictionary. Each part has been got up with great care, so that the little work before us is one of great utility, whilst, by avoiding:repetitions, the author has managed to avoid bulkiness, thus rendering it _available either for carrying in the pocket or for general use. It is well and clearly printed and neatly bound in cloth. CHIPS (London: F. Warne and Co.).—This is a touching tale of Manchester life by Silas K. Hocking. It is an ac- count of the struggle for life of two little fellows, who, whilst surrounded by sin and misery, continue unpolluted. One ales and the other lives to be a successful gardener. It is a very interesting, moral story, well suited for boys and girls, and, as the book is nicely illustrated, forms a very suitable present.
