div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman), S. B. Chadwick, and C. W. Hazlehurst. A Wegrox PUBLICAN FINED.—Mr. Samuel Barrow, of the Royal Oak public-house, Weston, was summoned for , having at 12-40 on the morning of the 10th ult. kept his pre- , raises opened for the sale of beer to persons who were not ! krut-fide travellers, or lodging therein ; and also for having, ! on the same date, allowed beer to be consumed on the pre- j mises by the said poises—Superintendent Williamson saidl that at the hour and date mentioned, P.C. Cooper was on I duty near the defendant's house, and, hearing a noise, he tried the back door, and in the kitchen found six men with , half a gallon jug of beer upon the table and several glasses. I In reply to the officer, defendant said the men bad each had ' bread, cheese and ale before ten o'clock, for which everyone paid a shilling. What drink they drank after was given to them by himself, as his step-eon was leaving the Weston Chemical Works to take a situation under Mr. Kirkham.— P.C. Cooper was called and gave evidence in support of this state:nent, and added that the men found in the house were all labourers, and their names were Thomas Murphy, Henry Mclver, John Mahoney, George Scanlon, and John *McEwin. There were also John Carson, defendant's step-son, and another man whose name he did not know.—Mr.W.H. Linaker, who appeared for the defence, said that on Friday evening the men, whose names are given above, went into defend- ant's and had a chat with his step-son about his leaving the chemical works. As they had known him a long time, it was suggested that he should treat them. It was agreed that they should come round about nine o'clock, and they did so, when the men and young Carson joined together, paying is. each, so that they might have supper in the kitchen. About supper time, Carson went to defendant and asked him if his companions might remain an hour or two after closing time. He saiel they could do so, but it must not be as customers, but as guests; upon his (Barrow's) invi- tation. He thought if be proved these facts the Bench would be of opinion that though the police might have been quite justified in bringing the case forward, the summons ought to be dismissed.—The defendant, the labourers, and the young man Carson were then celled by Mr. Linaker.— Mr. Brundrit considered that the statement made by Carson,' the principal witness, was not satisfactory as to who paid for the various lots of beer supplied and the bread and cheese. —Thomas Murphy, Henry Mclver (who did not ap- pear), John Mahoney, George Scanlon, and John McEwin were then charged with having been on Mr. Barrow's premises at the time mentioned, daring prohibited hours.— Mr Linaker also defended in this case, and after P.C. Cooper had given evidence in it, said that his clients had not made any effort to conceal their presence on the premises, and surely a landlord had a right to enterta!n his friends like any other man.—The Bench considered the case was quite clear, as it was not reasonable that defendant should keep his house open until nearly one o'clock in the morning. For allowing beer to be sold on his premises at prohibited hours, - he would be fined 405., and costs 14s. 6d.; and each of the " men found in the house 10s., and 10s. 6d. costs each.— Saperintendendent Williamson observed that he would with- , draw the second charge against Barrow.—A warranted was granted for the apprehension of the labourer who had not appeared in answer to the summons. THE CHARGE AGAINST A " LIVELY " DOCK BOARD ENGINEER.—Mr. William Talbot Code, described as bolding a very responsible position under the Liverpool Dock and Harbour Board (and who, it is said, has lately come into a considerable fortune), living at Fairfield, and also having a residence known as Maretown House, county Wexford, Ire- land, was summoned by Mr. S. Yarwood, livery stable pro- prietor and auctioneer, Church-street, for using violent and abusive language to him on the 11th ult.—Mr. Bartlett, of Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. Bradley and Son, of that city), represented the defendant, who did not put in an ap- pearance.—The case was a remanded one, and, on it being called upon, Mr. Bartlett said he was paced in a somewhat difficult position. It would be remembered that when the matter came before the Bench a fortnight ago they were kind enough to adjourn the hearing to that day. He might say that he was scarcely actually appearing for Mr. Code, but for Messrs. Bradley and Son, who had instructed him to be present. After the case had been before the Bench on the last occasion, he wrote to Messrs. Bradley telling them what had happened. He had not seen any of the firm or the defendant since. On Thursday, he communicated with Messrs. Bradley, saying he would be present at the Runcorn court that day; and on Friday last defendant's wife called upon him and informed him that her husband was unwell. Since arriving in Runcorn he had received a telegram from Dr. Quinlan, 29, Lower Fitzwilliam-street, Dublin,. marked 10-45, that morning, and addressed to Captain Code, at that court. It stated that on the 17th December he carefully examined defendant, and found him too ill to travel over to England to give evidence. At that time he gave Mr. Code a medical certificate, and he would send another copy by post. He (Mr. Bartlett) had not re- ceived any certificate, and he must now leave the matter with the magistrates.—The Chairman said the Bench had received a telegram addressed to the presiding magistrate, which was seat off from Dublin on the preceding night, stating that defendant would attend the court that day.— Mr. Lake: It is very evident that he does not intend to appear, unless he is made to do so.—The Chairman: We do not want to act vindictively, if there is any prospect of his coming, but it is a question of whether kis conduct is not a contempt of court.—Mr. Lake: This is twice that he has taken no notice of your worships' summons. Will your worships issue a warrant, and, in the meantime, Mr. Bartlett may try his best to get him here ?—The Chairman (to Mr. Bartlett) : You know what we said to you on the last occasion P—Mr. Bartlett : Yes, and I was very much obliged to the PNleli for their courtesy.—The Chairman : Ma. Bartlett; You know, from your lengthened experience, that such conduct cannot be tolerated. I think I told you very distinctly that if he was not here, we should issue a warrant. He seems to be keeping away.—Mr. Bartlett : I am afraid, from what I have heard, that he is hardly re- aponsible for his actions.—The Chairmaa : We don't reflect upon you at all, Mr. Bartlett. Do you ask for a warrant, Mr. Lake ?—Mr. Lake : Yes, sir—The Chairman : We grant it then.—This concluded the proceedings in the case. SERIOUS DISTURBANCE ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.—John Jos. Halpin, a ticket collector on the Cheshire side of Runcorn Bridge, Peter Blease, platelayer, and Samuel Walker, bridge lamplighter, all in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, were charged with having assaulted Samuel Gibbons, 39, Suffolk-street, Runcorn. The defendants' case was watched by Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department. Lime-street.—There was a cross- summons, Gibbons being charged with assaulting Blease and Walker.—Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared on behalf of com- plainant and briefly opened the case, after which he said the Bench would see that the matter in dispute was one which affected the public who crossed the bridge. He should pre- fer that the hearing be adjourned.—Mr. Ferrand said he had no objection to offer to the adjournment.—On being questioned as to their willingness to consent to it, each of the defendants said he had a strong objection to such a course being adopted. They would much prefer that it should be proceeded with.—Mr. Linaker remarked that, under the circumstances, he would go on with the case.— The complainant said he was a " burnerman " at Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon's, Widnes, where he had worked a little over eight years. On Sunday, the 25th ult., he left his work about five o'clock in the evening, and reached the Run- corn side of the bridge about ten minutes past five. When he was on the middle part of the last girder, he saw the defendant Walker causing a nuisance, and two females were passing at the time. He told him that as he was a regular passenger across the bridge it was his duty to report him at the ticket box. Walker said, "It is all right. Wait a minute, and I will come along with you, as I am going that way." He walked with him a few yards, and when on the arches Walker strnck him on the face. He seized him, and they fell down together. The defendant promised that he would not touch him if he would allow him to get up. They then rose, but had not gone far when he again struck him. A struggle ensued, and it was only when the defendant pro- mised to go quietly with him that he allowed him to get up. When they got to the top of the steps Walker tried to throw him down, and for the third time struck him. He (witness) then defended himself. When they reached the ticket box Blease came out, and Halpin was behind him. Halpin said, "Hallo! Sam, is that you?" Witness replied, "Yes," and commenced to tell him what had taken place, when Blease struck him over the right eye. He was again struck from behind by Walker, and on claiming the protection of Halpin he kicked him on the side of the face, and told him to get out of there, he being then on his knees. He then became unconscious, and did not remember anything else. Witness as sober. He bad had a pint of beer to his .dinner and a glass of rum about half-past two.- -The cross summons against Gibbons was then heard.— Samuel Walker said he was a lamplighter on the bridge. On the 25th ult. he left his cabin, which was on the Lancashire side of the bridge, to light the lamps down as far as the ticket box on that side. He left Blease near the cabin, and on his return found that he had gone to the Runcorn side and had lighted the lamps. He followed, intending to see him at the Cheshire side, and when he was on the last abut- ment of the bridge he stooped down to tie his boot lace. Some one from behind took hold of his collar and held him. When he got up he saw it was Gibbons, who then seized . him round the neck. He said to him, "Hold, or you will have my bat in the river." They walked along the bridge for several yards, Gibbcns with his arm round his neck, when suddenly he struck him in the right eye, and threw him backwards over his leg. Gibbons then ran away, and he gave chase, overtaking him nearly at the top of the steps. He told him that he should give him in charge when they reached the box, and he said he could not do it. They struck each other, and they struggled together until they reached the steps. He (witness) stuck to defendant's coat, which tore in his hand. They rolled in a close embrace down the three fliahts of steps from the top to the ticket office.—By Mr. Linaker: He was at the Runcorn ticket box in the afternoon looking after it in the absence of Hal- pin, who was dining with a friend. While he was there he had one pint of beer, which be sent a boy for. About three o'clock Halpin returned with a friend, who was the ticket collector on the alternate shift; and they went to his house, where he (witness) had two glasses of whiskey and water.— Peter Blease said that OR trying to lift Walker off Gibbons .1 the latter kicked and struck him. He returned the blow, and kicked Gibbons on the leg.—By Mr. Linaker: He was quite sober, having only had two pints of beer and two half glasses of whiskev.—John Joseph Halpin said he should have stopped the fighting himself, but he was unwell, and that day was only his second time of duty after three weeks' illness. Gibbons then crawled on his hands and knees to - the box, and asked to be allowed to come inside the hut, stating that he claimed his protection. The row then being over he did not think it necessary, and told him so. Gibbons went down the steps and in about five minutes zetired, and threatened Walker. Walker went away to have

his wounds dressed.—Mr. Linake'r asked their worships to I dismiss the case against his client. It was true his evidence ' was unsupported by any eye-witness; but he asked the Bench to consider the facts on both sides. Gibbons had been at his work during the whole day, and was returning to Runcorn for his tea, intending to go back to Widnes. They had heard what took place, and on Monday he ob- tained a summons against the men. What had the other men done? They had taken no action until they knew they were to be summoned. If it had been an unprovoked assault surely they would have made a complaint of it to the officials in the first place. They had all been holiday- making, as they admitted.—P.C. Hibbert gave evidence as to going to Gibbon'shouse shortly after the row. He noticed the man had been; that he smelled of drink; and that there were two doctors in the place. The Chairman remarked that the case was one of those in which there was such a deal of contradictory evidence that it made it rather difficult to decide. They had, however, carefully considered it. As to Halpin they should dismiss the case, and also the summons against Gibbons charging him with assaulting Blease and Walker. They found that Gibbons had been assaulted by Blease and Walker, and as Walker was the first to begin the row they would fine him 20s. and costs, in de- fault a month's imprisonment with hard labour; and Blease 10s. and costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment with bard labour. Seeing that a representative of the Railway Company was present, he would ask if they did not think it time to station a policeman on the bridge. They had had many interviews with the company on the matter; and he might say that rows were constantly occurring on the bridge. The expense of putting an officer there would really be very little compared with the public safety, and he hoped that the suggestion would receive the serious consideration of the company.—Mr. Ferrand promised to lay it before the proper quarter.—The costs were 14s. 63. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Frederick Atkinson was fined Is. and 9s. 6d. costs, on the evidence of Sergeant McMichael, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire. AN UNRULY SON. A young man named William Thomas Peck was summoned for using threatening language towards his father, James Peck, cab proprietor, on the 30th nit. The complainant stated that the defendant was very unruly, and had been the cause of several very good men leaving his employ. On the 30th ult., he came to his house and took one of his younger brothers by the throat. He afterwards threatened to do him several pounds worth of damage, and he was afraid that he weuld either fir his buildings or damage his property in some other way.—The Bench said as the complainant was not afraid of bodily harm they must dismiss the case.—Superintendent William- son remarked that the case was a most painful one, and said the defendant had done all in his power to annoy his father. He had himself on two or three occasions tried to make peace between them, but to no purpose. He thought if the chairman would caution him it might have a good effect.— The Chairman said the defendent evidently did not bear a good character, and they must caution him to conduct him- self better in the future or he might rely upon it that he I would end by getting himself into serious trouble.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. Jobn Brundrit (chairman) and Mr. C. %V. liazlehurst. _

EXTRAORDINARY SCENE IN COURT.—STRANGE CONDITCT OF A LIVERPOOL GENTLEMAN.—At the termination of the above case, Mr. Wm. Talbot Code, of Fairfield (who is re- ferred to in a report under Monday's police), for whose ap- prehension a warrant had been issued, and who had for some time been occupying a seat immediately before that part of the court used by the general public, was asked if he had any application to make to the Bench.—ln reply to this question, put by Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, Mr. Code said he was quite prepared to go on with the hearing of the summons issued against him by Mr. Yarwood.—The Clerk : Your solicitor was here from Liver- pool, yesterday.—Mr. Code: I am prepared to go on with the case without a solicitor. I may add that I have tele- graphed to him to attend here, but, as I have no wish to detain the court, I am prepared to go on with it now.—,The Chairman explained that owing to some misunderstanding , the warrant ordered to be issued hai not been served upon Mr. Code, and the solicitor for the complainant (Mr. Lace), who was under the impression that the warrant was to be held over until the following Monday, to see if the gentleman appeared in the meantime, had left the town that day. They did not wish to take any unfair advantage of him.— Mr. Code explained that he had done all in his power, by by using the means offered throngh express trains and boats, to get to the court on the previous day, but had not been able to do so. He arrived on the previous evening. He was detained in Dublin on Sunday, having then travelled about sixty miles; and could not get any further because there was no mail boat. He telegraphed from Dublin to the Bench stating that he was on his way.—The Chairman said that Mr. Cede knew very well that he had to be at the court on Monday, and he should have started on his journey in sufficieottime to get there.—Mr.:Code asked, if the hearing was adjourned until Monday next, might he rely upon the warrant for his arrest not being executed ? Superintendent Williamson: I will promise you that if you appear it shall not be executed.—Mr. Code: I appear now.— The Clerk: Will you take him into custody, superintendent? —Mr. Code: You cannot apprehend me in court.—A police officer then went up to defendant and read over the warrant to him.—The Superintendent (to Mr. Code) : Stand in the dock, where the other prisoners stand, sir.— The Clerk: You are apprehended, under a warrant, for disobeying a summons that on the 11th December last you 'did peke use of certain violent and abusive language, cal- culated to incite and promote a breach of the peace.— Prisoner : I deny that in toto.—ln reply to the Clerk, prisoner said his surname in Ireland was Codd, and in England Code.—fhe Clerk: You cannot have two names. —Prisoner: Oh. yes; I can have twenty.—The prisoner, in reply to the Clerk, saki that with the permission of the Bench, he wished to have the else gone into that day.— Mr. Linaker, solicitor, on behalf of Mr. Lake, asked that the case might be adjourned until Monday.—The Chairman Mr. Code, you will be protected from any effects of that warrant if von appear on Monday next; but, if not, it will be immediately executed. You will be allowed out on your own recognizances. I may add that I certainly issued the warrant against you with the intention that it should be im- mediately executed, but there seems to have been some doubt about the matter.—The Prisoner: It was utterly impossible for me to attend here in time after I got my solicitor's letter. The Chairman : You are in custody before us now, and you will be remanded until Monday next.—The prisoner: Am I at liberty to leave Runcorn P—The Clerk: No; you are in custody now—Prisoner: Will you accept my own recog- nisances ? I know nobody here except justices of the peace, and they cannot give bail, except the Superintendent of Police will kindly do so.—The Chairman: We will accept your OWR recognisances of £2O to appear here on Monday next—Prisoner: I am willing to deposit a cheque with the Bench for that amount, or to fetch the money from the bank. I have no wish to withdraw from this case; I would not do so for £s,ooo.—Prisoner ultimately agreed to be bound over to appear, and then said that he had an application to make to the Bench. That morning he received the letter he now produced from Mrs. Jackson,of Wilson's Hotel, opened. He called her atttention to its condition, and she said it was delivered by Police-constable Bossons about 8-20. Witness went to the post office, and they said the letter did not leave them in that state. He then went to the s3perintendent of police and complained that the letter had been tampered with, and he said, "You are a liar and a most abominable liar, and a blackguard." The superintendent then toek him by the shoulder, turned him out of the premises, and said that if he came there again he woeld lock him up.—The Clerk: Then what is your application to the Bench P—Mr. Code: To report the conduct of the superintendent.—Super- intendent Williamson, addressing the magistrates, said the man before them was either labouring under some delusion, or he must be still worse—a rogue. That morning he received the letter along with his own, and he at once gave it to the policeman to take to Wilson's Hotel. Police- constable Bossons noticed at the time that the communica- tion was intact, and it was given into the hands of Mrs. Jackson, at Wilson's Hotel, who had since been seen, and she now said that when she received the letter it was intact, and that she gave it to Mr. Code in the same condition as it was handed to her. The statement of Mr. Code was all a piece of infamy from beginning to end; and that was not the first time he had come upon those premises with false charges. On one occasion he came to the office and made a charge that two of the constables had taken a great coat, a £5 note, and a number cf other articles. He said he was going to take out warrants against the men the very next day, but he had never been near a magistrate, unless it be to disturb him at his dinner hour. [Mr. Code: Don't be too sure about that.] He told Mr. Code to take out the warrants, if he thought proper to do so, but he had done nothing. Notwithstanding this, the defendant came before the Bench that day making these charges. Something would have to be done to make him behave himself like a gentleman, and not come to the police office as if he were something superior to everyone else, and claiming to have the protection of a policeman wherever he went. [Mr. Code Even a beggar can do that.] The police had suffered a great deal at the hands of this man, with whom he certainly at first sympathised, but now he began to feel considerable irritation against him.— The Clerk (to Mr. Code): Do you wish the Bench to issue any process ?-31r. Code said he desired to report tne matter 1 to the Bench, who could take what steps they wished in ' regard to it. He had no 'wish to take up the time of the court, but he certainly considered that a greater outrage was never committed upon him than that perpetrated by Mr. Yarwood.—The Chairman: That will be heard on Monday next, so that you will not now have anything more to trouble the police about.—Mr. Code (pointing to the Super- intendent) : This man came to me, put up his band in my face, and said " Don't you come to this court until Monday next ;" and my solicitor said, "This man is drunk, sir."— The Superintendent: I must certainly have an understand- ing that he will keep away from me until Monday next. He is an intollerable nuisance. I shall certainly have to take some stringent means.—This terminated the proceedings in the case. THEFT FROM THE STANLEY ARMS HOTEL—James McManus, a sailor, of Bangor, North Wales, was charged with stealing a sugar crusher, the property of Mr. Thomas Harrison, of the Stanley Arms Hotel, High-street; and with assaulting P.C. Noden.—Thievidence of John Henry Har- rison, son of the prosecutor, was to the effect thatabout six o'clock on the previous evening, the prisoner entered the house, and, whilst having some rum, he put the crusher in his pocket. He and bis father spoke to him with the object of getting him to give up the article before an officer was sent for, but he denied having taken it. Noden was called in, and the crusher found in the prisoner's pocket.— The constable said that the prisoner refused to go to the police station, and whilst on the way kicked him several times, and tried to throw him down.—Prisoner, in reply to the Bench, said he was so much under the influence of liquor at the time that he had no recollection of what took

div.head: lIMININIMIMMIIIIi
div.p: lIMININIMIMMIIIIi
place.—He was fined ss. and costs for stealing the crusher, and 10s. and costs for the assault, and in default of payirg the 2 is. ordered to be imprisoned one month, with hal d labour.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, senr. (chairman) and George Pilkington. Two LICENSED VICTUALLERS IN TROUBLE. - Jacob Mottershead, licensed victualler, Ditton, was fined 10s. and costs for having been drunk in charge of a horse and cart, on the 26th ult.—Thos. Barrow, landlord of the Wellington Inn, Ditton, was charged with having been drunk on his licensed premises on tha 29th ultimo.--P.C. Palmer said that at seven in the evening he went to defendant's house, and found him drunk and incapable, in the kitcheu.—Defendant : I never saw the officer on that day; and if I was drunk then, I am so now. —P.C. Peddar was also called, and said that when he called at the house at six o'clock the same evening, defendant was drunk.—Henry Lowe said he went to the house at a quarter past six in the evening for some beer, and defendant went in the cellar for it himself.—ln cross-examination, the witness said he would not swear that Barrow was quite sober at the time, but he was not drunk.—The Chairman said it appeared that defendant was some short time ago convicted for having been drunk in charge of a horso and cart, and the only con- clusion which the Bench could come to was that he was a drunken man, and, as such, unfit to have charge of a public- house. He would be fined 20s. and costs. They should not endorse the license, but request Superintendent Barker to see that the matter was brought before the notice of the Justices at the Licensing Sessions. ALLEGED USE OF THREATENING LANGUAGE.-Hugh Nixon was charged with using threatening language to Jas. Harrison, who lives in King-street, and is employed by the Widnes Metal Co.—Mr. Husband defended, and on Nix )n undertaking that he would not do any harm to complainant, the summons was dismissed.

CRUELTY TO A Hons.—Hy. Wynne, senr. was 'sum- moned for causing a horse to be worked in an unfit state, and his son was charged with driving it in that condition.— Inspector Allen, of the R.S.P.C.A., proved seeing the animal in Milton-road, on the 21st ultimo, when it was driven by defendant's son, and had upon each shoulder a wound about the size of a fiorin.—Each defendant was fined 10s. and costs. BREA.E.ING i STREET LAMP.—Robert Brown, aged 17, was summoned by the Widnes Local Board, who were repre- sented by Mr. W. T. Husband, for breaking a street lamp in Walmsley-street, and doing da.nage to the amount of 2s. 6d. —Evidence was given as to the facts.—Defendant said he hit the lamp by accident.—He was fined 3s. and Costs. STEALING A SHlRT.—George Pearson, a travelling stone- mason, was charged, en remand, with stealing a shirt from the house of Mary Ann Gill, Wellington-street, on the 29th ult.—P.C. Laing proved the case, and the prisoner threw all the blame for his conduct upon "the drink."—He was sent to prison 14 days. YOUTHFUL POULTRY STEALERS.—John Tower and Robert Knights two lads, were brought up, on remand, charged with stealing a hen, value 2s. 6d., the property of Wm. Harvey, Victoria-road.—Evidence was given by the prosecutor's wife and P.C.'s Laing and Pitt, from which it appeared that on Mrs. Harvey going to the hen-house on the 13th ult., she found the two prisoners on the roof. She seized Power, on which he struck her on the hand with a stick he carried so so that she was compelled to let him go. She gave chase, and caught Power, who attempted to bite her on the hand so that she had to free him a second time. She could swear to the hen produced, and also to Power, but not to Knight. On Laing apprehending Knight, he said "it was all right," as he was with Power at the time of the robbery. He also offere to show the officer where the fowl was. Power knocked its head off after escaping from Mrs. Harvey, and threw the body into a ditch. Laing went to a spot near the Cheshire Lines Railway station, and found the hen.— Superintendent Barker said the prisoners had been previously convicted, and the magistrates committed them for trial to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.— John Power and Catherine Power, husband and wife k parents of the prisoner Power) were charged with obstruct- ing P.C. Pitt, on the 30th December, whilst in the execution of his duty,•and with assaulting him at the same time and place. The Officer stated that he went to the house oc- cupied by the prisoners for the purpose of apprehending John Power, their son, on suspicion of having stolen the hen. He found the boy Power at home, and took him into custody, but when they got to the door he resisted, and his father and mother assisted him in doing so. Witness was thrown down, and one of the prisoners struck him several times. The female prisoner called to the neighbours to come to their assistance, and a crowd soon assembled. He at last blew his whistle, and it was only when assistance arrived that he was able to get the prisoner to the police station.—Both the prisoners denied their guilt.—Each of them was fined 10s. and costs.

A LUCKY FIT.-At the Monday's conrt, James Webbe was charged with travelling on the Cheshire Lines Railwln on the Ist January, without having previously paid his fare. —On the arrival of the 947 train from Manchester on Sunday evening at the Central Station, the prisoner alighted, and asked one of tbe railway officials which was the way out. He was shown the right direction, but on coming to the gate and seeing the ticket collector there he turned back. He afterwards tried to push past the collector, but his design was frustrated; and on being asked for his ticket he failed to produce one. He said at first he had come from Man- chester, but afterwards asserted that he had only travelled from Warrington. As he had no money, he was banded over to the police and locked up.—Upon the case being called upon on Wednesday, the police stated that the young man was in a fit, and it would be impossible to bring him into court—After some discussion with the magistrates, the representative of the company present, agreed to with- draw the charge on being told that the expenses incident to the prosecution would be borne by the county.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
Mol*DAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), the Ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough), and Major Cart-

„ wright.. THE BLACK LisT.—The following persons were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly between the 24th and 26th December :—John Duane, John Burke, Thomas Houghton, David Murphy, Michael Kennedy, .Thomas Kelly, John Baggaley, and Wm. Preston. DOMESTIC INFELICITY.—Wm. Cooper, an aged man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Wash-lane, on Saturday night, and also with assaulting his son, James Cooper, and with using threatt towards him.—Mr. Percy Davies defended the prisoner.—The prosecutor said his father was abusing his mother most shamefully on Saturday night, and threatened to shoot them all. His mother put his supper on the table, when he said if she did not take it out of his sight he would run a knife through her. He ran at her, and witness stopped him, getting two cuts across the hand whilst doing so. Prisoner had previously struck wit- ness across the mouth with the "flat of a knife.” Prisoner had often threatened his mother, and she was in fear of her life, as was also witness.—ln cross-examination, prosecutor said his father had offered to give him £2O to go away from the house, so that he " could do what he liked at mother." —P.C. Rowbottom proved that the defendant was drunk, land stated that the prisoner used threats towards his son.— Mr. Davies said he was instructed that the prosecutor was the cause of all the disturbance, and that defendant had offered him Ss. per week to live away from home.— Prosecutor, recalled, said his father treated thent properly when sober.—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk, and for, the assault he was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognizances of £5O. CAUGHT WITH THE Srom—James Davenport, a young man, was charged with having stolen, on Saturday night last, a bag containing old iron and broken flasks, of the value of 55., the property of Alfred Wright Brundrett, landlord of the General Wolfe public-house, Church-street. P.C. Monaghan met the prisoner in Horsemarket-street with a bag upon his back. His suspicions being aroused by the pri- soner's answers to his questions, he apprehended him.— Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was committed to gaol for two months.

FOWL ROBBERY.—Thomas Leatherbarrow, a labourer, was charged with stealing, from the hencote of John Stringer, baker, St. James's Street, three fowls value 63. The fowls were stolen on Saturday night; and the constable found them the same night in the house of a man named Mitchell, who however, denied any knowledge of the matter. While Mitchell and his wife were on their way to the police station, in custody, the prisoner met them, and acknow- ledged the theft.—He now pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. REHANDS.—WiIIiam Moran, a factory hand, John Kearns, (10) bottle maker, Charles Poliitt mill furnaceman, and Michael Flannaghan, were charged with assaulting a flat- man named John Lee, near Bewsey Lodge, at half-past one o'clock on Sunday morning, and stealing from him about 7s, a silk neckerchief, and a pocket handkerchief. Prisoners were remanded until Friday, as was also Wm. Ducking, who was charred with stealing 203. and a pocket knife from the person of John Ward, at Bank Quay station, on Saturday night. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Monks. BEER THE CAUSE.—Henry Buckley, a fustian cutter, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by assault- ing his wife. The prosecurrix said her husband abused her on Saturday afternoon, Sunday night, and on Monday Morn- ing, when she had to get up in her nightdress, and go home to her father's house, with her baby in her arms. Prisoner was drunk.—Councillor Monks (to prisoner) : I wish you could keep clear of the beer. You would get on much better. —Prisoner: Up to last Saturday I had not tasted beer since May and that made me worse.— Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognizance of £lO. UNPAID BOORS' RATES.-17 persons were sumn..oned, by the assistant overseer, for arrears of poors' rates, and an order for payment with costs was made in each case.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Davies and Chandley, and

Councillor Fairclough. REMAND.—William McGowen, an ironworker, w 'as charged with baying, in company with William Lurking, stolen florn the person of John Ward, at Bank Quay railway station, on Saturday night, 20s. and a pocket knife. Prisoner was re- manded. How THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY IS SPENT—William Lee was charged with leaving his wife and family charge- able to the common fund of the Union. Mr. Garnett said the prisoner was a stonemason, and able to earn good wages, but he had habitually neglected his family for two years. The family had cost the Union £3o.—Prisoner had been twice previously convicted for similar offences, and he was committed to 'gaol 3 months with hard labour. .

div.head: EXAMINER, SATtRDAY JANUARY 7, 1882. ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATtRDAY JANUARY 7, 1882. ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
SPECIAL MEETING.

A special meeting of the Town Council was held on Wed- nesday, the Mayor (Mr. R. Pilkington) presiding. There were also present Aldermen Johnson, Gamble, Cook, Mcßryde ; Councillors J. C. Gamble, McKechnie, Hanson, Jamison, Belsher, Twyford, Brook, Baxter, and Foster.— The TONVN CLERK said that the meeting was a statutory meeting to confirm a resolution, passed on the 9th November, to apply to Parliament for powers to obtain water from linowsley and Kimby. It was necessary he said to comply with the act of Parliament and confirm the resolution at a second meeting of the Council, after the bill had been de- posited in Parliament.—Alderman MCBRYDE moved a resolu- tion to the effect that it is expedient to promote, in the next session of Parliament, a bill to make and maintain additional waterworks, abd otherwise to promote the waterworks under- taking; and that the expense of promoting such bill be charged to the borough funds.—Mr. BAXTER seconded the motion, which was carried without comment.

communications were submitted to the first Council. mek,t. lug, and the Council then said what was proper to done with them.—Mr. FOSTER seconded the motion.— i Alderman JoHNsow did not see why it should be referred to the Parliamentary Committee. The Home Secretary asked for information and he (Alderman Johnson) thought that information should be furnished now. He was sur- prised that one or two of those resolutions had beep made by the county magistrates, who acknowledged that the business had not been attended to. Those who had an opportunity of sitting on the Bench knew that for a long time the duties had not been attended to, simply because there was not a sufficient number of magistrates. The county magistrates alleged that this was in consequence of deaths and other causes, yet they had taken no action. Was it reasonable that the town should go on suffering day by day in consequence of the county magistrates' neglect ? Alderman GAMBLE was understood to say that the magis- trates did not appoint additional ones.—Alderman JOHNSON said that the a agistrates could make recommendations which might lead to the appointment of additional magis- trates. He had nat had much experience on the Bench ; he might be wrong, and Alderman Gamble might be right, but he thought if recommendations were made they would be listened to. He had no hesitation in saying that the duties could not be performed to the satisfaction of the public at large as things at present existed.—Alderman GAMBLE suggested that the matter be referred either to the Parliamentary Committee or the next Council meeting.— Mr. BROOK: A resolution has been passed by this Council that a Borough Bench is required, and I don't see why the subject should be dealt with again.—The MAYOR: We have to consider this letter, and give certain information. It is in the ordinary course of business, and we must do it. —lt was decided to bring the letter before the next meeting of the Council.

div.head: ORDINARY MONTHLY MEETING.
div.p: ORDINARY MONTHLY MEETING.

_ The monthly meeting of the Council was held im- mediately after, the Mayor presiding, when there were present, in addition to the above, Aldermen Hadley and Harrison, Councillors Bishop, Co3k, Fisher, E. Johnson, and Massey.

UNIVERSITY COLLEGE. A letter W. 19 read from the honarary secretary to the University College, Liverpool, acknowledging the receipt of the Town Clerk's letter enclosing extract, which stated that Alderman Gamble had been appointed a governor of the college.

THE BOROUGH BENCH. A letter was read from the Home Secretary enclosing copies of resolutions which had been sent to the right hon. gentleman from the county justices. The letter pointed out the narrow majority in favour of petitioning the Crown for the establishment of a borough:bench, and asked for the ob- servations of the Council upon the matter :—The following is a copy of the resolutions passed by five county magis- trates namely, Col. Gamble, W. L. Evans, Esq., W. Pilking- ton, Esa., Dr. Twyford, and W. Blinkhorn, Esq.; and referred to above :—Special meeting of Her Majesty's Justices, held 28th day of November, 1881. A letter, dated 19th inst., from the clerk of the peace, enclosing copy petition to Her Majesty the Queen from the Corporation of St. Helens, praying for the appointment of borough justices, and which said copy petition we read and considered. Resolved as follows :—That in the opinion of the justices the state- ments in the petition, except those which allege that juotices would be brought more within the means of the inhabitants, and that pecuniary benefit would be acquired if a separate commissiot of the peace were granted, are correct. That the borough of St. Helens is of sufficient importance to have a separate commission of the peace if the Corpora- tion desire it, but this meeting is informed that the resolu- tion of the Town Council to petition the Crown for a Borough Bench, was carried by a majority of one vote only. , at the meeting at which such resolution was passed one member did not vote, and four members (including the mayor) who had, a short time previously, opposed the motion, were absent. That the inconvenience said to have been sometimes experienced, in regard to magisterial matters, has aria sm principally from the reduction in. the number of acting justices of the division by the deaths or incapacity of four justices, and the increasing age and change of residence of others who used to attend regularly at petty sessions, but who do not now attend. That there are no facilities for the disposal of magisterial business to be got by establishing a Borough Bench which might not be attained by the • appointment of additional County magistrates residing in or near St. Helens. 1 hat no advantage to the borough would result by the establishment of a Borough Bench. On the other hand, from the fact of the borough not including parts of the present Petty Sessional Division, some of which are really residential outskirts of the town, much inconvenience would be caused which is avoided under the present county arrangement. Moreover county justices would still have to hold petty sessions for the dis- posal of cases arising within the present Petty Sessional Division, but outside the borough."—Mr. MASSEY observed that although the letter was received by the Mayor on the 17th that was the first occasion on which it had been brought before -the Council.—Mr. BROOK: I should like to ask, Mr. Mayor, who called that meeting of magistrates:—The MAYOR: I suppose that they have a right to call their own meetings, Mr. Brook.—Alderman GAMBLE thought the question ought to be answered.—Mr. BREWIS (town clerk) : i The magistrates' clerk convened the meeting n Pursuance of a request of the clerks of the peace who required the in- formation for the Lord Lieutenant. All the magistrates of the division were • summoned.—Mr. MASSEY said the matter had come upon him quite by surprise. He did not want to say that the communication was deliberately kept back so that it might come as a surprise. But he would point out, as a fact, that the Parliamentary Committee met on the 21st Dec., and that committee all along had special cognisance and management of the matter. A resolution was passed by the Council ; by which the getting up of the petition was referred to the Parliamentary Committee. It was drawn up, and afterwards submitted to the Council, and •approved. His point was this: That all along it had been perfectly well-known to the Parliamentary Committee, as a committee which had, and ought to have, to do with the matter; and he said deliberately tbat the Mayor's communication which was received on the 17th September ought to have been sub- mitted to the Parliamentary Committee, as it would then have had the advantage of appearing in the minutes, and if thought desirable, any member of the Council could have framed a resolution upon which that Council could have taken some action. Mr. Brook's question was a very per- tinent one.—The MAYOR: That has been answered.—Mr. Massey. : Well, I didn't say it was not, sir.—Mr. MASSEY, continuing, said that if they reviewed the circumstances they would find that the weight brought against the motion was simply from those interested—the county magistrates, men • who, he supposed, sought to continue the old system, and to keep what they might consider the government of the town in their own hands. The magistrates naturally were against it. He did not blame them if they considered it their duty to look after' their interests—pecuniary or otherwise. Those were the gentlemen who initiated that meeting, and in high-flown language which meant nothing at all tried to convey some- , thing which was scarcely the fact. They would find that I the document was got up by five magistrates who were the magistrates for St. Helens, and those were the gentlemen , who with others had given it their strenuous opposition, with the exception of one, he believed. The resolution of the Council must pass by, because according to the hole-and- corner meeting there was one of the Council who did not vote; and perhaps there was no one better able to give them reasons than Dr. Twyford himself, who, while believing that a borough bench was for the benefit of the town, at the same time did not care to vote against his brother magistrates. Pehaps, if he had followed the dictates of his conscience at the time. Dr. Twyford might have favoured them with his vote. The members of the Council were the conservators of the public interest, and knew better than anyone else what was of benefit to the town. And when the Town Council passed a resolution it ought not to be interfered with by county magistrates; and he viewed! the interference of those gentlemen in the proceedings of the I Council with disapprobation. He would not like to make I use of a stronger expression, although it was on the tip of his tongue. But there were opinions in the town that would be expressed in a stronger fashion than his. 'The resolutions of the magistrates distinctly alleged that the change would in no respect be better for the toren. He thought that was a very erroneous assertion,and one which would not bear the test of argument and the light of day. If one simply mentioned the question of fees it was sufficient. It was universally admitted, not only that the fees of the county were excessive, but high, as compared with those in borough courts.. No one could doubt for a moment that they were excessive. If the old system were continued they would be taking from the pocket of suitors something they ought not to pay, and putting it into the pockets of some- body else who Ought not to receive it. The object of the Borough Bench was to administer justice cheaply, and the question of expense could not be ignored, as it was at pre- sent a burden and injustice to the town. When the Act of incorporation was extended to the town, they took a step which gave them the right of governing themselves. What they wanted now was to complete what they had begun, and govern themselves entirely. Why they shou!d have gentlemen from Widnes, Woolton, and Liverpool to sit in judgment Over their fellow townsmen he did not know. It could not be that the townspeople bad greater confidence in those from a distance than in those who were acquainted with and understood them, and who were more likely to be sympathetic than a. etranger was. He would urge that the Town Clerk write in reply to the Home Secretary stating that the resolution of the Council was not passed on the spur of the moment, but that it had actually been twice under discussion; that the grievances complained of had been seriously pressed on the notice of the county magistrates, who promised to remedy the nuisance arising from an insufficient number of magis- trates or irregularity of attendance; that they had six months' time to do it in, but that no steps were taken; that the Council feeling that the ratepayers and the town were suffering, took advantage of what the Act of Parliament in• vited them to do—petition the Crown for a borough bench of magistrates. This had been done, and he would suggest that the facts be placed before the Home Secretary, and that his particular attention be called to the fact that only five magistrates attended the meeting; that two of the gentlemen were members of the Town Council, and that one opposed it very strongly; that the others were gentlemen who lived away from St. Helens; that Mr. Pilkington very seldom sat on the bench, and that Mr. Blinkhorn was not a very active citizen, and not a very active magistrate. And also that the Council still adhered to what they had done a being to the benefit of the town.—The MAYOR said the meeting termed the. hole-and-corner was called by the Clerk of the Peace; and it was called to elicit information res- pecting the petition that the Town Council had sent. As to the communication being deliberately kept back he was exceedingly hurt. .It was not deliberately kept back, and on no sooner occasion was it proper for him to bring it before the Council. It was not for him to bring it before the Parliamentary Committee. It was now brought before the Council as a maycr's communication, and he strongly repudiated the statement of Mr. Massey who, no doubt, made it thoughttessly (Hear, hear.)—Mr. MASSEY: I said it was open to the Fomment that it had been deliberately kept back. If it is many way hurtful to your feelings that it was uttered even in that way—(Colonel Gamble. Nonsense, and Mr. Massey sat down without finishing the sentence.)—Alderman C. 00K moved that the communication be referred to the Parliamentary Committee. All mayor's
i That

div.head: SMOKE NUISANCE.
div.p: THE SMOKE NUISANCE.

A communication to the Mayor was read, stating that a conference of manufacturers and members of the Council had been held, and that it was moved by Mr. Harris, seconded by Mr. Thomas Pilkington, that the manufacturers exert themselves to use every possible means to abate the nuisaace caused by the emission of black smoke, and that the Council be requested to allow reasonable time to elapse before instituting legal proceedings ha the matter.—The MAYOR said it was quite evident from , that resolution that no such meeting as that intended to be held a fortnight after date of the conference, was necessary. It was no use holding another meeting,!as the manufac,urers had already given their answer.—Alderman JOHNSON asked what was meant by a "reasonable time." One person might effect his object in a certain time while another might not do anything at all. —Dr. JAMISON did not think it necessary to hold another meeting, because each pledged himself to do something which was satisfactory so far as he knew. He would propose that the adjourned meeting of the Council and manufacturers be not held. If they accepted that resolution, would the Council have power to do something with the incorrigibles P—The MAYOR observed that if the Council tied itself to time it would make the matter far worse.—Dr. JAMISON : Will the Health Committee have power to deal with it after this ? The MAYOR: You have full powers now, doctor.—Mr. BELSIIER seconded Dr. Jamison's motion.—Dr. TWYFORD: I should like to ask whether our action now will interfere with the resolution moved by Alderman Gamble on a recent occasion, that the consideration of the matter be adjourned two months. If this resolution is passed will it interfere at all with the other ?—The MAYOR: The thing fits in per- fectly well. No action can be taken until February. Mr. Alderman Gamble's resolution carries us on to that time, and if the Council wish to do anything, the Council can do it in the first week in February.—Dr. TWYFORD thought it would have been better to have given them some definite time. —The MAYOR• The Council can carry out anything it chooses to do, after the time mentioned in Alderman Gamble's resolution.—The motion was carried.

div.head: LORD MAYOR AND IRELAND.
div.p: THE LORD MAYOR AND IRELAND.

A letter was read from the Lord Mayor of London, calling attention to the influential meeting held recently in London, on the subject of rendering aid to the law abiding people of Ireland, and asking the co-operation of the Mayor and Coun- cil in the matter.—No remarks were made on the subject. THE GAS &C. DEPARTMENT.

Mr. T. Coos moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Gas Committee, including a statement by the manager that, during the past month, 14,676,000 cubic feet of gas had been produced at the works, of an average illuminating power, ascertained by 25 tests, equal to 1967. sperm candles. INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL. On the minutes of the Health Committee being brought forward for confirmation, Alderman MCBRYDE said that the Medical Officer's report stated " The people of Sutton are dissatisfied with the water supplied to them. They com- plain of it being very hard, and one ratepayer says it has affected his health." Mr. Mcßryde said that the water from Collins Green was thoroughly mixed with the Eccleston water before it reached the town. It was the same with Windle, and it was alike all round the town. So far as he knew the water had not affected the health of the people.— The MAYOR: They have quite forgotten the fact that it goes nto the Brown Edge water.—Dr. TWYFORD : I am very glad of this explanation, because there is a general idea in the town that it is not mixed.— The minutes, which were con- firmed, contained the following resolution :—" That the fol- lowing scale of charges be adopted for use of the Infectious Diseases Hospital: The sum of is. per day for every patient whose wages when in work (or, in case of a child, the wages of whose parent or guardian when in work) do not exceed 205.; the sum of is. 3d. per day for every patient whose wages when in work (or, in case of a child, the wages of whose.parent or guardian when in work) exceed 205., but do not exceed 255. per week, and so on, in proportion to the wages of the patient (or parent or guardian of the patient as before mentioned), with a maximum of £2 2s. per week; the above charges not to include the provision of medicine or medical attendance."—Dr. TWYFORD said what the patient would get at the hospital would be simply more nursing. THE RAILINGS IN FRONT OF THF PARISH CHURCH. . _ _

Alderman COOK moved, and Mr. FOSTER seconded, the confirmation of the Parliamentary, &c., Committee, in which were comprised a report of a committee who waited on Canon Carr with respect to the removal of the Parish Church rail- ings, and that he had stated that the removal of the railings might be brought about in consideration of the payment by the Corporation of the sum of £250. The Surveyor pro- duced the minute book of the late Commissioners, and the report book of their Surveyor, and read therefrom extracts relating to the matter. He stated that he had ascertained that the Commissioners had spent £l5B 2s. f3d. in respect of the forming and making of the present footpath in front of the church in erecting new gates and palisades and pointing the end of the church under an arrangement between the Commissioners and Canon Carr. The deputation was requested to saek a further interview with Canon Carr and the churchwardens on the subject.—Alderman JornrsoN asked for what purpose another interview was sought?— Alderman COOK: To see if we cannot get it on better terms. He wants £250, and we have already spent £l5B 2s. 6d. on that improvement; and we think, taking that into considera- tion, that he should not ask us to give £2so.—Alderman JOHNSON. remembered when the arrangement was entered into. It was understood that the ground was to be thrown to the street. These rails were kept up afterwards, Dr. Carr refused to have them taken down, and then the Commis- sioners tried ta approach Dr. Carr for the purpose of making arrangements. It was, however, considered that the amount required for their removal was exorbitant, and the matter dropped. Now the matter was taken up again. Formerly It was £2OO, and now it reached £250. His opinion was that they should not give anything for the rails, and that they should come down.— Mr. Herssore : I would suggest that we get a provisional order to compel their removal, and let Dr. Carr prove that he sustains £250 worth of damage by it. I don't believe for a moment that they are a positive improvement to the church; and for him— I won't express any strong language.—Alderman GAMBLE: I think Alderman Johnson does not correctly remember what occurred in the time of the Commissioners. I am quite satisfied that the sum paid —XISB 2s. 6d.—was for for ming and making the present footpath in front of the church, which was no benefit to the church, and/or 'pointing the end of the church. The point- ing was necessary, and in consequence of haying taken down two little houses which existed between the church and St. Mary's-street. He recollected very well that Dr. Carr did not give up the land in front of the church, but only gave up the right of passing over it.t-Alderman JOHNSON said that when a person gave up land instead of being paid for the land it might be that the authotities agree to pave and flag and do all that was necessary for the land given up. And so it was in this case with the exception of pointing the end of the church. The idea of the Commissioners was to throw open to the street the street the whole of the land. They fixed railings a few inches from the wall of the church, and afterwards they found that Dr. Carr had not taken down the railings, which now are at the edge of the parapet. —Alderman GAMBLE said that Dr. Carr did not take down any of the railings, and it was not fair to say that Dr. Carr had failed to take them down, and claimed money. Dr. Carr, he was satisfied, had carried out the necessary arrange- ments which the Commissioners expected he would. carry out. Dr. Carr simply maintained the rails there to show that he had a right to the land.—Alderman HARRISON said that Alderman Johnson was nat correct with regard to Canon Carr's giving up the land. The land, he believed, measured 140 yards. He was one of the Commis- sioners at the time, and McManus was the surveyor. He believed the agreement was not carried out according to the churchwardens agreement, and so Dr. Carr retained the railings there to show that he had a claim on the land. It was extraordinary if the land was not worth £250, when other parts of the town were widened at a Cost of between £2,000 and £3,000. It would be a great advantage if the rails were removed at once, espe- cially as the tramways were now constructed.—Mr. T. COOK said that they had the minute book, and it was re- corded in the minute book that the rails were left standing. —Alderman JOHNSON still said that the understanding was to remove the rails. He emphatically asserted that Dr. Carr could not foreclose the land. the money had been spent for an object, and that object was to widen the street. That /and, he said, belongs to the public, and the public had paid for it, and were now using it. It was only a narrow strip upon which the rails stood that the amount was asked for, and it was not fair to say that the whole of the land was for that amount. No improvement was so expensive.—Mr. MASSEY : Pay £250 for something which ie simply a nuisance and a danger ! It should be the daty of this Council to make some arrangement, or take some action which will ultimately lead to this being removed.—Alder- man JOHNSON : The public already have the right of using that footpath. It is public property beyond all question, and cannot belong to Dr. Carr.—The MAYOR thought it was a duty which the Parliamentary Committee ought to dis- charge. He felt that the rails were an eye-sore and ought to come down.—Mr. FOSTER characterised the price asked
for the land as abominable. Dr. Carr could not sell the foot- path as it was a part of the street.—The minutes were con- firmed.

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT WHISTON. On Friday, a meeting of the ratepayers of Whiston was held in the National School, to consider the adoption of the Small Tenement Act. Mr. T. Molyneux presided, and there was only a moderate attendance.—The CHAIRMAN thought the adoption of the Act would be advantageous.—Ml'.l.llNT inquired whether the adoption of thA Act would benefit all parties, or only the landlords, the guardians, and the assis- tant overseers, who had promised to take the rates from the poorer ratepayers by instalments of 6d. and is , the same as the previous collector' Mr. Watkin, had done. *e thought the assistant overseer had more interest in getting the AeL passed than anybody else.—Mr. RANGE emphaticallY dis- claimed Any such interest, and said it did not matter to Dim which way he took the rates.—After further discussion, the CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the Act, under which owners of property, viiere the rateable value does not exceed XS, shall be rated to "Jae poor in future, instead of the occu pier.—Mr. WiLnitaitAm CLouGH seconded.—As an amend - ment, Mr. LUNT moved that the Act be not adopted, and this was also seconded.—On being put to the meeting, the ill its was lost, only the mover and seconder voting - its favour. -

TOWN HALL COMMITTEE. •11 The minutes of this committee, which were unimportat t, were confirmed.—Alderman GAMBLE complained of the,eL, Town Hall Keeper being in his shirt sleeves and lighting asa fire at 10-40 that morning, while the girls where making a tremendous dust in the Mayor's parlour. He considered that was not according to the contract, which stated that he should be dressed at eight o'clock.

div.p: _THE PAVING OF -CHURCH AND RAVEN STREETS.

Alderman GAMBLE drew attention i(Ttlre—s;aight line between the pavements of the Tramway Company and that of the Corporation; and the SURVEYOR being called in, he said it cost about £6O above the original estimate to pave the sides of the tramways and obviate the straight line.— It was decided to do this, the cost not to exceed £5OO.

div.head: LIBERALISM AT RAINHILL
div.p: LIBERALISM AT RAINHILL

' The importance of clubs as a means of uniting the party has been fully recognised by the Liberals of South-West Lancashire, and the interval since the last general election bas witnessed the establishment of Liberal clubs in many parts of the division. Not the least successful of these clubs is Rainhill Reform Club, which, after being in existence only three months, has a membership of 150. The club at present housed at the Victoria Hotel, Rainhill, but it seems that a number of the Liberals, were not disposed to join the club in its present quarters, as the officials have received an intimation that there will be a considerable influx of mem- bers so soon as they establish themselves in premises of their own. Success as also attended the club in financial matters, and the members are in the happy position of being free from debt. A re-union of the members took place at the clubroom, on Wednesday evening, when over 30 gentlemen sat down to dinner, served in excellent style by the proprietor of the hotel, Mr. Peter Foster. Afterwards the chair was taken by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, and the vice-chair by Mr. W. Evans, and amongst those present were Messrs. McKenzie (secretary of the Prescot Liberal Club,) G. Tompkinson, W. Lowe, W. C. Rawlins, dr.c. The loyal and patriotic toasts having been duly honoured, Mr. McKErrztE proposed the toast of the "Rainhill Reform Club," and coupled with it the name of Mr. W. Evans, the secretary. After expressing the pleasure he had in forming the acquaintance of the members of the Rainhill Reform Club, he remarked that he had been the instigator of, not only Rainhill Reform Club, but also the Prescot Con- servative Club. He took upon himself to suggest that unity was the strerfgtyof Liberalism—(hear, hear,)—and that they should form an association combining Prescot, Eccleston, Rainhill, and Whiston. In the two latter townships, how- ever, he had been forestalled by the chairman,who suggested a Reform Club for Rainhill—(applause,)—and he was very pleased indeed to notice his efforts had not been in vain. Mr. Rawlins informed him that they had about 150 members (applause,) —and that their financial position was very good indeed. There was truly nothing like unity, and so long as they united together, whether in a private or a public-house, they would find that unity would promote their objects in general and their welfare in particular. The Liberals of Prescot had not been so fortunate as the Liberals of Rainhill. They had endeavoured to establish a club there, but in consequence of being unable to meet with suitable premises, they had been obliged to take the course adopted at Rainhill, and occupy a room at a hotel. He was sorry their efforts had not gone a little further. Adverting to the Irish Land Act, he said its success was established by the fact that the court suggested by the Act was giving satisfaction to everyone, except perhaps those landlords who expected greater things from the commissioners appointed under the Act. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with enthusiasm.

Mr. W. EVANS responded. He thought he might say for the satisfaction of their Prescot friends, and also for their own satisfaction, that they were progressing very favourably indeed. (Hear, hear.) They were only infants yet in the political world. Their existence only commenced about three months ago, but he thought he might venture to say they had already begun to feel their feet, and for infants three months old that was not so bad. (Laughter.) He dared say there were some 'members audacious enough to believe they would be cutting their wisdom teeth directly. (Laughter.) But some were audacious enough to suppose the Rainhill Reform Club would make a stir in the political world by and by. It was a tremendous assertion to make in that neighbourhood. Some time ago they ventured to assert in that room that Rainhill Liberalism intended to assert its dignity in the future. He thought he was the adventurous spirit who had the temerity to make that asser- tion, and the editor of a local paper administered to them a smart castigation and informed them it would be better for the Rainhill Liberals instead of talking about asserting their dignity in the future would kindly observe how they had asserted their dignity ha the past. The " past " referred to was the last general election, when, they were informed, on the authority of the gentleman he had alluded to, the Conservatives polled two or three votes to one by the Liberals, and he seemed to think if they could call this asserting their dignity they were welcome to it. (Laughter.) He, personally, was perfectly willing to sit at the feet of any Gamaliel who was prepared to teach him anything; and as to the gentleman who held the responsible position of editor of the paper he had spoken of, he was prepared to sit at the feet of that Gamaliel if he could learn anything by so doing. But they were content to leave to their opponents the entire monopoly of what he considered the antiquated system of living in the past. (Applause.) The last general election had gone, and they were prepared to let the dead bury its dead. They preferred to act now, and knew if they acted unitedly and energetically, as he was sure they meant to do, the future was indeed bright with hope; and be had not the slightest doubt of the brilliant success of the Rainhill Reform Club. (Applause.) It was suggested in the article to which he had referred that if, instead of peer- ing into the dim and uncertain future, the Liberals would look at the clear and certain past, it would better become them. They were quite content to look at the clear and certain past, as they were not ashamed of it. The future must of necessity be dim and uncertain, but by the light of the time being they 'Are sometimes enabled even to peer into the dim and uncertain future; and if theenthusiasm of the Rainhill Liberals meant anything—and in his opinion it meant a great deal—that enthusiasm enabled them to look very cheerfully at the future prospects of that place. Coming events sometimes cast their shadows before, and they thought coming events were now casting their shadows before them, and that they saw the prospect of a great success for Liberalism in that district. (Hear, hear.) If they referred generally to the Liberalism of the past they found that he Liberal escutcheon was too extensively engraved with victories for them to be ashamed of it. (Hear, hear.) Those victories had not always been so com- plete as the Liberal party had desired, but that had not been the fault of the Liberal party, but of these gentle- men who had stood in the way of the party and prevented them carrying out those reforms they had contemplated. It was the fault of that branch of the constitution which preferred to legislate for class interests. (Hear, hear.) He was not presuming too much when be said it wast:l - - of the Liberal party to legislate for the people, and ,iass interests must go to the wall if the general welfare demanded it. Coming to the general election, he did not think the Liberals bad very much to be ashamed of. (Hear, bear.) But one did expect, when the editor of a paper touched upon figures, he would give them facts. (Hear, bear.) However, he thought lie was justified is saying the article to which he had referred was not altogether based upon facts. The electoral roll of Rainhill contained the names of about 100 of the voters. Of that number not more than 90 or 95 could be polled at any election, and he could assert, on undeniable authority, that any the last general election there were 45 promises given to the Liberal party. Under the Ballot Act they had no really reliable means of ascertaining how persons had voted, but the Liberal party had the same means at their disposal to obtain information as the Conservatives, and they fully believed they bad 45 votes for Rainhill. If out of 95 votes the Liberals secured 45, he failed to see how the remainder could be twisted into a majority for the Conservatives of two or three to one. If the Conservatives could make it into such a majority they were welcome to all the satisfaction they could derive from such a feat in arithmetic. (Laughter.) The result he had mentioned was achieved without organisation, and that being the case, what might they not hope to do in th( future with organisation? (Hear, hear.) If in three mo-aths they could so organise themselves as to have a roll of 150 members who were determined to do all in their power -
